a: The end of Swiss wars of conquest
The start of the Reformation in Bern
The founding of the federal state
14449.e: After Marignano the Confederates no longer conquered large territories. Many see this as the beginning of their later restraint in wars, although mercenary service continued.
14449.m: After Marignano the Confederates no longer pursued their own policy of conquest.

a: A new start for the Church
14450.e: Renaissance comes from French and means “rebirth”. It refers to the rediscovery of the art and knowledge of antiquity.
14450.m: Renaissance means the rebirth of antiquity.

14451.q: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
14451.e: The Renaissance began in Italy in the 14th and 15th centuries. There were rich cities there and many remains from Roman antiquity.
14451.m: The Renaissance has its origins in Italy.

14452.q: Which city is considered the cradle of the Renaissance?
14452.e: In Florence, rich bankers and merchants supported artists and scholars. Many of the first great works of the Renaissance were created there.
14452.m: Florence was the centre of the early Renaissance.

14453.q: Which rich banking family supported many artists in Florence?
14453.e: The Medici were bankers and ruled Florence for a long time. They gave artists such as Botticelli big commissions.
14453.m: The Medici made Florence a city of art.

14454.q: What do you call a person who supports artists with money and commissions?
14454.e: A patron supports art and science with their wealth. In the Renaissance, princes, popes and rich merchants were important patrons.
14454.m: A patron supports artists with their money.

14455.q: Which era did the people of the Renaissance want to bring back to life?
14455.e: The people of the Renaissance admired the art, buildings and writings of the ancient Greeks and Romans. This period is called antiquity.

14456.q: Which painting technique, developed in the Renaissance, makes pictures look deep and three-dimensional?
14456.e: In linear perspective, all lines meet at one vanishing point. This makes pictures look like a view into a real space.

14457.q: Which master builder created the great dome of Florence Cathedral?
14457.e: Filippo Brunelleschi built the huge dome without a conventional supporting scaffold. The cathedral was consecrated in 1436.
14457.m: Brunelleschi built the dome of Florence Cathedral.

14458.q: Which painter created the famous picture “The Birth of Venus”?
14458.e: Sandro Botticelli painted “The Birth of Venus” in Florence. The picture shows a goddess from ancient legend.
14458.m: Botticelli painted The Birth of Venus.

14459.q: Which Renaissance painter created the wall painting “The School of Athens” in the Vatican?
14459.e: Raphael painted “The School of Athens” in the Vatican. The picture shows famous ancient thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle.
14459.m: Raphael painted The School of Athens.

14460.q: Which invention by Johannes Gutenberg helped to spread the new ideas of the Renaissance quickly?
14460.e: Around 1450 in Mainz, Gutenberg invented printing with movable metal letters. Books could now be made much faster and more cheaply.
14460.m: Printing spread knowledge quickly across Europe.

14461.q: Which German artist brought Renaissance ideas from Italy to Nuremberg?
14461.e: Albrecht Dürer travelled to Italy and got to know the new art there. Among his famous works are his self-portrait and the “Young Hare”.
14461.m: Albrecht Dürer brought the Renaissance to Germany.

14462.q: Which Renaissance painter worked for a long time in Basel before becoming court painter in England?
14462.e: Hans Holbein the Younger lived and painted in Basel for many years. Later he became court painter to the English King Henry VIII.
14462.m: Hans Holbein the Younger painted in Basel and London.

14463.q: What is meant by a Renaissance “universal genius”?
a: A person who achieves great things in many fields
A king who rules many countries
A monk who copies many books
A trader who travels all over the world
14463.e: The Renaissance ideal was the all-round educated person. Leonardo da Vinci, for example, was a painter, inventor and researcher all at once.
14463.m: A universal genius is gifted in many fields.

14464.q: Which Florentine wrote the book “The Prince” about power and politics?
14464.e: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote “The Prince” around 1513. The book explains plainly how a ruler gains and keeps power.

14467.q: Which city fell to the Ottomans in 1453, after which Greek scholars came to Italy?
14467.e: In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople. Greek scholars with old manuscripts had already been coming to Italy, but now even more came.
14467.m: After the fall of Constantinople, scholars came to Italy.

14468.q: Which sculptor of the early Renaissance created a famous bronze statue of David?
14468.e: Donatello made a bronze David in Florence. It was one of the first free-standing nude statues since antiquity.
14468.m: Donatello was a great sculptor of the early Renaissance.

14469.q: In which two centuries was the Renaissance at its height in Europe?
14469.e: The Renaissance began in Italy in the 14th century and reached its peak in the 15th and 16th centuries. It forms the transition from the Middle Ages to the modern era.
14469.m: The Renaissance flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries.

14470.q: What was at the centre of humanism?
14470.e: The word humanism comes from the Latin “humanus”, meaning human. Humanists wanted to improve people through education and ancient writings.
14470.m: In humanism, people are at the centre.

14471.q: What does the humanists’ motto “ad fontes” mean?
14471.e: Humanists wanted to read the old texts in the original, instead of only in later copies and interpretations. “Ad fontes” means “to the sources”.
14471.m: “Ad fontes” means back to the sources.

14472.q: In which country did humanism begin in the 14th century?
14472.e: Italian scholars such as Francesco Petrarca searched for old Roman texts. From Italy, humanism spread all over Europe.

14473.q: Which two ancient languages did humanists learn especially eagerly?
14473.e: The most important writings of antiquity were written in Latin and Greek. Humanists wanted to read them in the original.

14474.q: Which famous humanist lived in Basel for a long time and died there in 1536?
14474.e: Erasmus of Rotterdam worked closely with printers in Basel. He died in Basel in 1536 and is buried in Basel Minster.
14474.m: Erasmus of Rotterdam worked and died in Basel.

14475.q: Which book did Erasmus publish in a new Greek edition in Basel in 1516?
14475.e: In 1516 in Basel, Erasmus published the New Testament in Greek with a new Latin translation. Luther used the second edition of 1519 for his translation of the Bible.
14475.m: Erasmus published the Greek New Testament in Basel.

14476.q: Why was Basel a centre of humanism in the 16th century?
a: It had a university and many printing workshops
It was the seat of the Emperor
It was right by the sea
14476.e: Basel had a university and many important printing workshops. That is why many scholars came to the city to teach and to have their books printed.
14476.m: Its university and printers made Basel a centre of humanism.

14477.q: In which year was the University of Basel, the oldest in Switzerland, founded?
14477.e: The University of Basel opened in 1460. It is the oldest university in present-day Switzerland.
14477.m: Founded in 1460, the University of Basel is the oldest in Switzerland.

14478.q: Which invention helped to spread the ideas of humanism quickly?
14478.e: With printing, books could be made quickly and in large numbers. That way the humanists’ writings reached many readers.
14478.m: Printing spread the ideas of humanism.

14479.q: Which Zurich reformer was strongly influenced by the humanist Erasmus?
14479.e: Huldrych Zwingli read the writings of Erasmus and learned Greek to read the Bible in the original. In this way humanism shaped his Reformation in Zurich.
14479.m: Zwingli was a humanist and reformer in Zurich.

14480.q: What does the word “utopia”, which goes back to a book from 1516, mean?
14480.e: In “Utopia”, Thomas More described an invented island with an ideal society. Today such a dream of an ideal world is called a utopia.
14480.m: A utopia is an imagined ideal world.

14481.q: Which subjects were especially important to the humanists?
14481.e: Humanists studied grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and philosophy. They called these subjects the “studia humanitatis”.
14481.m: Humanists studied languages, poetry and history.

14482.q: Where did humanists often search for forgotten ancient manuscripts?
14482.e: Many ancient texts had been copied and kept in monasteries. Humanists such as Poggio Bracciolini found valuable manuscripts there, for example at the Abbey of St Gallen.
14482.m: Humanists found old texts in monastery libraries.

14483.q: Which Swiss story was made especially well known by the chronicle of Aegidius Tschudi?
14483.e: Aegidius Tschudi wrote a large chronicle of the Swiss Confederation. His account of William Tell shaped Switzerland’s view of its history for a long time.
14483.m: Tschudi’s chronicle shaped the Tell story.

14484.q: What did the Zurich scholar Conrad Gessner describe in a huge work in the 16th century?
a: All the battles of the Confederates
14484.e: Conrad Gessner was a doctor and naturalist in Zurich. In his “Historia animalium” he described a great many animals.
14484.m: Conrad Gessner wrote a great book about animals.

14485.q: Which new attitude to knowledge did humanism encourage?
a: Reading, checking and thinking for yourself
Learning only on the king’s orders
14485.e: Humanists wanted to read texts carefully and find mistakes in copies. This led to a more critical attitude towards what had been handed down.
14485.m: Humanism encouraged independent and critical thinking.

14486.q: Which period did the humanists take as their model?
a: The antiquity of the Greeks and Romans
14486.e: Humanists admired the writings of the ancient Greeks and Romans. They wanted to learn from them and renew education.
14486.m: The humanists took antiquity as their model.

14487.q: What did the humanist Philipp Melanchthon especially work for?
14487.e: Philipp Melanchthon taught in Wittenberg and helped to set up many schools. That is why he was called the “Teacher of Germany”.
14487.m: Melanchthon worked for schools and education.

14488.q: What was the job of Johann Froben, Erasmus’s friend in Basel?
14488.e: Johann Froben printed many of Erasmus’s works in Basel. The two were friends and worked together for years.
14488.m: Johann Froben printed Erasmus’s works in Basel.

14489.q: In which language did most humanists write their scholarly works?
14489.e: Latin was the shared language of scholars all over Europe. That way humanists from different countries could understand each other.
14489.m: Scholars in Europe mostly wrote in Latin.

14490.q: In which era did Leonardo da Vinci live?
14490.e: Leonardo lived from 1452 to 1519. That is the time of the Renaissance, when art and science flourished in Italy.
14490.m: Leonardo da Vinci was a Renaissance artist.

14491.q: What does the “da Vinci” part of the name mean?
14491.e: “Da Vinci” means “from Vinci”. Vinci is a small place near Florence; Leonardo was born close by.
14491.m: “Da Vinci” means from the town of Vinci.

14492.q: Where does Leonardo’s famous picture “Mona Lisa” hang today?
a: In the National Gallery in London
14492.e: The “Mona Lisa” hangs in the Louvre in Paris. It is one of the best-known paintings in the world.
14492.m: The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

14493.q: In which city is Leonardo’s wall painting “The Last Supper”?
14493.e: Leonardo painted “The Last Supper” on the wall of the dining hall of the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. It shows Jesus with his twelve disciples.
14493.m: Leonardo’s Last Supper is in Milan.

14494.q: What does Leonardo’s drawing “Vitruvian Man” show?
a: A man in a circle and a square
14494.e: The drawing shows a man with arms and legs stretched out inside a circle and a square. It is about the ideal proportions of the body according to the Roman Vitruvius.
14494.m: Vitruvian Man shows ideal body proportions.

14495.q: How did Leonardo write many of his notes?
14495.e: Leonardo often wrote from right to left in mirror writing. You can read it easily with a mirror. He was left-handed.
14495.m: Leonardo wrote his notes in mirror writing.

14496.q: In which city did the young Leonardo learn to paint?
14496.e: Leonardo trained with an artist in Florence. There he learned painting, sculpture and craftwork.
14496.m: Leonardo learned to paint in Florence.

14497.q: Besides painting, what else did Leonardo work as in Milan?
14497.e: Leonardo worked for many years for the ruler of Milan. He planned fortresses, canals and machines and organised festivities.
14497.m: In Milan, Leonardo was also an engineer.

14498.q: What kind of machine did Leonardo sketch long before people could really fly?
14498.e: Leonardo watched birds closely and drew designs for flying machines. They were not built or flown in his time.
14498.m: Leonardo designed flying machines modelled on birds.

14499.q: Why did Leonardo examine human corpses?
a: To understand the structure of the body exactly
14499.e: Leonardo dissected corpses and drew muscles, bones and organs very precisely. He wanted to understand the human body and depict it better.
14499.m: Leonardo studied the human body very carefully.

14500.q: In which country did Leonardo spend the last years of his life?
14500.e: In 1516 Leonardo accepted an invitation to the French court. He spent his final years at the manor house of Clos Lucé in Amboise on the Loire.
14500.m: Leonardo spent his last years in France.

14501.q: Leonardo is considered a universal genius. What does that mean?
a: He was gifted in a great many fields
He travelled all around the world
He was the richest man in Italy
He spoke every language in the world
14501.e: Leonardo was a painter, sculptor, inventor, engineer and naturalist. People with so many talents are called universal geniuses.
14501.m: Leonardo was a universal genius with many talents.

14502.q: Roughly how old was Leonardo da Vinci when he died?
14502.e: Leonardo was born in 1452 and died in France in 1519. He lived to be 67.
14502.m: Leonardo da Vinci lived to be 67.

14503.q: What happened to the “Mona Lisa” in 1911?
a: It was stolen from the museum
It was destroyed in a fire
It was sold to the USA
14503.e: In 1911 the Italian Vincenzo Peruggia, who had worked at the museum, stole the “Mona Lisa”. It was found in Florence at the end of 1913 and returned at the beginning of 1914.
14503.m: The Mona Lisa was stolen in 1911 and found again in 1913.

14504.q: Which way of painting, in which outlines blur softly like smoke, is typical of Leonardo?
14504.e: Sfumato comes from the Italian word for smoke. Leonardo made transitions very soft, for example in the smile of the “Mona Lisa”.

14505.q: Why is Leonardo’s “Last Supper” in poor condition today?
a: He used a new technique on dry plaster
It was only drawn in chalk
It lay under water for centuries
14505.e: Leonardo did not paint a true fresco on wet plaster but experimented on a dry wall. The paint soon began to flake off.
14505.m: Leonardo’s painting technique made the Last Supper very fragile.

14506.q: Roughly how many paintings by Leonardo have survived?
14506.e: Leonardo painted slowly and left much unfinished. That is why there are only a few paintings by him, but thousands of pages of drawings and notes.
14506.m: Only a few paintings by Leonardo exist.

14507.q: Which animal is the woman holding in Leonardo’s picture that hangs in Kraków today?
14507.e: The painting is called “Lady with an Ermine”. Today it is in Kraków in Poland.
14507.m: The Lady with an Ermine hangs in Kraków.

14508.q: What are Leonardo’s collections of notes and drawings called?
14508.e: Leonardo’s notebooks are known as codices, for example the “Codex Atlanticus”. They contain thousands of pages of sketches and ideas.

14509.q: Which huge work did Leonardo plan in Milan that was never cast?
14509.e: Leonardo planned a giant bronze horse for the Sforza family and made a clay model. In 1494 the bronze was needed for cannons, and the model was later destroyed.
14509.m: Leonardo’s great bronze horse was never cast.

14510.q: Which country did Michelangelo come from?
14510.e: Michelangelo was born in Tuscany and worked mainly in Florence and Rome.
14510.m: Michelangelo was an artist from Italy.

14511.q: In which century was Michelangelo born?
14511.e: Michelangelo was born in 1475. That belongs to the 15th century, the time of the Renaissance.
14511.m: Michelangelo was born in the 15th century.

14512.q: What material is Michelangelo’s famous statue “David” made of?
14512.e: Michelangelo carved David from a single large block of marble. The figure is over 5 metres tall.
14512.m: Michelangelo’s David is made of marble.

14513.q: In which city is the original of Michelangelo’s “David”?
14513.e: David now stands in the Galleria dell’Accademia in Florence. A copy stands in front of the Palazzo Vecchio.
14513.m: The original David is in Florence.

14514.q: In the Bible story shown by Michelangelo’s statue, whom does David defeat?
14514.e: According to the Bible, the young David defeats the giant Goliath with a sling. Michelangelo shows David just before the fight.

14515.q: Which ceiling did Michelangelo paint from 1508 to 1512?
a: The ceiling of the Sistine Chapel
14515.e: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican with scenes from the Bible. It took him around four years.
14515.m: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

14516.q: Who commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
14516.e: The Sistine Chapel is part of the Vatican. Pope Julius II commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling in 1508.
14516.m: A pope commissioned Michelangelo to paint the Sistine ceiling.

14517.q: Which famous scene on the Sistine Chapel ceiling shows two fingers almost touching?
14517.e: In “The Creation of Adam”, God stretches out his finger towards Adam. The almost touching hands are among the best-known images in the world.
14517.m: The Creation of Adam shows two fingers almost touching.

14518.q: Which huge wall painting did Michelangelo later paint on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel?
14518.e: From 1536 to 1541, Michelangelo painted “The Last Judgement”. It shows the end of the world according to Christian belief.
14518.m: Michelangelo painted the Last Judgement in the Sistine Chapel.

14519.q: What is Michelangelo’s marble sculpture in St Peter’s Basilica, showing Mary with the dead Jesus, called?
14519.e: The Pietà shows Mary holding her dead son on her lap. Michelangelo created it as a young man, around 1498 to 1499.
14519.m: The Pietà in St Peter’s shows Mary with the dead Jesus.

14520.q: What is special about the Pietà in St Peter’s Basilica?
a: It is the only work Michelangelo signed
It is made of pure gold
It is the largest painting in the world
14520.e: Michelangelo carved his name on a sash across Mary’s chest. He did not sign any other works.
14520.m: The Pietà is Michelangelo’s only signed work.

14521.q: For which great building in Rome did Michelangelo design the dome?
14521.e: In old age, Michelangelo became chief architect of St Peter’s Basilica. He designed the mighty dome, which was completed after his death.
14521.m: Michelangelo designed the dome of St Peter’s Basilica.

14522.q: Which statue did Michelangelo create for the tomb of Pope Julius II?
14522.e: The figure of Moses is part of the tomb of Julius II in the church of San Pietro in Vincoli in Rome. It shows Moses with the tablets of the law.
14522.m: Michelangelo’s Moses is part of the tomb of Julius II.

14523.q: Where did the marble that Michelangelo liked best come from?
14523.e: The quarries of Carrara in Tuscany supply especially beautiful white marble. Michelangelo chose his blocks there himself.
14523.m: Michelangelo liked to use white marble from Carrara.

14524.q: How did Michelangelo work on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
a: Lying in a basket hanging from ropes
On the floor, then the ceiling was put up
14524.e: Michelangelo mostly painted standing on a scaffold with his head tilted back. The common idea that he painted lying down is not quite right.
14524.m: Michelangelo painted the ceiling standing on a scaffold.

14525.q: Which painting technique did Michelangelo use on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
14525.e: In fresco, paint is applied to fresh, wet lime plaster. As it dries, the paint bonds firmly with the wall.
14525.m: Michelangelo painted the Sistine ceiling as a fresco.

14526.q: What did Michelangelo see himself as above all?
14526.e: Michelangelo was a painter, architect and poet. But what mattered most to him was sculpting in marble.
14526.m: Michelangelo saw himself above all as a sculptor.

14527.q: Roughly how old was Michelangelo when he died?
14527.e: Michelangelo died in Rome on 18 February 1564, shortly before his 89th birthday. For those times that was a very great age.

14528.q: Which family took the young Michelangelo into their home in Florence?
14528.e: Lorenzo de’ Medici discovered the young Michelangelo’s talent. He was allowed to live in the Medici palace and study ancient sculptures.
14528.m: The Medici supported Michelangelo even as a teenager.

14529.q: Besides painting, sculpture and architecture, which other art form did Michelangelo practise?
14529.e: Michelangelo wrote many poems, especially sonnets. They were published after his death.

14530.q: What is at the centre of the geocentric view of the universe?
14530.e: “Geo” means earth. In the geocentric view, the Sun, Moon and planets circle around the motionless Earth.
14530.m: In the geocentric view, the Earth is at the centre.

14531.q: What is at the centre of the heliocentric view of the universe?
14531.e: “Helios” is Greek for sun. In the heliocentric view, the Earth, like the other planets, circles around the Sun.
14531.m: In the heliocentric view, the Sun is at the centre.

14532.q: Which ancient scholar shaped the geocentric view of the universe that was accepted in the Middle Ages?
14532.e: In the 2nd century, Claudius Ptolemy described a view of the universe with the Earth at the centre. It was accepted for over 1,000 years.
14532.m: Ptolemy shaped the geocentric view of the universe.

14533.q: Which astronomer founded the heliocentric view of the universe in the early modern period?
14533.e: Nicolaus Copernicus described how the Earth circles the Sun and spins on its own axis. That is why it is also called the Copernican view of the universe.
14533.m: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre.

14534.q: In which language did Copernicus write his main work about the heavenly bodies?
14534.e: At that time scholars all over Europe wrote in Latin. That way researchers from every country could read the book. It came out in 1543.
14534.m: In Copernicus’s time, scholars wrote in Latin.

14535.q: Which instrument did Galileo Galilei point at the sky from 1609 onwards?
14535.e: Galileo built an improved telescope and used it to observe the Moon, stars and planets. In this way he made many new discoveries.
14535.m: Galileo explored the sky with a telescope.

14536.q: What did Galileo Galilei discover at the planet Jupiter?
14536.e: In 1610 Galileo saw four moons circling Jupiter. This showed that not everything revolves around the Earth.
14536.m: Galileo discovered four of Jupiter’s moons.

14537.q: Why was Galileo Galilei brought before the court of the Inquisition in 1633?
a: He had set fire to a church
14537.e: At that time the Catholic Church considered the heliocentric view to be wrong. Galileo had to renounce his teaching and was then kept under house arrest until his death.
14537.m: Galileo was convicted because of the heliocentric view.

14538.q: Which sentence is said to have been spoken by Galileo after his trial, but is probably a legend?
14538.e: After taking back his teaching, Galileo is supposed to have said that the Earth moves all the same. There is no evidence for this from his own time; it is probably a legend.
14538.m: “And yet it moves” is probably a legend.

14539.q: Which astronomer realised that the planets orbit the Sun in ellipses?
14539.e: Johannes Kepler showed that the planets’ orbits are not circles but ellipses. His laws made the heliocentric view much more accurate.
14539.m: Kepler discovered the elliptical orbits of the planets.

14540.q: Which Danish astronomer provided the precise observations that Kepler worked with?
14540.e: Tycho Brahe measured the positions of the planets very precisely without a telescope. Kepler used this data for his laws.
14540.m: Tycho Brahe provided precise observations of the sky.

14541.q: In which year did Christopher Columbus reach America?
14541.e: Columbus wanted to sail west to India and in 1492 reached islands in the Caribbean. Until his death he believed he had been in Asia.

14543.q: Did educated people in the Middle Ages know that the Earth is a sphere?
a: Yes, it had been known since antiquity
No, everyone thought it was a disc
14543.e: The ancient Greeks already knew that the Earth is a sphere. Educated people in the Middle Ages knew this too; the idea of a flat disc is a later myth.
14543.m: The round shape of the Earth had been known since antiquity.

14544.q: After which seafarer was the continent of America named?
14544.e: In 1507 the mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller named the New World after Amerigo Vespucci. In his reports, Vespucci had described it as a “New World” and not Asia.
14544.m: America is named after Amerigo Vespucci.

14545.q: Which seafarer found the sea route around Africa to India in 1498?
14545.e: The Portuguese Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached India in 1498. This made direct sea trade in spices possible.
14545.m: Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India in 1498.

14546.q: When did the Catholic Church officially declare that Galileo had been wronged?
14546.e: In 1992, Pope John Paul II acknowledged that Galileo’s conviction had been a mistake. That was around 350 years after Galileo’s death.

14547.q: Which observation by Galileo of the planet Venus supported the heliocentric view?
a: Venus shows phases like the Moon
14547.e: Galileo saw that Venus waxes and wanes like the Moon. This could best be explained if Venus circles the Sun.
14547.m: The phases of Venus supported the heliocentric view.

14548.q: In which present-day country was Nicolaus Copernicus born?
14548.e: Copernicus was born in 1473 in Thorn, which is now called Toruń and is in Poland.
14548.m: Copernicus was born in what is now Poland.

14549.q: Why was the heliocentric view so shocking for many people at the time?
a: The Earth was no longer the centre of the universe
The Sun was suddenly supposed to go out
It banned travelling across the sea
14549.e: For a long time people believed God had placed the Earth and humans at the centre. The new view made the Earth one planet among many.
14549.m: The new view took away the Earth’s place at the centre.

14551.q: Which destination did Columbus actually want to reach when he sailed west?
14551.e: Columbus believed he could reach Asia faster by sailing west instead of around Africa. He did not know that a whole continent lay in between.
14551.m: Columbus was looking for a western sea route to Asia.

14552.q: Which royal couple paid for Columbus’s first voyage?
a: Henry VIII and Catherine of England
Louis XII and Anne of France
Manuel I and Maria of Portugal
14552.e: The Catholic Monarchs, Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon, supported Columbus in 1492. Before that, the King of Portugal had turned him down.
14552.m: The Spanish monarchs Isabella and Ferdinand financed Columbus.

14553.q: With how many ships did Columbus set off on his first voyage in 1492?
14553.e: Two of the three ships were the caravels Pinta and Niña. There were around 90 men on board altogether.
14553.m: Columbus set sail in 1492 with three ships.

14554.q: What was the name of Columbus’s flagship on the first voyage?
14554.e: The Santa María ran aground off the island of Hispaniola at Christmas 1492. The settlement of La Navidad was built from her timber.
14554.m: Columbus’s biggest ship was the Santa María.

14555.q: In which city was Christopher Columbus born?
14555.e: Columbus came from the Italian port city of Genoa and was born around 1451. Later he sailed in the service of Spain.
14555.m: Columbus was a seafarer from Genoa.

14556.q: Why did Columbus call the people he met in America “Indians”?
a: Because he believed he had arrived in India
Because they had come from India
Because the Pope had ordered that name
14556.e: Columbus thought he had reached islands off Asia, which at that time were called “the Indies”. That is also where the name “West Indies” comes from.
14556.m: Calling the native peoples of America “Indians” goes back to Columbus’s mistake.

14557.q: How many voyages to America did Columbus make in total?
14557.e: Between 1492 and 1504, Columbus crossed the Atlantic four times. He explored Caribbean islands and coasts of Central and South America.
14557.m: Columbus sailed to America four times in all.

14558.q: Roughly how long did Columbus’s first crossing from the Canary Islands to America take?
14558.e: Columbus left the Canary Islands at the beginning of September 1492 and sighted land on 12 October. The crew became very restless on the way.
14558.m: Columbus’s first Atlantic crossing took about five weeks.

14559.q: Who was the continent of America named after?
14559.e: In 1507 the mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller named the new continent after the seafarer Amerigo Vespucci. Vespucci had described it as a “New World”.
14559.m: America bears the name of Amerigo Vespucci.

14560.q: Which Europeans were in North America around 500 years before Columbus?
14560.e: Around the year 1000, Vikings from Greenland reached Newfoundland. But their settlement only lasted a short time and had no lasting effects.
14560.m: Vikings reached North America around the year 1000.

14562.q: What mistake did Columbus make when planning his voyage?
a: He thought the Earth was much too small
He believed the Earth was a disc
He forgot to take drinking water
14562.e: Educated Europeans at that time knew that the Earth is a sphere. But Columbus calculated with a far too small circumference of the Earth, so he thought the way to Asia was short.
14562.m: Columbus greatly underestimated the size of the Earth.

14563.q: For which country did Vasco da Gama sail?
14563.e: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese seafarer in the service of King Manuel I. Portugal was looking for a sea route to India at the time.
14563.m: Vasco da Gama was a seafarer from Portugal.

14564.q: What did Vasco da Gama achieve in 1498 as the first European?
a: Finding the sea route to India
14564.e: Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached India in May 1498. With that, the sea route from Europe to India had been discovered.
14564.m: Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India in 1498.

14565.q: Roughly how long did Vasco da Gama’s voyage from Lisbon to India take?
14565.e: Vasco da Gama set off from Lisbon in July 1497 and reached India in May 1498. The voyage all the way around Africa was long and dangerous.
14565.m: The voyage to India took about ten months.

14566.q: Around which cape at the southern tip of Africa did Vasco da Gama have to sail?
14566.e: The Cape of Good Hope is in what is now South Africa. Anyone who wanted to sail from Europe to India had to go around it.
14566.m: The route to India went around the Cape of Good Hope.

14567.q: Which Portuguese seafarer was the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa, back in 1488?
14567.e: In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias showed that you can sail around the south of Africa. Vasco da Gama used this knowledge ten years later.
14567.m: In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias was the first to round the southern tip of Africa.

14568.q: Which goods made the sea route to India so valuable for Portugal?
14568.e: Spices such as pepper, cinnamon and cloves were very expensive in Europe. Anyone who bought them directly in Asia could make huge profits.
14568.m: The spice trade made Portugal rich.

14569.q: Why did Europeans look for a sea route to Asia in the 15th century?
a: To avoid the expensive overland middlemen
Because the land routes were completely unknown
Because ships were cheaper than horses then
Because the Pope had banned all land routes
14569.e: Asian goods reached Europe through many middlemen, for example in the Ottoman Empire and in Venice. Each trader added a mark-up, so the goods were very expensive.
14569.m: A sea route to Asia promised cheaper goods without middlemen.

14570.q: In which year did Vasco da Gama set off from Lisbon for India?
14570.e: The fleet left Lisbon in July 1497. After around ten months it reached India.
14570.m: Vasco da Gama set off from Lisbon in 1497.

14571.q: Who helped Vasco da Gama find his way from East Africa across the Indian Ocean to India?
14571.e: In the East African city of Malindi, Vasco da Gama took an experienced pilot on board. He knew the monsoon winds and the way to India.
14571.m: A pilot from East Africa showed Vasco da Gama the way across the Indian Ocean.

14572.q: Which Portuguese prince supported voyages of discovery along Africa early in the 15th century?
14572.e: From about 1420, Henry the Navigator sent ships along the African coast. This laid the foundation for the later voyages to India.
14572.m: Henry the Navigator laid the foundation for Portugal’s voyages of discovery.

14573.q: Which nimble type of ship was especially important for the Portuguese voyages of discovery?
14573.e: The caravel was small and fast and could also tack against the wind. That made it well suited to exploring unknown coasts.
14573.m: The caravel was a typical explorers’ ship.

14574.q: What did Vasco da Gama achieve on his voyage from 1497 to 1499?
a: He found the sea route from Europe to India
He was the first to sail around the Earth
14574.e: Vasco da Gama sailed around the southern tip of Africa and on across the Indian Ocean to India. This gave Portugal a sea route to the spices of Asia.
14574.m: Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India.

14575.q: Which country did Ferdinand Magellan come from?
14575.e: Magellan was Portuguese. Because his king, Manuel I, did not support him, he entered Spanish service.
14575.m: The Portuguese Magellan sailed for Spain.

14576.q: In which year did Magellan’s fleet set off on its voyage west?
14576.e: The fleet put to sea in September 1519 from the port of Sanlúcar de Barrameda in southern Spain. Before that it had been in Seville.

14577.q: With how many ships did Magellan’s expedition start?
14577.e: The five ships were called Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepción, Victoria and Santiago. Magellan’s flagship was the Trinidad.
14577.m: Magellan started out with five ships.

14578.q: Which sea passage at the southern tip of South America bears Magellan’s name?
14578.e: In 1520, Magellan found a passage between the mainland of South America and Tierra del Fuego. That is how he got from the Atlantic into the Pacific.
14578.m: Through the Strait of Magellan, Magellan reached the Pacific.

14579.q: Why did Magellan call the great ocean the “Pacific”?
a: Because the sea was calm when they crossed it
Because there were many islands there
Because the water was especially warm
Because the Pope had named it that
14579.e: “Pacific” means “the peaceful one”. After the storms in the strait, the crew at first found the ocean calm.

14580.e: In 1521, Magellan died on the Philippine island of Mactan in a fight with local people led by the chief Lapulapu. So he did not live to see the end of the voyage around the world.
14580.m: Magellan died in the Philippines in 1521.

14581.q: Which islands did Magellan’s expedition actually want to reach?
14581.e: The Moluccas, in what is now Indonesia, were famous for cloves and nutmeg. Spain wanted to reach them by a western route.
14581.m: Magellan wanted to reach the Spice Islands, the Moluccas.

14582.q: Who led Magellan’s expedition back to Spain after his death?
14582.e: The Spaniard Juan Sebastián Elcano took command of the last remaining ship. He brought it back to Spain in 1522.
14582.m: Elcano completed the first voyage around the world.

14583.q: How many men returned to Spain in 1522 on the last ship of Magellan’s fleet?
14583.e: Of well over 200 men who had set off in 1519, only 18 came back on this ship. Many died of hunger, disease or in fighting.
14583.m: Only 18 men came back on the last ship.

14584.q: Which illness especially troubled Magellan’s crew on the long voyage across the Pacific?
14584.e: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C. Because there was no fresh fruit or vegetables, many sailors fell ill and died.
14584.m: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.

14585.q: Why do we know so much about Magellan’s voyage around the world today?
a: A member of the crew wrote an account of the journey
Magellan wrote a book after returning
A painter drew a picture every day
14585.e: The Italian Antonio Pigafetta went along and survived. His account is the most important source. Magellan himself died on the way.
14585.m: An eyewitness account tells the story of Magellan’s voyage.

14586.q: For which Spanish king, who later also became emperor, did Magellan sail?
14586.e: In 1519, Charles I of Spain was elected Holy Roman Emperor as Charles V. He supported Magellan’s plan.
14586.m: Magellan sailed on behalf of Charles I of Spain.

14587.q: What is it called when a ship’s crew rises up against the captain, as happened on Magellan’s voyage?
14587.e: There were several mutinies on Magellan’s voyage. The crew of the San Antonio even secretly sailed back to Spain.
14587.m: A mutiny is a rebellion by the crew against the captain.

14588.q: By which route did the Victoria sail back from the Spice Islands to Spain?
a: Across the Indian Ocean and around the Cape of Good Hope
Back across the Pacific and through the Strait of Magellan
Through the Mediterranean and the Strait of Gibraltar
Through the Arctic Ocean past Siberia
14588.e: The Victoria kept sailing west across the Indian Ocean and rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1522. So it returned to Spain from the other side, having gone once around the Earth.
14588.m: On the way home, the Victoria sailed around the southern tip of Africa.

14589.q: Which ship completed the first voyage around the world?
14589.e: The Victoria was the only one of Magellan’s five ships to return to Spain. It reached the port of Sanlúcar de Barrameda in September 1522.
14589.m: The Victoria was the first ship to sail around the Earth.

14590.q: What did the first voyage around the world prove in practice?
a: That you can go around the Earth by sea
That the Earth is a disc
That America is joined to Asia
14590.e: The voyage showed that all the oceans are connected and that you can sail around the Earth. It also made clear how huge the Pacific is.
14590.m: The first voyage around the world showed that all oceans are connected.

14591.q: What did those who returned from the first voyage around the world notice about their calendar?
a: They had one day too many
They had lost a whole month
14591.e: Because they had always sailed west, they had seen one sunrise fewer. Today the International Date Line deals with this difference.
14591.m: If you go around the Earth westwards, you lose a day.

14592.q: Which Englishman led the second voyage around the world, which ended in 1580?
14592.e: Francis Drake sailed around the world from 1577 to 1580. He was the first Englishman to sail around the Earth, and he led the whole voyage himself.
14592.m: Francis Drake sailed around the Earth from 1577 to 1580.

14593.q: Which queen knighted Francis Drake after his voyage around the world?
14593.e: Queen Elizabeth I of England honoured Drake on board his ship in 1581. His voyage had brought England a lot of fame and treasure.
14593.m: Francis Drake was knighted by Elizabeth I.

14594.q: How did Jeanne Baret, the first woman to go around the Earth, travel on the ship at the start?
14594.e: At that time women were not allowed on naval ships. So in 1766 the botanist Jeanne Baret disguised herself as a man.
14594.m: Jeanne Baret was the first woman to go around the Earth.

14595.q: Which Swiss man, together with Brian Jones, was the first to fly around the Earth nonstop in a balloon in 1999?
14595.e: In 1999, Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones flew around the world without landing in the balloon “Breitling Orbiter 3”. They took off from Château-d’Oex in the canton of Vaud.
14595.m: Bertrand Piccard flew around the world in a balloon in 1999.

14596.q: Which Swiss aeroplane flew around the Earth in 2015 and 2016 without any fuel at all?
14596.e: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar energy alone. Two Swiss pilots took turns at the controls.
14596.m: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the Earth on solar power alone.

14597.q: Which notorious cape at the southern tip of South America was first sailed around in 1616?
14597.e: The Dutchmen Schouten and Le Maire sailed around the cape in 1616 and named it after the town of Hoorn. The waters there are known for storms.
14597.m: Cape Horn is named after the Dutch town of Hoorn.

14598.q: Which British seafarer explored the Pacific on several voyages around the world in the 18th century?
14598.e: From 1768, James Cook made three great voyages to the Pacific. Among other things, he mapped New Zealand and the east coast of Australia.
14598.m: James Cook explored the Pacific on three great voyages.

14599.q: What happened to Magellan during the first voyage around the world?
a: He died on the way, in the Philippines
He returned to Spain as a hero
He became king of an island
He chose to stay in South America
14599.e: Magellan was killed in a fight in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano then led the Victoria back to Spain.
14599.m: Magellan did not live to see the end of his voyage around the world.

14600.q: In which region did the Maya live?
14600.e: The Maya lived in what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras and El Salvador. An important area is the Yucatán Peninsula.
14600.m: The Maya lived in Central America.

14601.q: Which number did the Maya know long before the Europeans?
14601.e: The Maya used a sign for zero that looks like a shell. In Europe, zero only caught on much later.
14601.m: The Maya were calculating with zero early on.

14602.q: Which base number was the Maya number system built on?
14602.e: The Maya counted in a base-20 system, probably because of fingers and toes. A dot stood for 1 and a bar for 5.
14602.m: The Maya counted in a base-20 system.

14603.q: Which crop was the most important food of the Maya?
14603.e: Maize was the basis of their diet and also played an important role in myths. According to a Maya story, humans were created from maize.
14603.m: Maize was the most important food of the Maya.

14604.q: Which famous Maya city is on the Yucatán Peninsula and has the pyramid “El Castillo”?
14604.e: Chichén Itzá was an important Maya city. The step pyramid El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
14604.m: The pyramid El Castillo stands in Chichén Itzá.

14605.q: Which large Maya city is in the rainforest of present-day Guatemala?
14605.e: In the Classic period, Tikal was one of the largest Maya cities. Its tall temple pyramids rise above the rainforest.
14605.m: Tikal is a large Maya city in Guatemala.

14606.q: What did the Maya have, unlike the Inca?
a: A road network in the Andes
14606.e: The Maya wrote with glyphs, signs for words and syllables. They carved texts in stone and wrote books known as codices.
14606.m: The Maya had their own writing made of glyphs.

14607.q: What did the Maya write their books on?
14607.e: The Maya made a kind of paper from the bark of fig trees. They folded it into books like a concertina.
14607.m: Maya books were made of bark paper.

14608.q: Why are there only a few Maya books left today?
a: Spanish missionaries had many of them burned
The Maya only wrote on stones
An earthquake destroyed all the libraries
The Maya burned them themselves as offerings
14608.e: In 1562 the monk Diego de Landa had many Maya writings burned because he thought they were heathen. As a result, a lot of knowledge was lost.
14608.m: Many Maya books were destroyed by Spanish missionaries.

14609.q: What happened to many large Maya cities in the lowlands around the year 900?
a: They were conquered by the Spanish
They became capitals of the Inca
They were buried by a volcano
14609.e: Many cities in the southern lowlands were abandoned between about 800 and 900. Possible reasons include droughts, wars and overused soils.
14609.m: Around 900, many Maya cities were abandoned.

a: Yes, millions of people are Maya
No, they died out during the conquest
Yes, but only a few dozen
14610.e: Maya culture did not disappear. Today millions of Maya live in Mexico and Guatemala and speak many different Mayan languages.
14610.m: The Maya still live in Central America today.

14611.q: Which drink did the Maya make early on from the beans of a plant?
14611.e: The Maya drank bitter cocoa, often mixed with spices. Later cocoa came to Europe and was developed into chocolate.

14612.q: What was the name of the Aztec capital?
14612.e: Tenochtitlan was on an island in Lake Texcoco. Long causeways connected the city to the shore.
14612.m: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztecs.

14613.q: Which present-day capital stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan?
14613.e: After the conquest, the Spanish built their city right on top of Tenochtitlan. Remains of the Great Temple have been dug up in the middle of Mexico City.
14613.m: Mexico City stands where Tenochtitlan once was.

14614.q: Where was the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan?
a: On an island in a lake
In the middle of the desert
14614.e: Tenochtitlan was on an island in Lake Texcoco. Causeways and canals connected the city to the shore.
14614.m: Tenochtitlan was on an island in a lake.

14615.q: According to their legend, which sign showed the Aztecs where to found their city?
a: An eagle on a cactus with a snake
A jaguar under a maize field
A llama on a mountain top
14615.e: According to the founding legend, the Aztecs saw an eagle on a prickly pear cactus holding a snake. This picture can be seen on the flag of Mexico today.
14615.m: The eagle on the cactus is the sign from the founding legend of Tenochtitlan.

14616.q: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Aztec empire?
14616.e: Hernán Cortés landed on the coast of Mexico in 1519. With the help of local allies, he conquered the Aztec capital.
14616.m: Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec empire.

14617.q: What was the name of the Aztec ruler when the Spanish arrived in 1519?
14617.e: Moctezuma II received Cortés in Tenochtitlan. He was later taken prisoner and died in 1520 in unexplained circumstances.
14617.m: Moctezuma II ruled the Aztecs when Cortés came.

14618.q: In which year did Tenochtitlan fall to the Spanish?
14618.e: After a long siege, Cortés and his allies captured the city in August 1521. That was the end of the Aztec empire.

14619.q: Besides weapons and allies, what contributed greatly to the Spanish victory over the Aztecs?
14619.e: The Spanish brought smallpox, against which the people in America had no defences. In 1520 a great many people in Tenochtitlan died of this disease.
14619.m: Diseases brought in from outside greatly weakened the Aztecs.

14620.q: Which people fought as allies of the Spanish against the Aztecs?
14620.e: The Tlaxcaltecs were enemies of the Aztecs. Thousands of them fought on Cortés’s side.
14620.m: Without local allies, Cortés could hardly have won.

14621.q: Which language did the Aztecs speak?
14621.e: Nahuatl is still spoken by over a million people in Mexico today. Words such as “avocado” and “coyote” also come from Nahuatl.

a: Artificial garden beds in the lake
14622.e: Chinampas were fields built up in the shallow water of the lake. The Aztecs grew maize, beans and vegetables on them.
14622.m: On chinampas, the Aztecs grew plants in the lake.

14623.q: Which god did the Aztecs worship as the “Feathered Serpent”?
14623.e: Quetzalcoatl was an important god in Central America. The Maya worshipped a similar god called Kukulcán.
14623.m: Quetzalcoatl is the Feathered Serpent of the Aztecs.

14624.q: In which European city is the famous feather headdress known as “Moctezuma’s Penacho”?
14624.e: The headdress made of quetzal feathers is kept in the Weltmuseum in Vienna. Mexico has long wanted it returned.
14624.m: Moctezuma’s feather headdress is in Vienna today.

14625.q: What was the name of the capital of the Inca empire?
14625.e: Cusco is in the highlands of present-day Peru. The Inca saw the city as the centre of their empire.
14625.m: Cusco was the capital of the Inca.

14626.q: In which mountain range was the Inca empire?
14626.e: The Inca empire stretched along the Andes in South America. It reached from what is now southern Colombia to Chile.
14626.m: The Inca empire was in the Andes.

14627.q: Which famous Inca city lies high on a mountain in Peru and became internationally known in 1911?
14627.e: The American Hiram Bingham made Machu Picchu world-famous in 1911. But local farmers already knew the place before that.

a: A knotted cord for recording numbers
A temple for the sun god
14628.e: With knots in coloured cords, the Inca recorded numbers, for example for taxes and stores. Specialists could “read” these cords.
14628.m: The Inca stored numbers with knotted cords.

14629.q: Which language did the Inca speak?
14629.e: Quechua was the official language of the Inca empire. Millions of people in the Andes still speak Quechua today.
14629.m: The language of the Inca is called Quechua.

14630.q: Which animals did the Inca use as pack animals and for wool?
14630.e: Llamas can carry loads over steep mountain paths. For fine wool, the Inca also kept alpacas.
14630.m: The Inca kept llamas as pack animals.

14631.q: Which important crop originally comes from the Andes and was grown by the Inca?
14631.e: The potato was grown in the Andes long before the Inca. It came to Europe via Spain and later became a staple food in Switzerland too.
14631.m: The potato comes from the Andes.

14632.q: Which Spaniard conquered the Inca empire?
14632.e: Francisco Pizarro came to the Inca empire in 1532 with only around 170 men. A civil war between two claimants to the throne had weakened the empire.
14632.m: Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca empire.

14633.q: What did the Spanish demand as ransom for the captured Inca ruler Atahualpa?
14633.e: Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532. Although the Inca filled a room with gold and silver, the Spanish had him executed in 1533.
14633.m: The Spanish wanted gold and silver from the Inca.

14634.q: Into how many large parts was the Inca empire divided?
14634.e: The Inca called their empire “Tawantinsuyu”, the land of four parts. The borders of the parts met in the capital, Cusco.
14634.m: The Inca empire was made up of four parts.

14635.q: How did the Inca carry messages quickly through their empire?
14635.e: The runners were called chasquis and waited at stations along the roads. That way messages could cover long distances in a short time.
14635.m: Inca runners carried messages through the empire in relays.

14636.q: Which way of building is typical of Inca buildings?
a: Houses made of bamboo and paper
14636.e: The Inca cut stones so precisely that they held together firmly without mortar. Many of these walls even survived earthquakes.
14636.m: Inca walls hold together without mortar.

14637.q: Which treaty divided the newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal in 1494?
14637.e: In the Treaty of Tordesillas, a line was drawn through the Atlantic. Lands to the west of it were to go to Spain, lands to the east to Portugal.
14637.m: In 1494, the Treaty of Tordesillas divided the world between Spain and Portugal.

14638.q: Why do people in Brazil speak Portuguese and not Spanish?
a: Because Brazil was a Portuguese colony
Because Portuguese was a native language
14638.e: The Portuguese Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, after which it became a colony of Portugal. Brazil only became independent in 1822.
14638.m: Brazil was a colony of Portugal.

14639.q: What were the Spanish conquerors in America called?
14639.e: The word comes from the Spanish “conquistador”, meaning “conqueror”. The conquistadors were mainly looking for gold, land and glory.
14639.m: Conquistadors were the Spanish conquerors of America.

14640.q: What did many Indigenous people in the Spanish colonies have to do for the settlers?
a: Do forced labour and pay dues
14640.e: Under the encomienda system, Spaniards were allowed to demand work and dues from the local people. This often led to harsh exploitation.
14640.m: Many Indigenous people had to work for Spanish settlers.

14641.q: What did the Spanish priest Bartolomé de las Casas fight for in the 16th century?
a: The rights of the native peoples
14641.e: Bartolomé de las Casas described the violence of the conquerors and criticised the exploitation. He demanded better protection for the Indigenous people.
14641.m: Bartolomé de las Casas fought for the rights of the native peoples.

14642.q: Where were millions of people from Africa taken by force in the transatlantic slave trade?
14642.e: From the 16th to the 19th century, around 12 million Africans were taken to America by force. They had to do forced labour, mainly on plantations and in mines.
14642.m: The slave trade took millions of people from Africa to America by force.

14643.q: Which plant came to Europe as a result of the colonisation of America?
14643.e: Peppers, pumpkins and peanuts also come from America. This exchange between the Old and New Worlds is called the “Columbian Exchange”.

14644.q: Which animal did the Europeans bring to America, where it did not exist at the time?
14644.e: The Spanish brought horses to America, because America’s prehistoric horses had died out thousands of years earlier. Later, horses became very important to many Indigenous peoples of North America.
14644.m: Horses only came to America with the Europeans.

14645.q: Which precious metal from the mountain of Potosí, in present-day Bolivia, made Spain rich?
14645.e: From 1545, huge amounts of silver were mined at Potosí. The Indigenous workers had to work in very harsh conditions.
14645.m: Silver from Potosí brought Spain great wealth.

14646.q: Which country founded its first permanent settlement in North America, Jamestown, in 1607?
14646.e: Jamestown was in the colony of Virginia. The first years were marked by hunger and disease.
14646.m: In 1607, Jamestown was the first permanent English settlement in North America.

14647.q: On which ship did the so-called Pilgrim Fathers come to North America in 1620?
14647.e: The Pilgrim Fathers were English Protestants who wanted to practise their faith freely. They founded the settlement of Plymouth.
14647.m: The Pilgrim Fathers came on the Mayflower in 1620.

14648.q: Which city was first called “New Amsterdam” as a Dutch settlement?
14648.e: The Dutch founded New Amsterdam on the island of Manhattan. In 1664 the English took over the city and called it New York.
14648.m: New York was first called New Amsterdam.

14649.q: Which town in North America was founded in 1710 by settlers from Switzerland and the Palatinate?
14649.e: Christoph von Graffenried from Bern founded New Bern in what is now North Carolina. The town still has a bear in its coat of arms today.
14649.m: New Bern in America was founded by a man from Bern.

14650.q: Roughly when did Martin Luther live?
14650.e: Martin Luther was born in 1483 and died in 1546. So he lived about 500 years ago, at the same time as Zwingli.
14650.m: Martin Luther lived about 500 years ago.

14651.q: In which present-day country did Martin Luther live and work?
14651.e: Luther was born in Eisleben in 1483 and worked mainly in Wittenberg. Both towns are in today’s Germany.
14651.m: Martin Luther lived in today’s Germany.

14652.q: Which experience made Luther become a monk in 1505?
14652.e: On 2 July 1505 Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm near Stotternheim and, terrified of dying, vowed to become a monk. Soon after, he entered a monastery in Erfurt.
14652.m: A thunderstorm made Luther go into a monastery.

14653.q: Where did Luther live as a monk from 1505?
14653.e: In 1505 Luther became a monk in the Augustinian monastery in Erfurt. There he lived with other monks by strict rules.
14653.m: Luther lived as a monk in a monastery.

14654.q: What was Martin Luther supposed to study, as his father wished?
14654.e: His father wanted Luther to become a lawyer and have a career. Luther began studying law in Erfurt in 1505 but soon gave it up and went into a monastery.
14654.m: Luther’s father wanted him to become a lawyer.

14655.q: Before which ruler did Luther have to answer for himself at the Diet of Worms in 1521?
14655.e: At the Diet of Worms in 1521, Luther was supposed to take back his writings before Emperor Charles V. He refused, because no one had proved him wrong using the Bible.
14655.m: At Worms in 1521 Luther refused to take back his views before Emperor Charles V.

14656.q: What did the imperial ban imposed on Luther after the Diet of Worms mean?
a: He was an outlaw and anyone could seize him
He had to pay a large fine
He could only preach in Wittenberg
He had to leave the empire for a year
14656.e: With the Edict of Worms, Luther was outlawed. No one was allowed to protect him, and his writings were to be banned.
14656.m: The imperial ban made Luther an outlaw.

14657.q: In which castle did Luther hide after the Diet of Worms?
14657.e: Luther’s prince had him “kidnapped” for show and taken to Wartburg Castle near Eisenach. There Luther lived under the name “Junker Jörg” (Squire George).
14657.m: At Wartburg Castle Luther was safe as “Junker Jörg”.

14658.q: Why was Luther “kidnapped” for show in 1521 and taken to Wartburg Castle?
a: A prince wanted to protect him this way
He was to be punished there
The Pope wanted to question him
14658.e: Elector Frederick the Wise of Saxony was Luther’s prince. He had him “kidnapped” for show so that no one could harm him after the Diet of Worms.
14658.m: A prince took Luther to Wartburg Castle to protect him.

14659.q: Which important work did Luther begin during his time at Wartburg Castle?
a: Translating the New Testament into German
14659.e: At Wartburg Castle Luther translated the New Testament from Greek into German in about eleven weeks. It was printed in 1522.
14659.m: At Wartburg Castle Luther translated the New Testament into German.

14660.q: Why was Luther’s translation of the Bible so important for ordinary people?
a: They could now read the Bible in their own language
They got the Bible for free
Only priests were allowed to read the Bible
14660.e: Before, the Bible in church was mostly in Latin, which only scholars understood. Luther wanted all Christians to be able to read the Bible for themselves.
14660.m: Thanks to Luther’s translation many people could read the Bible in German.

14661.q: Whom did Martin Luther marry in 1525?
14661.e: Katharina von Bora was a former nun who had escaped from her convent. The marriage showed that Luther rejected the rule that clergy must not marry.
14661.m: In 1525 Luther married the former nun Katharina von Bora.

14662.q: What did the Pope do to Martin Luther in 1521?
14662.e: On 3 January 1521 Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther. Luther had refused to take back his teachings.
14662.m: In 1521 the Pope expelled Luther from the Church.

14663.q: What did Luther do in December 1520 with the papal bull that threatened him with excommunication?
a: He sent it to the emperor
He hung it up in church
14663.e: In front of the Elster Gate in Wittenberg, Luther burned the bull together with books of Church law. With that, he openly broke with the Pope.
14663.m: In 1520 Luther burned the Pope’s bull in public.

14664.q: What was Luther’s attitude to the rebelling peasants in the Peasants’ War of 1525?
a: He fought alongside them as a soldier
14664.e: Luther first called on the peasants to keep the peace, but then wrote sharply against the uprising and took the side of the princes. Many peasants felt betrayed by him.
14664.m: In the Peasants’ War Luther turned against the rebelling peasants.

14665.q: Which well-known hymn did Martin Luther write?
a: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
Holy God, We Praise Thy Name
14665.e: “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God” was written by Luther and became the best-known song of the Reformation. Luther encouraged the whole congregation to sing in church services.
14665.m: Luther wrote the hymn “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God”.

14666.q: In which town is Luther said to have published his 95 Theses in 1517?
14666.e: Luther taught at the University of Wittenberg. In 1517 he published his 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences there. This is seen as the start of the Reformation.
14666.m: The Reformation began in Wittenberg in 1517.

14667.q: In which year did Luther publish his 95 Theses?
14667.e: In 1517 Luther made his 95 Theses against indulgences known. This year is seen as the start of the Reformation.

14668.q: Which practice of the Church were the 95 Theses mainly aimed against?
14668.e: Luther criticised the Church for selling letters of indulgence. People believed they could buy their way out of punishment for their sins with them.
14668.m: The 95 Theses were aimed against the sale of indulgences.

14669.q: What were people promised when they bought a letter of indulgence?
a: Being let off punishment for sins
14669.e: An indulgence was supposed to shorten punishment for sins, including in purgatory. For money you could even buy indulgences for people who had died.
14669.m: A letter of indulgence was supposed to cancel punishment for sins.

14670.q: Which Dominican monk preached for indulgences near Wittenberg and so angered Luther?
14670.e: Johann Tetzel sold letters of indulgence for the Church with great business sense. Many people from Wittenberg travelled to him to buy indulgences.
14670.m: Johann Tetzel was a well-known preacher of indulgences.

14671.q: Which saying is linked to the sale of indulgences in Tetzel’s time?
a: As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs
One God, one faith, one baptism
14671.e: The saying is attributed to the indulgence preacher Tetzel, but it is not proven that he really said it like that. It sums up what many people believed about indulgences, and that is exactly what Luther criticised.
14671.m: The saying about the coin ringing in the coffer shows how indulgences were sold.

14672.q: What was part of the money from the sale of indulgences at that time used for?
a: Rebuilding St Peter’s Basilica in Rome
14672.e: Half of the money from this indulgence was meant for rebuilding St Peter’s. The other half went to a German archbishop, who used it to pay debts to the banker Jakob Fugger.
14672.m: Indulgence money helped pay for St Peter’s in Rome, among other things.

14673.q: In which language did Luther write his 95 Theses?
14673.e: Latin was then the language of the Church and the universities. Only translations into German made the Theses known among ordinary people.
14673.m: Luther wrote the 95 Theses in Latin.

14674.q: What was Martin Luther when he wrote the 95 Theses in 1517?
a: A monk and professor of theology
A knight at the emperor’s court
14674.e: Luther was an Augustinian monk and taught at the University of Wittenberg. As a professor he was allowed to invite people to a scholarly debate.
14674.m: Luther was a monk and professor in Wittenberg.

14675.q: According to tradition, on which church door did Luther nail the 95 Theses?
a: The door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg
The door of St Peter’s Basilica
14675.e: Tradition tells of the Theses being posted on the Castle Church in Wittenberg. At that time this door served as a kind of notice board for the university.
14675.m: According to tradition, Luther posted the Theses on the Castle Church in Wittenberg.

14676.q: What do historians say today about the famous posting of the Theses with a hammer?
a: It is uncertain whether it really happened like that
14676.e: Luther himself never mentioned posting them. Only years later did Melanchthon and Luther’s assistant Georg Rörer report it, so the posting of the Theses is still disputed today.
14676.m: Whether Luther really posted the Theses is disputed.

14677.q: Which invention helped the 95 Theses spread widely within a few weeks?
14677.e: Thanks to Gutenberg’s printing press, the Theses could be reprinted quickly and cheaply. So they were soon being read in many regions.
14677.m: Printing spread the ideas of the Reformation very quickly.

14678.q: Which holiday recalls the publication of the 95 Theses?
14678.e: Protestant Christians celebrate Reformation Day on 31 October. In some German states it is a public holiday.
14678.m: Reformation Day is celebrated on 31 October.

14679.q: What did Luther originally want to achieve with his 95 Theses?
a: A debate among scholars about indulgences
The founding of a new church
14679.e: Luther wanted to improve the Church and invited people to a scholarly debate. At first, splitting the Church was not his aim.
14679.m: At first Luther only wanted to improve the Church, not split it.

14680.q: What is a “thesis” in the sense of Luther’s 95 Theses?
a: A statement that can be debated
14680.e: Theses are statements that are defended or disproved in a debate. Luther put forward 95 such statements.
14680.m: A thesis is a statement people can argue about.

14681.q: What did the excommunication imposed on Luther by the Pope in 1521 mean?
a: Luther was expelled from the Church
Luther had to move to Rome
Luther could only write in Latin
14681.e: Because Luther did not take back his teaching, the Pope expelled him from the Church. Shortly afterwards the emperor also declared him an outlaw.
14681.m: In 1521 Luther was expelled from the Church.

14682.q: According to Luther’s Theses, what is more important for a Christian than a bought indulgence?
14682.e: In the very first thesis Luther says that the whole life of believers should be one of repentance. In his view, anyone who truly repents does not need a letter of indulgence.
14682.m: For Luther, true regret counted for more than a bought indulgence.

14683.q: What does the Latin word “reformation” mean?
14683.e: “Reformatio” means restoration or renewal. The reformers wanted to renew the Church following the example of the Bible.

14684.q: What does the principle “sola scriptura” mean?
a: Holy Scripture alone is the measure of faith
14684.e: For the reformers the Bible was the only basis of faith. Church traditions only counted if they agreed with the Bible.
14684.m: “Sola scriptura” means that only the Bible counts.

14685.q: According to Luther’s teaching, how is a person made right before God?
a: By faith and God’s grace alone
14685.e: Luther taught “sola fide” and “sola gratia”: God gives salvation out of grace, and people accept it in faith. Good works follow from faith but buy nothing.
14685.m: According to Luther, people are made right by faith and grace alone.

14686.q: Where does the name “Protestants” come from?
a: From the protest of Protestant princes at the Diet of Speyer in 1529
From the name of a pope
14686.e: In 1529 Protestant princes and towns in Speyer protested against a decision of the Catholic majority. Since then the followers of the Reformation have also been called Protestants.
14686.m: The name Protestants goes back to the protest at Speyer in 1529.

14687.q: Which peace settlement in 1555 allowed the princes in the empire to decide the faith of their land?
14687.e: In the Peace of Augsburg, Lutherans and Catholics in the empire were legally recognised. The Reformed were not yet clearly included in it.
14687.m: The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 let the princes decide on religion.

14688.q: What does the principle “cuius regio, eius religio” mean?
a: The Church stands above the king
14688.e: The phrase was only coined by a lawyer around 1600, but it describes the arrangement of 1555. Anyone who did not want to accept their ruler’s faith was allowed to emigrate.
14688.m: “Cuius regio, eius religio” means that the ruler decides the religion.

14689.q: What is the reform movement of the Catholic Church in response to the Reformation called?
14689.e: The Catholic Church responded with inner reforms and tried to win back lost areas. A great council and new religious orders helped with this.
14689.m: The Catholic response to the Reformation is called the Counter-Reformation.

14690.q: Which council of the Catholic Church met from 1545 to 1563 to respond to the Reformation?
14690.e: The Council of Trent clearly set out Catholic teaching and got rid of abuses. With breaks, it lasted almost 20 years.
14690.m: The Council of Trent was the Catholic Church’s great answer to the Reformation.

14691.q: Which religious order was confirmed by the Pope in 1540 and became an important force of the Counter-Reformation?
14691.e: Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, which was confirmed in 1540. The Jesuits worked mainly in schools and in missions.
14691.m: The Jesuits were an important force of the Counter-Reformation.

14692.q: Which forerunner of the Reformation was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415?
14692.e: The Czech theologian Jan Hus criticised the Church much as Luther did later. Despite being promised safe conduct, he was burned in Constance in 1415.
14692.m: Jan Hus was a forerunner of the Reformation and died in Constance in 1415.

14694.q: Which sacraments remained in most Protestant churches?
a: Confession and anointing of the sick
14694.e: The Catholic Church has seven sacraments. The reformers kept only those they saw as set up directly by Jesus in the Bible.
14694.m: Protestant churches usually have only baptism and Communion as sacraments.

14695.q: What happened to many monasteries in areas that brought in the Reformation?
a: They were given to the Pope
14695.e: The reformers rejected life in a monastery as a way to salvation. The property often went to the authorities and was used, for example, for schools and care of the poor.
14695.m: In Reformed areas many monasteries were closed down.

14696.q: What did the peasants fight for in the Peasants’ War of 1525?
a: For more rights and lower dues
For a war against the Turks
14696.e: The peasants had to give their lords many dues and services. They demanded more freedom but were bloodily defeated in 1525.
14696.m: In the Peasants’ War the peasants fought for more rights.

14697.q: Which group in the Reformation period rejected infant baptism and only baptised adults?
14697.e: The Anabaptists believed that only people who consciously believe should be baptised. They were persecuted by Catholics and Reformed alike.
14697.m: The Anabaptists only baptised people who could believe for themselves.

14698.q: Which two reformers met in Marburg in 1529 for talks?
14698.e: Landgrave Philip of Hesse invited Luther and Zwingli to Marburg. They wanted to unite the Protestants, but did not fully succeed.
14698.m: Luther and Zwingli met in Marburg in 1529.

14699.q: On which question could Luther and Zwingli not agree in Marburg?
14699.e: Luther believed Christ was really present in the bread and wine. Zwingli saw it differently, so agreement failed on this point.
14699.m: Luther and Zwingli argued about Holy Communion.

14700.q: In which city did Huldrych Zwingli bring in the Reformation?
14700.e: Zwingli came from Wildhaus in the Toggenburg. As a priest in Zurich he began to renew the Church from 1519.
14700.m: Zwingli brought the Reformation to Zurich.

14701.q: In which church in Zurich did Zwingli preach?
14701.e: Zwingli took up his post at the Grossmünster in 1519. The Reformation in Zurich began from here.
14701.m: Zwingli preached at the Grossmünster in Zurich.

14702.q: What is the renewal of the Church that Zwingli led in Zurich called?
14702.e: Zwingli and his helpers wanted to renew the Church according to the Bible. This movement is called the Reformation.
14702.m: Zwingli was a reformer in Zurich.

14703.q: What was Zwingli’s job before he became a reformer?
14703.e: Zwingli was first a Catholic priest in Glarus and Einsiedeln. Only in Zurich did he begin to reform the Church.
14703.m: Zwingli was first a Catholic priest.

14704.q: What happened at the famous “sausage eating” in Zurich in 1522?
a: People ate sausage during Lent on purpose
The Bishop of Constance was honoured
14704.e: Sausage was eaten during Lent in the house of a Zurich printer. Zwingli was there but did not eat any himself; afterwards, though, he defended breaking the fast using the Bible.
14704.m: The sausage eating of 1522 was a public break with the fasting rules.

14705.q: Which invention helped Zwingli to spread his ideas quickly?
14705.e: Zurich printers like Christoph Froschauer printed Zwingli’s writings and the Zurich Bible. That way his ideas reached many people.
14705.m: Printing spread the ideas of the Reformation.

14706.q: What happened at the First Zurich Disputation in January 1523?
a: The council allowed Zwingli to keep preaching from the Bible
14706.e: On 29 January 1523 Zwingli defended his teaching in front of about 600 people. Afterwards the Zurich council decided that he could go on preaching, which opened the way to the Reformation.
14706.m: After the First Zurich Disputation in 1523 Zwingli was allowed to keep preaching.

14707.q: What was the most important guide for faith for Zwingli?
14707.e: Zwingli only wanted to accept what is written in the Bible. That is why he preached straight from the Bible.
14707.m: For Zwingli the Bible counted most.

14708.q: What was removed from the churches in Zurich from 1524?
14708.e: Zwingli rejected the worship of images as idolatry. In 1524 pictures, statues and altars were removed from the churches in an orderly way.
14708.m: In Zurich the pictures were removed from the churches in 1524.

14709.q: What did Zwingli do publicly in 1524 that Catholic priests were not allowed to do?
14709.e: Catholic priests were not allowed to marry. In 1524 Zwingli publicly married the widow Anna Reinhart and so openly broke this rule.
14709.m: Zwingli married as a priest and so broke with celibacy.

14710.q: Which Swiss practice did Zwingli fight against in particular, because he had seen it as an army chaplain?
a: Going off to fight as a mercenary
14710.e: Zwingli went with troops from Glarus as an army chaplain, including to the Battle of Marignano in 1515. After that he sharply criticised mercenary service and the payments from foreign princes.
14710.m: Zwingli fought against the Confederates serving as mercenaries.

14711.q: How did Huldrych Zwingli die in 1531?
a: He fell in the Battle of Kappel
He died of plague in Zurich
14711.e: In the Second War of Kappel, Zwingli marched with the Zurich troops against the Catholic cantons. He fell on 11 October 1531 at Kappel am Albis.
14711.m: Zwingli fell in the Battle of Kappel in 1531.

14712.q: Who became Zwingli’s successor at the Grossmünster after his death in 1531?
14712.e: Heinrich Bullinger led the Zurich church for over 40 years. He strengthened the Reformation and was in contact with Protestants all over Europe.
14712.m: Heinrich Bullinger became Zwingli’s successor in Zurich.

14713.q: How did Zwingli understand Holy Communion?
a: As a meal of remembrance in which bread and wine stand for Christ
As a sacrifice offered by the priest
As a feast only for priests
14713.e: For Zwingli, Communion was a meal of remembrance for the congregation. He understood the words “this is my body” as “this means my body”.
14713.m: For Zwingli, Communion was a meal of remembrance.

14714.q: Which translation of the Bible was made in Zurich in Zwingli’s time?
14714.e: Zwingli and other scholars translated the Bible into German in Zurich. The complete Zurich Bible was published in 1531.
14714.m: The Zurich Bible was made in Zurich.

14715.q: Which meal in the First War of Kappel in 1529 became a symbol of reconciliation among the Confederates?
14715.e: According to tradition, soldiers from both sides ate milk soup with bread together from one pot. The war ended in 1529 without a big battle.
14715.m: The Kappel milk soup stands for reconciliation among the Confederates.

14716.q: In which country was John Calvin born?
14716.e: Calvin came from Noyon in northern France. Because Protestants were persecuted, he had to leave France.

14717.q: Was Calvin older or younger than Luther and Zwingli?
14717.e: Calvin was born in 1509, Luther in 1483 and Zwingli in 1484. So he belonged to the second generation of reformers.
14717.m: Calvin was younger than Luther and Zwingli.

14718.q: In which Swiss city did Calvin work for most of his life?
14718.e: Calvin came to Geneva in 1536 and shaped the city until his death. As a result Geneva became a centre of the Reformation.

14719.q: How did Calvin explain the Reformed faith in detail?
14719.e: Calvin’s main work, the “Institutes”, was published in Basel in 1536. He revised and expanded it several times.
14719.m: Calvin explained the faith in a big textbook.

14720.q: Why did Calvin have to flee from France?
a: He was looking for work in a factory
14720.e: In France followers of the Reformation were persecuted. So Calvin fled and came to Geneva in 1536.
14720.m: Calvin fled France as a Protestant.

14721.q: What role did Calvin have in Geneva?
a: He was a pastor and preacher
14721.e: Calvin preached in Geneva and led the Reformed church. He held no political office, yet he still shaped the city strongly.
14721.m: Calvin was a pastor in Geneva.

14724.q: How was life in Geneva regulated under Calvin’s influence?
a: With strict rules on behaviour and church attendance
By the laws of the Pope
By the orders of the emperor
14724.e: Calvin’s church order of 1541 created the Consistory, which watched over the lives of the citizens. Dancing, gambling and luxury were strictly limited.
14724.m: In Calvin’s Geneva strict rules applied to daily life.

14725.q: How were people treated in Calvin’s Geneva who held a different religious teaching?
a: They were punished harshly, one even with death
They were allowed to preach freely
14725.e: In 1553 the Geneva council had the scholar Michael Servetus burned because of his teaching. Calvin had spoken against him. This is a dark chapter of the Reformation.
14725.m: People of other beliefs were persecuted in Calvin’s Geneva too.

14727.q: What did Calvin wish for his grave?
a: A simple grave with no special marking
A place in St Peter’s Basilica
14727.e: Calvin died in Geneva in 1564. He did not want to be worshipped, so his grave was not specially marked.

14728.q: Which nickname did Geneva get because of Calvin?
14728.e: Under Calvin, Geneva became the most important centre of the Reformed. That is why the city was called the “Protestant Rome”.
14728.m: Geneva was called the Protestant Rome.

14729.q: What were the French followers of Calvinism called?
14729.e: The Huguenots were persecuted in France for a long time. Many fled to Reformed areas, including Geneva and other parts of Switzerland.
14729.m: The French Calvinists were called Huguenots.

14730.q: Which monument in Geneva shows Calvin together with Farel, Beza and Knox?
a: The Reformation Wall in the Parc des Bastions
