15231.e: The “Middle Passage” was the middle section of the triangular trade. People were crammed together below deck, and many died of disease and mistreatment.
15231.m: The Middle Passage was the deadliest part of the triangular trade.

15232.q: According to estimates, how many people died during the crossing of the Atlantic?
15232.e: Estimates suggest about 1.5 to 2 million deaths at sea. In addition, many died during capture in Africa and after arrival.
15232.m: The crossing alone cost millions of those carried off their lives.

15233.q: Which European sea power was the first to carry off people from West Africa, from the 1440s?
15233.e: In 1441 Portuguese sailors first brought captives from the West African coast to Portugal. From the 16th century this grew into the transatlantic trade.
15233.m: Portugal was at the beginning of the European slave trade with Africa.

15234.q: What was an “asiento” in connection with the slave trade?
a: A licence from the Spanish Crown to deliver enslaved people to its colonies
A revolt of enslaved people in the Caribbean
A type of ship for crossing the Atlantic
A law to free enslaved children
15234.e: The Spanish Crown granted asientos to traders and companies, giving them the right to sell people in the Spanish colonies. These contracts were highly sought after.
15234.m: Through the asiento the Spanish Crown also earned money from the slave trade.

15235.q: For which plantation product were especially many enslaved people carried off to the Caribbean in the 17th and 18th centuries?
15235.e: Sugar was in great demand in Europe and brought high profits. Work on the sugar plantations was extremely hard, and the death rate among the enslaved was correspondingly high.
15235.m: Demand for sugar drove the slave trade to the Caribbean.

15236.q: In which year did Great Britain ban its subjects from the slave trade?
15236.e: The British Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act in 1807. Slavery itself was only abolished in the British Empire in 1833.
15236.m: Great Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833.

15237.q: Which state was created in 1804 by a successful revolution of enslaved people?
15237.e: In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the enslaved rose up from 1791. On 1 January 1804 Haiti declared its independence.
15237.m: Haiti was the first state founded by freed enslaved people.

15238.q: Which country, with the “Golden Law” of 1888, was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery?
15238.e: The Lei Áurea of 13 May 1888 ended slavery in Brazil. In the USA it had already been banned in 1865 by the 13th Amendment.
15238.m: In 1888 Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery.

15239.q: At which congress in 1815 did European powers condemn the slave trade in a joint declaration?
a: At the Peace Congress of Westphalia
At the Paris Peace Congress of 1856
15239.e: In 1815 the Congress of Vienna adopted a declaration condemning the slave trade. The ban, however, was only enforced much later.
15239.m: In 1815 the European powers condemned the slave trade in Vienna.

15240.q: How were people from Switzerland involved in the Atlantic slave trade, even though Switzerland had no colonies?
a: As investors, merchants, bankers and plantation owners
Not at all, there were no links whatsoever
Only as sailors in a Swiss war fleet
As a colonial power with its own ports in West Africa
15240.e: Swiss trading houses and private individuals invested in slave ships, supplied trade goods such as printed cotton cloth or owned plantations. Researchers have been examining these links more closely in recent years.
15240.m: Swiss people also profited from the Atlantic slave trade.

15241.q: Which formerly enslaved man published an autobiography in 1789 that strengthened the British movement against the slave trade?
15241.e: In “The Interesting Narrative”, Olaudah Equiano described how he was carried off and enslaved. The book is an important source from the point of view of someone affected.
15241.m: Olaudah Equiano gave enslaved people a voice of their own in the abolition movement.

15635.q: Which period in Swiss history is called the Restoration?
15635.e: After the end of the Mediation period in 1813/14, the old elites tried to restore the conditions before the Revolution. The era ended when liberal reforms began in many cantons in 1830.
15635.m: In Switzerland the Restoration lasted from 1814 to 1830.

15636.q: Which treaty regulated relations between the cantons from 1815?
15636.e: The Federal Treaty was sworn on 7 August 1815 in Zurich’s Grossmünster. It made Switzerland a loose confederation of states again.
15636.m: The Federal Treaty of 1815 created a loose confederation of states again.

15637.q: How many cantons swore the Federal Treaty of 1815?
15637.e: With three new cantons admitted, the number rose to 22. This number stayed the same until the canton of Jura was founded in 1979.
15637.m: From 1815 the Confederation consisted of 22 cantons.

15638.q: Which three territories joined the Confederation as new cantons in 1815?
a: The Grisons, St Gallen and Thurgau
15638.e: The Congress of Vienna recognised the enlargement of the Confederation in the west. With this, Switzerland essentially got its present borders.
15638.m: Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel became Swiss cantons in 1815.

15639.q: What was special about the canton of Neuchâtel after 1815?
a: It was also a principality of the King of Prussia.
It had no vote in the Federal Diet.
It was a subject territory of Bern.
15639.e: Neuchâtel was a Swiss canton and at the same time a principality owned by the Prussian king. This double status later led to a serious conflict with Prussia.
15639.m: After 1815 Neuchâtel was both a canton and a Prussian principality.

15640.q: Which cities took turns as the leading canton (Vorort) after the Federal Treaty of 1815?
15640.e: The Vorort ran the business of the Federal Diet and changed every two years. However, it had no special privileges.
15640.m: Zurich, Bern and Lucerne took turns as the Vorort of the Confederation.

15641.q: When did the great powers formally recognise Switzerland’s perpetual neutrality?
15641.e: The declaration of 20 November 1815 was connected with the Second Peace of Paris. The Congress of Vienna had already promised recognition in March 1815.
15641.m: Swiss neutrality was recognised by the great powers in 1815.

15642.q: What did the old elites in Switzerland want to achieve during the Restoration from 1814?
a: To restore conditions as they were before the French Revolution
To found a modern federal state
15642.e: Restoration means bringing back. After Napoleon’s fall, the old rulers wanted to win back their privileges from before 1798.
15642.m: The Restoration tried to bring back the old order from before 1798.

15643.q: Under whose pressure did the Federal Diet restrict press freedom and asylum for political refugees in 1823?
a: Under pressure from great powers such as Austria and Prussia
15643.e: The conservative great powers wanted to stop liberal refugees from spreading propaganda from Switzerland. The Federal Diet therefore decided on stricter rules in 1823.
15643.m: Under pressure from the great powers, Switzerland restricted the press and asylum in 1823.

15644.q: What caused the famine years of 1816 and 1817 in Switzerland?
a: The eruption of the Tambora volcano and failed harvests
A cattle plague on the Central Plateau
15644.e: The eruption of Tambora in Indonesia led to the “Year Without a Summer” in 1816. The failed harvests caused the last great famine in Swiss history.
15644.m: A volcanic eruption caused the famine of 1816 and 1817.

15645.q: Which alliance of monarchs did Switzerland join in 1817?
15645.e: The Holy Alliance of Russia, Austria and Prussia was meant to secure the monarchical order. Switzerland joining in 1817 shows the conservative direction of the Restoration period.
15645.m: Switzerland joined the Holy Alliance in 1817.

15646.q: How did the old elites in cities such as Bern secure their power during the Restoration?
a: By restoring the patriciate and voting rights based on wealth
15646.e: In Bern, Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn the old patrician families ruled again. Voting rights based on wealth and indirect elections kept most citizens away from power.
15646.m: The patriciate and wealth-based voting rights secured power for the old elites.

15647.q: Which event abroad triggered the Regeneration in many cantons in 1830?
15647.e: The July Revolution in Paris encouraged the liberals in Switzerland. In 1830 and 1831 many cantons got new, liberal constitutions.
15647.m: The July Revolution of 1830 set off the Regeneration in Switzerland.

15648.q: What is meant by the Regeneration in Swiss history?
a: The liberal renewal of many cantonal constitutions from 1830
The rebuilding after the Sonderbund War
The return to the old order after 1815
The reforestation of the woods in the 19th century
15648.e: From 1830 many cantons gave themselves new, liberal constitutions with popular sovereignty and civil liberties. This period is called the Regeneration, meaning renewal.
15648.m: The Regeneration from 1830 brought liberal cantonal constitutions.

15649.q: What was the Ustertag of 22 November 1830?
a: A popular assembly of the Zurich countryside calling for a new constitution
A battle between Zurich and Schwyz
The first sitting of the National Council
An uprising against the Federal Constitution
15649.e: In Uster the rural population demanded more political say and fairer representation in the Grand Council. The Ustertag led to the liberal Zurich constitution of 1831.
15649.m: At the Ustertag in 1830 the Zurich countryside demanded more rights.

15650.q: Which freedom did the liberals of the Regeneration demand most, so they could spread their ideas in newspapers?
15650.e: For the liberals, newspapers were the most important way to promote their ideas. The regenerated constitutions therefore guaranteed freedom of the press.
15650.m: The liberals of the Regeneration fought for freedom of the press.

15651.q: Which principle did the regenerated cantonal constitutions establish against the old order?
15651.e: The new constitutions declared the people to be the source of state power. They also guaranteed equality before the law, separation of powers and civil liberties such as freedom of the press.
15651.m: The Regeneration made the people the source of state power.

15652.q: Which canton was split in 1833 after fierce conflicts between town and countryside?
15652.e: After fighting between the city and the countryside, the division into Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft was finally recognised in 1833. Basel-Landschaft had already set itself up as a canton of its own in 1832.
15652.m: Basel was split into two half-cantons in 1833.

15653.q: Which liberal cantons joined together in the Concordat of Seven in 1832?
a: Zurich, Bern, Lucerne, Solothurn, St Gallen, Aargau and Thurgau
Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Zug, Lucerne and Valais
Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Fribourg, Valais, Ticino and Bern
Basel, Schaffhausen, Glarus, Appenzell, the Grisons, Zug and Uri
15653.e: The seven cantons guaranteed each other’s new liberal constitutions. In this way they wanted to protect themselves against conservative coups.
15653.m: In the Concordat of Seven, seven liberal cantons protected their constitutions.

15654.q: What was the alliance of conservative cantons formed in response to the Concordat of Seven called?
15654.e: In November 1832 Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Neuchâtel and Basel-Stadt, among others, joined together in the League of Sarnen. It rejected the liberal innovations.
15654.m: The League of Sarnen was the conservative counter-alliance of 1832.

15655.q: What did the Rossi Plan of 1832/33 aim to achieve?
a: A reform of the loose Federal Treaty of 1815
The division of the canton of Basel
The restoration of the Helvetic Republic
15655.e: Pellegrino Rossi’s draft wanted to bring the Confederation more closely together. It did not go far enough for the radicals and went too far for the conservatives, and it failed in the cantons in 1833.
15655.m: The Rossi Plan aimed to reform the Federal Treaty and failed in 1833.

15656.q: Which university was founded in 1833 in the spirit of the Regeneration?
15656.e: Liberal governments promoted education as the basis of responsible citizens. Zurich founded its university in 1833, and Bern followed in 1834.
15656.m: The University of Zurich was founded in 1833 during the Regeneration.

15657.q: What led to the Züriputsch in 1839?
a: The appointment of the theologian David Friedrich Strauss
The introduction of new taxes on wine
The building of the first railway
The closing of the monasteries in Aargau
15657.e: The appointment of the controversial theologian as professor outraged the conservative rural population. On 6 September 1839 an uprising overthrew the liberal government.
15657.m: The dispute over David Friedrich Strauss led to the Züriputsch in 1839.

15658.q: Which word, now also used in English, spread through the whole German-speaking world because of the Zurich coup of 1839?
15658.e: The Swiss German word for a violent push became known through the reports on the Züriputsch. Today it generally means a violent overthrow of a government.
15658.m: The word “putsch” comes from Swiss German.

15659.e: The Catholic conservative cantons formed a defensive alliance at the end of 1845. The liberal majority saw this as a breach of the Federal Treaty.
15659.m: The Sonderbund was founded in December 1845.

15660.q: Which canton did NOT belong to the Sonderbund?
15660.e: The members were Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais. Catholic Solothurn, like Appenzell Innerrhoden, stayed out of the alliance.
15660.m: Solothurn did not join the Sonderbund despite its Catholic majority.

15661.q: Which city was the centre of the Sonderbund?
15661.e: The Sonderbund was founded in Lucerne, and its war council sat there. Lucerne was also the member canton with the largest population.
15661.m: Lucerne was the political centre of the Sonderbund.

15662.q: Who chaired the war council of the Sonderbund?
15662.e: The Lucerne government councillor Constantin Siegwart-Müller was the leading figure of the Sonderbund. After the defeat he fled abroad.
15662.m: Constantin Siegwart-Müller led the war council of the Sonderbund.

15663.q: What happened in the Aargau monastery dispute of 1841?
a: The canton of Aargau closed the monasteries.
The Pope banned all Swiss monasteries.
The Federal Diet founded new monasteries.
15663.e: In January 1841 Aargau decided to close all its monasteries, which broke the Federal Treaty. The dispute poisoned relations between liberals and Catholic conservatives.
15663.m: The closing of the Aargau monasteries in 1841 sharpened the religious dispute.

15664.q: Which decision by the canton of Lucerne in 1844 particularly outraged the liberals?
a: Bringing the Jesuits in to run the higher school
15664.e: For the radicals, the Jesuits were a symbol of Rome and backwardness. Their appointment in Lucerne in 1844 triggered the Freischarenzüge.
15664.m: Bringing the Jesuits to Lucerne in 1844 fuelled the conflict.

15665.q: What were the Freischarenzüge of 1844 and 1845?
a: Armed attacks on Lucerne by radical volunteers
Campaigns by the Federal Diet against Valais
15665.e: Radical volunteers tried to overthrow the conservative government of Lucerne. Both expeditions failed, the second on 31 March 1845 with many taken prisoner.
15665.m: The volunteer expeditions against Lucerne failed in 1844 and 1845.

15666.q: Which later member of the first Federal Council led the second volunteer expedition in 1845?
15666.e: Ulrich Ochsenbein from Bern led the failed expedition against Lucerne. In 1848 he was elected to the first Federal Council.
15666.m: Ulrich Ochsenbein led the second volunteer expedition.

15667.q: Why did the liberal majority consider the Sonderbund illegal?
a: The Federal Treaty banned alliances that harmed the Confederation or other cantons.
It had been founded by France.
It had introduced its own currency.
It consisted only of Protestant cantons.
15667.e: The Federal Treaty of 1815 forbade the cantons from forming harmful separate alliances. The Federal Diet therefore declared the Sonderbund dissolved in 1847.
15667.m: In the majority’s view the Sonderbund broke the Federal Treaty.

15668.q: Which change in Geneva and St Gallen gave the liberals a majority in the Federal Diet in 1847?
a: Both cantons were occupied by Austria.
15668.e: Through the change of power in Geneva and the liberal election victory in St Gallen, the liberals reached the majority they needed. Only then could the Federal Diet decide to dissolve the Sonderbund.
15668.m: Only the turnaround in Geneva and St Gallen gave the liberals their majority in 1847.

15669.q: From which great power did the Sonderbund mainly hope for military help?
15669.e: The Sonderbund cantons negotiated in Vienna, Paris and Turin. Austria supplied some money and weapons but sent no troops.
15669.m: The Sonderbund hoped in vain for help from Austria.

15670.q: Who led the federal troops as general in the Sonderbund War of 1847?
15670.e: Dufour from Geneva ended the war in less than four weeks with few casualties. He ordered his troops to treat the wounded and prisoners well.
15670.m: General Dufour led the Federal Diet’s troops in 1847.

15671.q: Who was commander-in-chief of the federal troops in the Sonderbund War?
15671.e: The Federal Diet elected Dufour from Geneva as general. He led a quick campaign and tried to keep losses low.
15671.m: General Dufour led the federal army in the Sonderbund War.

15672.q: Roughly how long did the Sonderbund War last?
15672.e: The fighting began on 3 November 1847 and ended on 29 November with the surrender of Valais. So the war lasted only 26 days.
15672.m: The Sonderbund War lasted less than a month.

15673.q: Which Sonderbund canton was the last to surrender?
15673.e: On 29 November 1847 Valais surrendered as the last canton. With that, the war was over.
15673.m: The Sonderbund War ended with the surrender of Valais.

15674.q: Which battle on 23 November 1847 decided the fight for Lucerne?
15674.e: At Gisikon on the river Reuss the federal troops prevailed. The next day the city of Lucerne surrendered.
15674.m: The battle at Gisikon decided the fight for Lucerne.

15675.q: What was the Sonderbund that was defeated in the war of 1847?
a: A defensive alliance of Catholic conservative cantons
An alliance of the liberal cities
15675.e: Seven Catholic conservative cantons joined together in 1845 to form the Sonderbund. The liberal majority of the Federal Diet declared the alliance incompatible with the Federal Treaty.
15675.m: The Sonderbund was an alliance of Catholic conservative cantons.

15676.q: With which attack did the Sonderbund War begin on 3 November 1847?
a: With an advance by Sonderbund troops into Ticino
15676.e: Sonderbund troops advanced over the Gotthard into Ticino. On 4 November the Federal Diet decided to enforce its decision by force of arms.
15676.m: The war began with a Sonderbund advance into Ticino.

15677.q: How is the number of dead in the Sonderbund War usually estimated?
15677.e: Recent research gives just over 90 dead, official figures about 150. Compared with other civil wars, the losses remained low.
15677.m: The Sonderbund War caused relatively few deaths.

15678.q: Why is Dufour’s conduct of the war considered especially moderate?
a: He ordered that the wounded and prisoners be treated humanely.
He had the Sonderbund cantons occupied and looted.
He left the fighting to foreign mercenaries.
15678.e: Dufour did not want to humiliate his opponents, because they were to be fellow Confederates again after the war. He spared civilians and demanded good treatment of the wounded.
15678.m: Dufour fought the war with the later peace in mind.

15679.q: In which later founding did General Dufour play an important role?
a: The International Committee of the Red Cross
15679.e: In 1863 Dufour was part of the founding committee in Geneva from which the ICRC emerged. The highest Swiss summit, the Dufourspitze, is also named after him.
15679.m: General Dufour was one of the founders of the Red Cross.

15680.q: What important consequence did the quick victory in the Sonderbund War have?
a: The way was clear for the Federal Constitution of 1848.
The Jesuits became the state church.
The Federal Diet was strengthened and remained.
15680.e: After the liberals’ victory, the Federal Diet was able to revise the Federal Treaty completely. Because the great powers did not intervene, the federal state was created in 1848.
15680.m: Victory in the Sonderbund War made the Federal Constitution of 1848 possible.

15681.q: Why did the conservative great powers not intervene in the Sonderbund War in 1847?
a: The war was over too quickly and they had problems at home.
Switzerland was a member of NATO at the time.
An alliance with Great Britain forbade it.
15681.e: Austria and Prussia hesitated, and in 1848 revolutions broke out across Europe. The short war created a fait accompli before any intervention was possible.
15681.m: The shortness of the war prevented foreign interference.

15682.q: What date does Switzerland’s first Federal Constitution bear?
15682.e: The Federal Diet declared the constitution adopted on 12 September 1848. With that, the confederation of states became a federal state.
15682.m: The first Federal Constitution is dated 12 September 1848.

15683.q: Which model did the two-chamber system of the 1848 Federal Constitution follow?
a: The Reichstag of the German Empire
15683.e: The National Council and the Council of States correspond to the House of Representatives and the Senate of the USA. In this way the interests of the people and the cantons were taken into account equally.
15683.m: Switzerland’s two-chamber system follows the American model.

15684.q: Which compromise was the basis of the two-chamber system of 1848?
a: A balance between large and small cantons
A balance between the nobility and the middle class
A balance between church and state
A balance between the city of Bern and the city of Zurich
15684.e: In the National Council, cantons with large populations have more seats; in the Council of States, all cantons have the same number of seats. This made the small, defeated cantons more likely to accept the federal state.
15684.m: The two-chamber system combines representation of the people and of the cantons.

15685.q: Which cantons mostly rejected the Federal Constitution of 1848?
15685.e: A clear majority of men voted in favour. The constitution was rejected mainly by Catholic cantons such as Uri, Schwyz or Valais, which had been defeated in the Sonderbund War in 1847.
15685.m: In 1848 the constitution was rejected mainly by the losers of the Sonderbund War.

15686.q: How was the Federal Constitution decided on in the canton of Fribourg in 1848?
a: By the cantonal parliament instead of a popular vote
By the Bishop of Lausanne and Geneva
15686.e: The radical Fribourg government let the parliament decide in order to avoid rejection by the people. This shows that the votes of 1848 were not equally democratic everywhere.
15686.m: In Fribourg in 1848 the cantonal parliament decided on the constitution.

15687.q: Which responsibility passed from the cantons to the federal government in 1848?
15687.e: Internal customs duties between the cantons were dropped, and the federal government collected the border duties. This created a single economic area.
15687.m: Since 1848 customs have been a federal matter.

15688.q: Which areas were also standardised with the new federal state?
a: Post, coins, and weights and measures
Police, street names and public holidays
15688.e: Before that, almost every canton had its own coins and measures. Standardisation made trade and transport much easier.
15688.m: The federal state standardised post, money, and weights and measures.

15689.q: To whom did the freedom of establishment in the 1848 Federal Constitution at first apply?
a: Only to Swiss citizens of Christian denomination
Only to citizens of the towns
15689.e: Jews were excluded from the freedom of establishment. Only the partial revision of 1866 gave them equal rights on this point.
15689.m: In 1848 freedom of establishment applied only to Christian Swiss citizens.

15690.q: Which religious order was banned in Switzerland by the Federal Constitution of 1848?
15690.e: The ban on the Jesuits was a direct result of the Sonderbund conflict. It was only lifted in a popular vote in 1973.
15690.m: The Federal Constitution of 1848 banned the Jesuit order.

15691.q: Who was allowed to vote and stand for election in federal matters in 1848?
a: Men and women aged 21 and over
15691.e: The constitution introduced voting rights for men without any wealth requirement. However, the cantons often excluded people receiving poor relief, for example, and women only got the vote in 1971.
15691.m: In 1848 Swiss men got the right to vote and stand for election.

15692.q: Which popular right was already contained in the Federal Constitution of 1848?
a: The popular initiative for partial revision
15692.e: Every change to the Federal Constitution had to be put to the people and the cantons. In addition, 50,000 voters could demand a total revision.
15692.m: Since 1848 the people and the cantons have decided on changes to the constitution.

15693.q: How was the Federal Constitution of 1848 prepared?
a: By a revision committee of the Federal Diet
By a constitutional council elected by the people
By envoys of the great powers
15693.e: The Federal Diet set up a committee on 16 August 1847, which met from February 1848. It presented a draft in April 1848.
15693.m: A committee of the Federal Diet drew up the constitution of 1848.

15694.q: Who elected the members of the first Federal Council in November 1848?
a: The people at the ballot box
15694.e: The National Council and the Council of States met for the first time in November 1848 and together elected the seven Federal Councillors. To this day the United Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council.
15694.m: The Federal Assembly has elected the Federal Council since 1848.

15695.q: Which politician from Ticino belonged to the first Federal Council of 1848?
15695.e: Stefano Franscini represented Italian-speaking Switzerland in the first Federal Council. He especially promoted statistics and education.
15695.m: Stefano Franscini was the first Federal Councillor from Ticino.

15696.q: What is Bern officially called, since Switzerland legally has no capital?
15696.e: In November 1848 the Federal Assembly chose Bern as the seat of the federal authorities. But the constitution says nothing about a capital, so Bern is called the federal city (Bundesstadt).
15696.m: Bern is the federal city of Switzerland.

15697.q: Which cities were Bern’s main rivals in the choice of the federal seat in 1848?
15697.e: Zurich was already the economic centre and was not to gain even more weight. Lucerne was politically weakened as the centre of the Sonderbund.
15697.m: Zurich and Lucerne lost out to Bern in the choice of the federal city.

15698.q: Which institution did Zurich get to make up for not becoming the federal city?
15698.e: ETH (then the Federal Polytechnic) opened in Zurich in 1855. It became the first federal university.

15699.q: When was the present Federal Palace in Bern inaugurated?
15699.e: The parliament building with the large dome opened in 1902. Before that, parliament met in other buildings in Bern.
15699.m: The Federal Palace in Bern was inaugurated in 1902.

15700.q: Which businessman and politician shaped railway building and the Gotthard Tunnel in the young federal state?
15700.e: Alfred Escher founded the Swiss Credit Institute (Schweizerische Kreditanstalt) and pushed forward the Gotthard Railway. He is considered one of the most influential business leaders of the 19th century.
15700.m: Alfred Escher was a pioneer of Swiss railway building.

15701.q: Who built most of the railway lines in Switzerland after the first Railway Act of 1852?
15701.e: The Act left railway building to the cantons and private companies. Only after the popular vote of 1898 were the large private railways nationalised.
15701.m: In the young federal state, private companies built the railways.

15702.q: Which party provided all the members of the Federal Council from 1848 to 1891?
a: The Free Democrats, also called Liberal Radicals
15702.e: The winners of the Sonderbund War governed alone for over four decades. Only in 1891 did the Catholic Conservatives get a seat.
15702.m: Until 1891 only Free Democrats sat in the Federal Council.

15703.q: Which political group got a seat on the Federal Council for the first time in 1891?
15703.e: After more than forty years of sole rule by the Free Democrats, Josef Zemp from Lucerne was elected in 1891. In this way the losers of the Sonderbund War were brought into government.
15703.m: In 1891 the Catholic Conservatives entered the Federal Council.

15704.q: Which conflict with Prussia was resolved in 1856/57 when the king gave up his rights?
15704.e: In 1856 royalists in Neuchâtel attempted a coup in favour of the Prussian king. After mediation, the king gave up his claims in 1857.
15704.m: With the Neuchâtel affair, Neuchâtel broke away from Prussia completely.

15705.q: What does it mean that the Federal Constitution was “totally revised” in 1874?
a: It was rewritten as a whole
Only a single article was changed
It only applied to some cantons
15705.e: In a total revision the whole constitution is revised and adopted again. In a partial revision only individual articles are changed. Switzerland had total revisions in 1874 and 1999.
15705.m: A total revision renews the whole constitution.

15706.q: What happened to the first draft of a total revision in 1872?
a: It was rejected by the people and the cantons.
It was introduced without a vote.
It was blocked by the army.
It only came into force in French-speaking Switzerland.
15706.e: The centralist draft was narrowly rejected by the people and clearly by the cantons on 12 May 1872. French-speaking Swiss and Catholics in particular feared too much centralisation.
15706.m: The overly centralist draft of 1872 was rejected.

15707.q: Which new popular right did the Federal Constitution of 1874 bring?
a: Election of the Federal Council by the people
15707.e: A referendum could now be called against federal laws. At first this needed 30,000 signatures.
15707.m: Since 1874 the people have been able to vote on federal laws.

15708.q: Where did the permanent Federal Supreme Court get its seat after 1874?
15708.e: The Federal Supreme Court became a permanent court based in Lausanne. This also gave French-speaking Switzerland an important federal institution.
15708.m: The Federal Supreme Court has its seat in Lausanne.

15709.q: What did the Federal Constitution of 1874 require for primary school teaching?
a: It had to be compulsory, free and religiously neutral.
It had to be given by monasteries.
It was only intended for boys.
It had to be in German in all cantons.
15709.e: The cantons remained responsible for schools but had to guarantee adequate primary teaching under state control. This limited the church’s influence on schools.
15709.m: Since 1874 primary school has been compulsory and free.

15710.q: To which wider context do the church policy articles of the 1874 constitution belong?
a: The Kulturkampf between the state and the Catholic Church
15710.e: After the dogma of papal infallibility in 1870, the conflict with the Catholic Church grew sharper. The 1874 constitution, for example, banned new monasteries and required approval for new dioceses.
15710.m: The 1874 constitution was shaped by the Kulturkampf.

15711.q: Which change in marriage law did the Federal Constitution of 1874 introduce?
a: Marriage only from the age of 30
15711.e: Getting married became a matter for the state, and the right to marry was guaranteed. This was part of separating the tasks of state and church.
15711.m: Since 1874 marriages have been concluded before the state.

15712.q: How did the Federal Constitution of 1874 change military affairs?
a: The federal government got more powers over training and weapons.
Each canton was allowed its own navy.
15712.e: The Franco-Prussian War of 1870/71 had shown weaknesses in the cantonal troops. Training and equipment were therefore largely centralised at federal level.
15712.m: The 1874 constitution strengthened the federal role in the army.

15713.q: Which federal law protecting workers was narrowly accepted in a referendum in 1877?
15713.e: The federal Factory Act limited working hours, among other things, and restricted child labour. It was an early example of federal social policy.
15713.m: The Factory Act of 1877 protected workers.

15714.q: How long did the Federal Constitution of 1874 remain in force?
15714.e: It was often partially revised over more than 100 years. On 1 January 2000 the new Federal Constitution of 18 April 1999 replaced it.

15715.q: Which punishment did the Federal Constitution of 1874 abolish in civil criminal law?
15715.e: The 1874 constitution banned the death penalty outside military criminal law. As early as 1879, after a narrow popular vote, the cantons were allowed to bring it back for non-political crimes.
15715.m: The 1874 constitution abolished the death penalty for a time.

15716.q: Which principle of economic life was laid down in the Federal Constitution of 1874?
15716.e: In principle, anyone could run a business anywhere in the country. Cantonal restrictions from the time of the guilds were greatly reduced.
15716.m: The 1874 constitution guaranteed freedom of trade and industry.

15717.q: Which fundamental right did the Federal Constitution of 1874 guarantee more fully than that of 1848?
a: Election of judges by the people
15717.e: In 1848 only the worship of the recognised Christian denominations was protected. The 1874 constitution declared freedom of belief and conscience inviolable.
15717.m: Since 1874 the Federal Constitution has guaranteed freedom of belief and conscience.

15718.q: What could voters do with the “veto” that St Gallen introduced in 1831?
15718.e: With the veto a law could be stopped if enough citizens were against it. It was an early form of the legislative referendum.
15718.m: The veto was a forerunner of the legislative referendum.

15719.q: What did the Democratic Movement of the 1860s demand in cantons such as Zurich?
a: More direct popular rights instead of purely representative government
A return to rule by the patricians
15719.e: The Democrats criticised the “Escher system”, the power of a small liberal elite. They demanded the referendum, the initiative and election of the government by the people.
15719.m: The Democratic Movement demanded more direct popular rights.

15720.q: Which canton adopted a constitution with far-reaching direct democratic rights in 1869?
15720.e: On 18 April 1869 the people of Zurich adopted the new constitution. Among other things it brought the mandatory legislative referendum and the popular initiative.
15720.m: The Zurich constitution of 1869 became a model for direct democracy.

15721.q: Which popular right was introduced at federal level in 1891?
a: The popular initiative for partial revision of the constitution
15721.e: Since 1891 voters have been able to demand a change to individual articles of the constitution. Before that, only an initiative for total revision was possible.
15721.m: The popular initiative for partial revision has existed since 1891.

15722.q: Which popular initiative was the first to be accepted in Switzerland, in 1893?
a: A ban on slaughtering animals without stunning them first
Proportional election of the National Council
15722.e: The ban on slaughter without stunning (shechita) was accepted on 20 August 1893. Researchers also see the vote as an expression of antisemitic attitudes of the time.
15722.m: The first accepted popular initiative, in 1893, concerned ritual slaughter.

15723.q: How many signatures does a federal popular initiative need today?
15723.e: The signatures must be collected within 18 months of publication in the Federal Gazette. To be accepted, it needs a majority of the people and of the cantons.
15723.m: A popular initiative today needs 100,000 signatures.

15724.q: How does an optional referendum against a federal law come about today?
a: With 50,000 signatures or eight cantons within 100 days
With the approval of the Federal Council
15724.e: The deadline starts when the act is published. If the referendum succeeds, only the popular majority decides.
15724.m: A referendum today needs 50,000 signatures or eight cantons.

15725.q: Why were the numbers of signatures for referendums and initiatives raised in 1977?
a: Because of population growth and women’s right to vote
Because of a ban by the Council of Europe
Because there were too few votes
Because the cantons lost their vote
15725.e: Since 1971 women had also been allowed to vote, which roughly doubled the number of voters. The required numbers of signatures were therefore raised.
15725.m: With more voters, the numbers of signatures were raised in 1977.

15726.q: What does the majority of the cantons mean in a vote on the Federal Constitution?
a: Most of the cantons must agree.
The Council of States must agree unanimously.
At least two thirds of the people must agree.
The Federal Council decides if there is a tie.
15726.e: Constitutional changes need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons. The result of the vote in each canton counts as that canton’s vote.
15726.m: Constitutional changes need a majority of the people and of the cantons.

15727.q: Which electoral reform did a popular initiative bring in in 1918, greatly changing the party system?
a: Proportional election of the National Council
Election of the Federal Council by the people
Abolition of the Council of States
15727.e: After proportional representation was introduced, the Free Democrats lost their absolute majority in the National Council in 1919. The Social Democrats and the Farmers’ Party made clear gains.
15727.m: Proportional representation ended the Free Democrats’ majority in the National Council in 1919.

15728.q: Which popular right was added in 1921?
a: The referendum against certain international treaties
The popular initiative for partial revision
15728.e: Since 1921 important treaties under international law can be put to the people. This right was later extended several times.
15728.m: Since 1921 the people can also vote on international treaties.

15729.q: What did the initiative “Return to direct democracy”, narrowly accepted in 1949, want?
a: To limit the emergency powers of parliament and the Federal Council
To introduce women’s right to vote
To have federal judges elected by the people
15729.e: During the crisis and the war, the Federal Council and parliament had declared many decisions urgent, so no referendum could be held on them. The initiative restored the popular rights.
15729.m: The 1949 initiative strengthened popular rights against emergency law.

15730.q: Which canton had to introduce women’s right to vote at cantonal level in 1990 because of a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court?
15730.e: The men at the Landsgemeinde had rejected women’s right to vote several times. On 27 November 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that this violated the equality guaranteed in the Federal Constitution.
15730.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to introduce women’s right to vote, in 1990.

15731.q: What does the “double yes” with a deciding question, introduced in 1987, allow?
a: You can vote for an initiative and the counter-proposal at the same time.
You may vote twice on the same proposal.
The Federal Council can overrule a no from the people.
Two cantons can call a referendum together.
15731.e: Before that, supporters of a reform had to choose between the initiative and the counter-proposal, which could weaken both. The deciding question settles which proposal applies if both get a yes.
15731.m: Since 1987 you can accept an initiative and the counter-proposal at the same time.

16230.q: In which treaty did the European powers recognise Switzerland’s permanent neutrality on 20 November 1815?
a: In the Second Peace of Paris
16230.e: On 20 November 1815 in Paris, the signatory powers recognised and guaranteed the permanent neutrality and the inviolability of Swiss territory. The groundwork had been laid at the Congress of Vienna.
16230.m: Switzerland’s permanent neutrality was recognised internationally in 1815.

16231.q: In which set of treaties were the rights and duties of neutral states in war laid down in 1907?
a: In the Charter of the United Nations
16231.e: The law of neutrality was codified in the Hague Conventions in 1907. It also applied to Switzerland in the Second World War.
16231.m: The law of neutrality comes from the Hague Conventions of 1907.

16232.q: What duty does a neutral state have under the law of neutrality?
a: It may provide neither troops nor its territory to parties at war
It must stop all trade with parties at war
It may not keep an army of its own
It must supply all parties at war with the same number of weapons
16232.e: A neutral state may not take part militarily in a war, provide troops or open its territory to parties at war. Private trade, however, remained allowed in principle, which raised tricky questions during the war.
16232.m: A neutral state does not take part militarily in any war.

16233.q: What did Switzerland’s return to “integral neutrality” in 1938 mean?
a: It no longer took part in League of Nations sanctions
It made an alliance with France
16233.e: Since joining the League of Nations in 1920, Switzerland had followed a “differential” neutrality that included taking part in economic sanctions. In 1938 it returned to full, integral neutrality and no longer joined in sanctions.
16233.m: From 1938 Switzerland no longer took part in League of Nations sanctions.

16234.q: What does the term “armed neutrality” mean?
a: Switzerland defends its neutrality with its own army
Switzerland supplies weapons only to neutral states
Switzerland lets foreign armies into the country for protection
Switzerland does without any arms industry
16234.e: Swiss neutrality is self-chosen, permanent and armed. The state intends to defend its independence with its own army if necessary.
16234.m: Switzerland protects its neutrality with its own army.

16235.q: What was Switzerland’s geographical situation from the summer of 1940?
a: It was surrounded by the Axis powers and territories they controlled
It bordered an unoccupied, Allied France
It had free access to the Mediterranean
It was completely surrounded by Allied states
16235.e: After France’s defeat in 1940, Switzerland was enclosed by Germany, Italy and territories they controlled. From the end of 1942 it was completely surrounded.
16235.m: From 1940 Switzerland was surrounded by the Axis powers.

16236.q: Which President of the Confederation gave a radio speech on 25 June 1940 that many saw as adapting to a Nazi-ruled Europe?
16236.e: Shortly after France surrendered, Pilet-Golaz spoke of an “inner rebirth”. Terms such as armed neutrality and independence were missing, which many interpreted as adapting to the new situation.
16236.m: Pilet-Golaz’s speech in June 1940 was criticised as adapting to Nazi Germany.

16237.q: Which meeting held by Federal Councillor Pilet-Golaz in September 1940 caused fierce criticism?
a: Receiving leaders of the Frontist National Movement of Switzerland
16237.e: Pilet-Golaz received representatives of the pro-Nazi National Movement of Switzerland. The movement was banned in November 1940.
16237.m: Pilet-Golaz receiving Frontists in 1940 caused outrage.

16238.q: Which diplomatic task did Switzerland take on for many states in the Second World War?
a: As a protecting power, it represented the interests of states at war with each other
It led the negotiations on Germany’s surrender
It provided peacekeeping troops for the Allies
It chaired the League of Nations Council in Geneva
16238.e: Especially after the USA entered the war, Switzerland took on many protecting power mandates. It represented the interests of states that no longer had direct relations with each other.
16238.m: As a protecting power, Switzerland represented the interests of many states in the war.

16239.q: Which political and cultural movement from the 1930s was meant to strengthen Swiss values against totalitarian ideologies?
16239.e: Spiritual National Defence stressed multilingualism, democracy and freedom as a defence against Nazism and fascism. It shaped culture and politics into the 1960s.
16239.m: Spiritual National Defence strengthened Swiss identity against dictatorships.

16240.q: Which event is considered the most powerful expression of Spiritual National Defence?
a: The National Exhibition of 1939 in Zurich
The World Exhibition of 1937 in Paris
The 1928 Olympic Games in St Moritz
16240.e: The “Landi” of 1939 in Zurich gave a strong sense of national independence shortly before the war began. People therefore speak of the “Landi spirit”.
16240.m: The Landi of 1939 became a symbol of Switzerland’s will to stand firm.

16241.q: What is the name of the form of government in which the Federal Council governed largely without parliament during the war, using extraordinary powers?
16241.e: The Federal Assembly gave the Federal Council extraordinary full powers on 30 August 1939. After the popular initiative “Return to direct democracy” was accepted in 1949, the regime of full powers was completely lifted by the end of 1952.
16241.m: During the war the Federal Council governed with extraordinary full powers.

16242.q: What did General Guisan do on the Rütli on 25 July 1940?
a: He called on the officers to resist and presented the Réduit
He signed a treaty with Germany
He announced his resignation as general
He announced the end of active service
16242.e: At the Rütli Report, Guisan gathered the senior officers at the symbolic place. He made it clear that Switzerland would defend itself, if necessary from the Alpine Réduit.
16242.m: With the Rütli Report in 1940, Guisan strengthened the will to resist.

16243.q: Shortly before which event was Henri Guisan elected general in 1939?
a: Before the German attack on Poland
Before the attack on Pearl Harbor
16243.e: The United Federal Assembly elected Guisan on 30 August 1939, two days before the German attack on Poland.
16243.m: Guisan became general shortly before the war began in 1939.

16244.q: Which body elects the general in Switzerland?
16244.e: The general is elected jointly by the National Council and the Council of States, that is, by the United Federal Assembly. This is also what happened with Henri Guisan in 1939.
16244.m: The general is elected by the United Federal Assembly.

16245.q: What was the result of Henri Guisan’s election as general in 1939?
a: A clear majority of the Federal Assembly
A narrow lead of one vote
Drawing lots because of a tie
No election, appointment by the Federal Council
16245.e: Guisan received 204 of 229 valid votes. The clear result showed broad support in parliament.
16245.m: Guisan was elected general with a clear majority.

16246.q: What is special about the rank of “general” in the Swiss Army?
a: A general is only elected in times of serious threat or war
The general is elected directly by the people
The general is also President of the Confederation
16246.e: In peacetime the Swiss Army has no general. Only when a large number of troops are called up to protect the country does the Federal Assembly elect a commander-in-chief.
16246.m: Switzerland only has a general in times of serious threat.

16247.q: Which canton did Henri Guisan come from?
16247.e: Guisan was born in Mézières in the canton of Vaud in 1874. He later lived on the Verte Rive estate in Pully.

16248.q: What job did Guisan do before his military career?
16248.e: Guisan worked as a farmer, among other places in Chesalles-sur-Oron, and took over an estate in Pully in 1902. As was usual in the militia army, he pursued a military career alongside.
16248.m: Guisan was a farmer and a militia officer.

16249.q: After which event did Guisan hold the Rütli Report in July 1940?
a: After the end of the war
After the Allied landings in Normandy
After the German attack on the Soviet Union
16249.e: After the fall of France, Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers. On 25 July 1940 Guisan wanted to strengthen the army’s will to resist.
16249.m: The Rütli Report followed the fall of France in 1940.

16250.q: What did Guisan announce at the Rütli Report?
a: The will to resist and the new Réduit strategy
16250.e: Guisan called for resistance and announced defence in the Alpine region, the Réduit. The report was seen as a counterpart to Pilet-Golaz’s speech, which was felt to be timid.
16250.m: On the Rütli in 1940, Guisan called for resistance.

16251.q: Why did Guisan choose the Rütli meadow for his report in 1940?
a: It is the symbolic place of the founding tradition of the Confederation
It was at the centre of the Gotthard fortress
He had started his military service there himself
16251.e: According to tradition, which is partly legend, the first Confederates swore their alliance on the Rütli. The place was meant to express unity and the will to be free.
16251.m: Guisan used the Rütli as a symbol of freedom and unity.

16252.q: When did Henri Guisan’s time as general end?
a: After the end of the war in summer 1945
In 1943 after the landings in Italy
16252.e: Active service ended on 20 August 1945. With that, Guisan stepped down as general.
16252.m: Guisan’s time as general ended in August 1945.

16253.q: How does Switzerland still remember General Henri Guisan today?
a: With monuments and streets and squares named after him
With a national holiday of its own
With his picture on all coins
With a permanent seat for his family on the Federal Council
16253.e: Guisan died in 1960, and his funeral was a great national event. Many places have an Avenue Général-Guisan or a General-Guisan-Quai.
16253.m: Many streets and monuments recall General Guisan.

16254.q: How does more recent historical research judge Guisan’s role?
a: It questions the myth that he alone saved Switzerland from occupation
It considers him a supporter of Nazism
It denies that he was ever general
It sees him as the founder of neutrality
16254.e: People who lived through the time often saw Guisan as the saviour of the country. More recent historians also stress other factors such as economic relations and put the myth around him into perspective.
16254.m: Research today sees Guisan’s role in a more nuanced way than before.

16255.q: Which troops did the Federal Council call up at the end of August 1939, even before general mobilisation?
16255.e: On 28 August 1939 the Federal Council ordered the mobilisation of the border guard with about 80,000 men; the border troops reported on 29 August. General mobilisation only followed after the German attack on Poland.
16255.m: The border troops were the first to be called up at the end of August 1939.

16256.q: When did the general war mobilisation of the Swiss Army begin?
16256.e: After the German attack on Poland on 1 September 1939, the whole army was called up. The first day of mobilisation was 2 September 1939, and a second general mobilisation followed on 10 May 1940.

16257.q: Roughly how many soldiers were called up in the general mobilisation of 1939?
16257.e: In the general mobilisation about 430,000 combat troops reported for duty. Over the whole war, about 450,000 soldiers were called up.
16257.m: About 430,000 soldiers reported for duty in the general mobilisation of 1939.

16258.q: Which group also supported the regular troops in large numbers in 1939?
a: about 200,000 men in the auxiliary service
16258.e: In the general mobilisation, about 200,000 men liable for auxiliary service reported alongside the combat troops; over the whole war about 250,000 were called up. They took on guard, transport and medical duties, for example.
16258.m: Men in the auxiliary service supported the army during active service.

16259.q: What was the organisation founded in 1939 in which at times over 20,000 women served the army voluntarily?
16259.e: In the Women’s Auxiliary Service, women worked in administration, communications, transport, kitchens or aircraft spotting, for example. At the end of 1941 about 23,000 women were serving, which freed men for duty with the troops.
16259.m: In the Women’s Auxiliary Service, women served the army voluntarily.

16260.q: On average, how many days of active service did Swiss soldiers do in the Second World War?
16260.e: On average the soldiers did about 800 days of service. This is why people speak of the “active service generation”.
16260.m: The active service generation did about 800 days of service on average.

16261.q: Which social scheme replaced soldiers’ lost wages from 1940 and is seen as paving the way for the AHV?
a: The Wage and Earnings Compensation Scheme
16261.e: Unlike in the First World War, soldiers received compensation financed by wage contributions from employers and employees as well as public money. This model influenced the financing of the AHV in 1948.
16261.m: The wage compensation scheme supported soldiers’ families and was a model for the AHV.

16262.q: How were troop numbers mostly organised from autumn 1940?
a: Through about 80 partial mobilisations with troops taking turns
Through permanent full mobilisation of all troops
Through a professional army of 20,000 men
16262.e: After the move into the Réduit, the number of troops called up fell sharply. Throughout active service there were about 80 partial mobilisations, so that industry and agriculture kept enough workers.
16262.m: From 1940 troops took turns in partial mobilisations.

16263.q: How did the air battles between the Swiss Air Force and the German Luftwaffe go in May and June 1940?
a: 11 German aircraft were shot down, 3 Swiss were lost
Switzerland lost all its fighter aircraft
16263.e: During violations of Swiss airspace, the Air Force shot down 11 German aircraft and lost 3 of its own. Germany responded with a sharp protest.
16263.m: The air battles of 1940 led to a crisis with Germany.

16264.q: What did General Guisan order the Air Force to do on 20 June 1940 under German pressure?
a: He banned it from air combat over Switzerland
He ordered attacks on German airfields
He placed it under the French army
16264.e: After sharp German protests about the air battles, Guisan banned the Air Force from air combat over Switzerland. After that, mainly the anti-aircraft defence protected the airspace; the ban lasted until the end of 1943.
16264.m: From June 1940, under German pressure, the Air Force was no longer allowed to fight in the air.

16265.q: How many Swiss soldiers died during active service from 1939 to 1945?
16265.e: About 4,050 soldiers died during active service, mainly through accidents and illness. Switzerland was not drawn into fighting on the ground.
16265.m: Even without war in the country, about 4,000 soldiers died during active service.

16266.q: How many Swiss sentenced to death for treason were executed in the Second World War?
16266.e: In 1940 the death penalty in military criminal law was extended to espionage and treason. Of 33 death sentences, 17 were carried out.
16266.m: In the Second World War, 17 traitors were executed in Switzerland.

16267.q: Which three fortress areas formed the cornerstones of the Réduit?
16267.e: Sargans in the east, St-Maurice in the west and the Gotthard in the centre were the most important fortresses. The Gotthard was considered the heart.
16267.m: Sargans, St-Maurice and Gotthard were the cornerstones of the Réduit.

16268.q: Where did General Guisan explain the Réduit strategy to senior officers on 25 July 1940?
a: In the Federal Palace in Bern
16268.e: At the Rütli Report, Guisan gathered the commanders at the symbolic place of the Confederation. He called for resistance and explained the withdrawal into the Réduit.
16268.m: At the Rütli Report in 1940, Guisan explained the Réduit strategy.

16269.q: Which general led the Swiss Army when it moved into the Réduit in 1940?
16269.e: Henri Guisan was general of the Swiss Army from 1939 to 1945. In 1940 he pushed through the Réduit strategy.
16269.m: General Henri Guisan led the army into the Réduit.

16270.q: Roughly what part of Swiss territory lay within the Réduit?
16270.e: The Réduit covered about a quarter of the country, mainly mountain areas. The densely populated regions lay outside it.
16270.m: The Réduit covered about a quarter of Switzerland.

16271.q: Which criticism of the Réduit is made most often?
a: The Central Plateau, with most of the population, would largely have been given up
It was too close to the German border
It was far too small for the army
It was never manned with troops
16271.e: In an attack, the army would hardly have defended the cities and economic centres of the Central Plateau. The civilian population would largely have been left unprotected.
16271.m: Under the Réduit plan, the Central Plateau would hardly have been defended.

16272.q: What idea was the effect of the Réduit mainly based on?
a: Deterrence through a long and costly mountain war
The superiority of the Swiss Air Force
16272.e: The Réduit was meant to make an attack so costly that it would not be worth it. Such a strategy is called dissuasion.
16272.m: The Réduit was meant to deter an attacker.

16273.q: Which means of pressure on the Axis powers was linked to the Réduit?
a: The prepared destruction of the Alpine crossings such as Gotthard and Simplon
The threat of an alliance with the Soviet Union
16273.e: In case of an attack, tunnels, bridges and railway lines were to be blown up. Germany and Italy would then have lost the important north-south link through the Alps.
16273.m: The Alpine transit routes were an important means of pressure for Switzerland.

16274.q: What was the name of the German plan for an attack on Switzerland from summer 1940?
16274.e: After the victory over France, the German general staff drew up attack plans, called “Tannenbaum” (fir tree) from September 1940. Italian troops were to attack from the south.
16274.m: With Operation Tannenbaum, Germany planned an attack on Switzerland in 1940.

16275.q: Which reasons helped ensure that Operation Tannenbaum was not carried out?
a: Other war aims and German interest in Swiss industry and Alpine transit
A peace treaty between Germany and Switzerland
16275.e: The Wehrmacht concentrated on other aims such as the planned invasion of Great Britain. In addition, Swiss deliveries and the Gotthard transit were useful to Germany.
16275.m: Economic interests helped ensure that Switzerland was not attacked.

16276.q: Which British military commander called the Réduit impractical nonsense?
16276.e: Montgomery thought the strategy made no military sense, because it gave up the Central Plateau. Opinions on the Réduit are still divided today.

16277.q: Until when were the course and boundaries of the Réduit kept secret?
a: Until the end of the war in 1945
16277.e: The installations remained important during the Cold War and were kept secret. Especially since the army reform of 1995 many have been dismantled, and some are museums today.
16277.m: The Réduit remained secret into the 1990s.

16278.q: What did the federal government want to prevent with a purchase ban on sugar, fats and grain shortly before the war began in 1939?
16278.e: With the purchase ban of 29 August 1939, important foods could temporarily no longer be sold. This was meant to prevent panic buying, and regular rationing followed shortly afterwards.
16278.m: A purchase ban prevented panic buying in 1939.

16279.q: From when were basic foods such as sugar, pulses and fats officially rationed?
16279.e: Rationing with ration cards began at the end of October 1939. Without ration coupons you could no longer buy these goods.

16280.q: Why was Switzerland better prepared for supplies in the Second World War than in the First?
a: The war economy system was ready to operate as early as 1938
It had enough oil wells of its own
It got all its food free from the USA
16280.e: In the First World War rationing only began hesitantly in 1917, and in 1918 there was hardship. Learning from this, the federal government prepared the war economy early.
16280.m: Learning from the mistakes of the First World War, Switzerland prepared early.

16281.q: How many meat-free days per week applied from May 1941?
16281.e: From May 1941 there were two meat-free days per week. From March 1942 meat was also rationed.
16281.m: From 1941 there were two meat-free days per week.

16282.q: From when was bread rationed in Switzerland?
16282.e: From July 1940 bread could no longer be sold fresh, so that people would eat less. From October 1942 it was rationed.
16282.m: Bread was rationed in Switzerland from 1942.

16283.q: What did you need in Switzerland in the Second World War, as well as money, to buy sugar or fat?
a: A voucher from the municipality for every purchase
16283.e: Every person received monthly ration cards with coupons. Without the right coupons you could not buy rationed goods, even if you had enough money.
16283.m: Rationed goods were only available for coupons and money.

16284.q: What daily calorie requirement for an adult did wartime nutrition plans assume?
16284.e: The planners assumed 2,160 calories per day. From 1943 this figure was reached only in a few months; things were tightest in the post-war period.
16284.m: Rationing assumed about 2,160 calories per day.

16285.q: When were the last foods released from rationing?
16285.e: Rationing was gradually lifted from spring 1945. The last foods only became freely available again in July 1948.

16286.q: By which name is the wartime programme to expand arable farming known?
16286.e: The agronomist Friedrich Traugott Wahlen drew up the plan to increase self-sufficiency. He later became a Federal Councillor.
16286.m: With the Wahlen Plan, Switzerland grew more of its own food during the war.

16287.q: Where in Zurich were potatoes planted in the middle of the city during the Cultivation Battle?
a: In the courtyard of the National Museum
16287.e: For the Wahlen Plan, parks, sports grounds and squares in the cities were also planted. The picture of potatoes on the Sechseläutenplatz became a symbol of the Cultivation Battle.
16287.m: During the Cultivation Battle, potatoes even grew on the Sechseläutenplatz.

16288.q: How did Switzerland’s open arable land change from 1940 to 1945?
16288.e: The arable land almost doubled. Parks and sports grounds were also planted, but the planned target of 500,000 hectares was not reached.
16288.m: The Cultivation Battle almost doubled the arable land.

16289.q: Roughly how did the degree of self-sufficiency in food change because of the Cultivation Battle?
a: From about 52 to about 70 per cent
From about 10 to about 100 per cent
From about 90 to about 50 per cent
From about 30 to about 40 per cent
16289.e: Self-sufficiency rose from about 52 per cent in 1939/1940 to about 70 per cent in 1945. Figures vary depending on the estimate, but Switzerland remained dependent on imports.
16289.m: The Cultivation Battle clearly increased self-sufficiency, but not completely.

16290.q: What was the so-called J stamp?
a: A mark in the passports of German Jews that made them identifiable at the border
A stamp on Swiss ration cards
A visa for Jewish refugees to the USA
16290.e: From October 1938 the passports of German Jews were marked with a “J”. This was based on an agreement between Germany and Switzerland.
16290.m: The J stamp made Jewish travellers immediately identifiable at the border.

16291.q: Which independent commission of experts examined Switzerland’s role in the Second World War in the 1990s?
16291.e: The Independent Commission of Experts Switzerland Second World War, led by the historian Jean-François Bergier, examined refugee policy among other things from 1996. Its final report appeared in 2002.
16291.m: The Bergier Commission examined Switzerland’s role in the Second World War.

16292.q: According to more recent research, why did the German authorities propose the J stamp in 1938?
a: To avoid a general visa requirement for Germans in Switzerland
To make it easier for Jews to emigrate
16292.e: Switzerland threatened a visa requirement for all Germans. Germany wanted to avoid this and offered to mark Jewish passports, which the Federal Council approved on 4 October 1938.
16292.m: Switzerland agreed to the J stamp so as not to have to introduce a general visa requirement.

16293.q: What position did Heinrich Rothmund hold during the Second World War?
a: Head of the Police Division in the Department of Justice and Police
Chief of the General Staff of the army
16293.e: Rothmund led the Police Division, including the aliens police, and shaped the restrictive refugee policy. Historians criticise his attitude as antisemitic.
16293.m: As head of police, Heinrich Rothmund shaped refugee policy.

16294.q: What did the directive of 13 August 1942 order?
a: Closing the border to refugees who fled only “for reasons of race”
Opening the border to children from France
16294.e: Refugees “only for reasons of race”, meaning mainly Jews, were not considered political refugees and were to be turned away. This happened when deportations to the extermination camps were already under way.
16294.m: With the border closure of 1942, Jewish refugees were turned away.

16295.q: How did the Federal Council react shortly after the border closure of August 1942?
a: After public protests it temporarily eased the turning back of refugees
It closed the border to diplomats too
16295.e: The directive caused fierce protests among the population, churches and press. On 23 August 1942 the turning back of refugees was temporarily eased.
16295.m: Public protests led to an easing of the border closure in 1942.

16296.q: Which slogan is often used to sum up Switzerland’s harsh refugee policy in the Second World War?
16296.e: In 1942 Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger compared Switzerland to a small lifeboat that could not take everyone. This became the well-known slogan “The boat is full”.
16296.m: “The boat is full” stands for the refugee policy of turning people away during the war.

16297.q: Roughly how many people did Switzerland host in total during the war, including military internees?
16297.e: They included over 100,000 interned soldiers, refugees at the border, children on recovery stays and civilian refugees. Their stay was often limited in time.
16297.m: During the war Switzerland at times hosted about 300,000 people seeking protection.

16298.q: Roughly how many civilian refugees did Switzerland take in during the Second World War?
16298.e: About 51,000 civilian refugees were taken in, about 21,000 of them Jews. At the same time, many were turned away at the border.
16298.m: About 51,000 civilian refugees found refuge in Switzerland.

16299.q: Why do the estimates of the number of refugees turned away vary so widely?
a: Because of incomplete records and different ways of counting
Because Switzerland had no border controls
Because all records are published and clear
Because only refugees from Italy were counted
16299.e: Depending on the study, the estimates differ many times over. Repeated attempts by the same person, destroyed records and different definitions make an exact number difficult.
16299.m: With refugee numbers, you must check sources and ways of counting critically.

16300.q: How did the St Gallen police captain Paul Grüninger help refugees in 1938 and 1939?
a: He backdated entries so that refugees could stay legally
He hid refugees in the Réduit
He issued letters of protection in Budapest
16300.e: Grüninger enabled several hundred refugees to enter by backdating entry dates or falsifying documents. He was dismissed in 1939 and fined in 1940.
16300.m: Paul Grüninger saved refugees by getting round the rules.

16301.q: When was Paul Grüninger acquitted by a court?
a: In 1945, shortly after the end of the war
In 1971, while he was still alive
16301.e: The St Gallen district court overturned the verdict in 1995. Yad Vashem had already honoured him as “Righteous Among the Nations” in 1971.
16301.m: Paul Grüninger was only fully rehabilitated in 1995.

16302.q: Roughly how many Hungarian Jews did the Swiss vice-consul Carl Lutz save in Budapest in 1944?
16302.e: Lutz issued letters of protection that saved people from deportation. In 1964 Yad Vashem honoured him as “Righteous Among the Nations”.
16302.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest with letters of protection.

16303.q: Which agreement did Switzerland conclude with Germany on 9 August 1940?
16303.e: The economic agreement secured supplies of coal and raw materials. In return Switzerland supplied industrial goods, including armaments, to the Axis powers.
16303.m: From 1940 an economic agreement tied Switzerland closely to Germany.

16304.q: What is meant by clearing in trade between Switzerland and Germany?
a: Settling payments through state offices without direct payment in foreign currency
16304.e: In clearing, exports and imports were offset against each other through state accounts. Swiss clearing credits allowed Germany to obtain goods before it paid.
16304.m: In clearing, payments between states were offset against each other.

16305.q: What did Switzerland get in return for the clearing credit to Germany of February 1941?
16305.e: Switzerland granted a credit of 165 million francs. In return it was promised 150,000 tonnes of coal per month.
16305.m: Coal from Germany was vital for the Swiss economy.

16306.q: According to the Bergier Commission, how much gold did the Swiss National Bank buy from the Reichsbank between 1940 and 1945?
16306.e: The National Bank bought gold worth about 1.23 billion francs, and commercial banks about 100 million. Part of it was looted gold.
16306.m: During the war the National Bank bought over a billion francs’ worth of gold from the Reichsbank.

16307.q: Why was the Swiss franc important to Germany during the war?
a: It was freely convertible and was used to buy raw materials such as tungsten and oil
It was the official currency throughout Europe
It was tied to the Reichsmark
16307.e: With francs, Germany could buy raw materials in neutral countries such as Portugal or Spain. Gold was therefore exchanged for francs in Switzerland.
16307.m: Germany needed freely convertible francs to buy raw materials.

16308.q: Which goods were among the most important Swiss exports in the Second World War?
a: Machine tools, watches and precision parts
16308.e: Precision goods such as machine tools, watches and jewel bearings were in demand, also for fuses and aiming devices. Electricity and dairy products were added to this.
16308.m: Swiss precision goods were in great demand during the war.

16309.q: When did Switzerland stop exporting war material?
16309.e: Under Allied pressure, the Federal Council banned the export of war material in autumn 1944. Before that, Switzerland had supplied mainly the Axis powers.
16309.m: Switzerland only stopped exporting war material in 1944.

16310.q: What was the largest share of German armaments production that Swiss arms deliveries ever reached?
16310.e: The deliveries never reached more than about one per cent of German production. For some individual goods, however, they could still be significant.
16310.m: Compared with German production, Swiss arms deliveries were small.

16311.q: Which transport link through Switzerland was particularly important for Germany and Italy?
a: The Gotthard Railway as a north-south transit route
16311.e: Goods traffic between the Axis partners ran over the Alpine railways, especially coal to Italy. War material and troops could not be transported for reasons of neutrality.
16311.m: The Gotthard transit was of great importance to the Axis powers.

16312.q: How did the Allies punish Swiss companies that traded with Germany?
a: By excluding them from the ICRC
By having the Federal Council seize them
16312.e: Companies on blacklists were boycotted by the Allies. The lists were only lifted with the Washington Agreement of 1946.
16312.m: The Allies boycotted companies by putting them on blacklists.

16313.q: What measure did the USA take against Swiss assets in 1941?
a: It froze Swiss assets, including a large part of the gold reserves
It introduced the franc as a second currency
16313.e: About three quarters of the Swiss gold reserves were held in the USA and were frozen. Only the Washington Agreement released them.
16313.m: During the war the USA froze Swiss assets.

16314.q: What sum did Switzerland pay the Allies under the Washington Agreement of 25 May 1946?
16314.e: The payment was made as compensation for the gold purchases, but expressly without accepting any legal obligation. In return, Swiss assets were released.
16314.m: Under the Washington Agreement, Switzerland paid 250 million francs in 1946.

16315.q: What did the Washington Agreement of 1946 decide about German assets in Switzerland?
a: They were to be sold off and the proceeds shared between the Allies and Switzerland
They were to be returned to Germany
They went entirely to the Soviet Union
16315.e: One half was to go to the Allies for rebuilding Europe, the other to Switzerland for its claims against Germany.
16315.m: After 1946, German assets in Switzerland were to be shared.

16316.q: What is the official name of the Bergier Commission?
a: Independent Commission of Experts Switzerland Second World War
16316.e: The commission is named after its president Bergier; officially it is called the Independent Commission of Experts (ICE). It examined Switzerland’s role in the Second World War.
16316.m: The Bergier Commission’s official name is the Independent Commission of Experts.

16317.q: When did the Federal Council set up the Bergier Commission?
16317.e: It was based on a federal decree passed by parliament in December 1996. The Federal Council set up the commission on 19 December 1996.
16317.m: The Bergier Commission was created at the end of 1996.

16318.q: What was the profession of Jean-François Bergier, the president of the Independent Commission of Experts?
16318.e: Bergier taught economic history at ETH Zurich. The commission is named after him.
16318.m: Jean-François Bergier was an economic historian at ETH Zurich.

16319.q: Why did the Bergier Commission also include historians from abroad?
a: To strengthen its independence and credibility
Because there were too few historians in Switzerland
Because the records were only available in English
16319.e: The commission had an international membership, including Saul Friedländer and Harold James. That way, nobody could accuse it of going easy on Switzerland.
16319.m: The Bergier Commission had international members so that it would be credible.

16320.q: Which debate in the 1990s was the main trigger for setting up the Bergier Commission?
a: The debate about dormant assets of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks
The dispute about joining the EEA
The debate about joining the UN
A dispute about abolishing the army
16320.e: The World Jewish Congress and lawsuits in the USA accused Swiss banks of holding back assets belonging to Holocaust victims. The international pressure led to a reappraisal of the past.
16320.m: The dormant assets triggered the reappraisal of the past in the 1990s.

16321.q: Which special right did the Bergier Commission get for its research?
a: Access to the archives of private companies such as banks and insurers
The right to overturn court verdicts
16321.e: The companies had to open their archives and were not allowed to destroy records from the period. This was unusual for historical research in Switzerland.
16321.m: The commission was also allowed to study the archives of private companies.

16322.q: Apart from looted gold and banking business, what else did the Bergier Commission examine?
a: Neutrality in the First World War
The founding of the federal state in 1848
16322.e: Its mandate was extended, and the budget rose from 5 to 22 million francs. The commission also examined how Switzerland dealt with refugees.
16322.m: The Bergier Commission also examined refugee policy.

16323.q: When did the Bergier Commission present its final report?
16323.e: The final report is called “Switzerland, National Socialism and the Second World War”. Many individual studies had appeared before it.
16323.m: The Bergier final report appeared in 2002.

16324.q: According to the Bergier Commission, where did part of the looted gold that reached Switzerland come from?
a: From the central banks of occupied countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, and from persecuted people
16324.e: The Reichsbank had stolen gold from the central banks of occupied states and from private individuals. Gold from victims of the extermination policy also ended up in its stocks.
16324.m: Part of the gold sold to Switzerland was looted gold.

16325.q: According to the Bergier Commission’s final report, how many refugees did Switzerland turn away or deport during the war?
16325.e: The commission gave a figure of over 20,000 refusals. Other studies arrive at lower or higher numbers, which shows how difficult the sources are.
16325.m: According to the Bergier Commission, Switzerland turned away over 20,000 refugees.

16326.q: What did the security guard Christoph Meili do at the Union Bank of Switzerland in January 1997?
a: He saved bank records from being destroyed
He published account data on the internet
He set up a foundation for refugees
16326.e: Meili took away records that were to be shredded, even though destroying them had been banned since December 1996. The case increased international pressure on the banks.
16326.m: In 1997 Christoph Meili saved records from the shredder.

16327.q: Which sum did the major Swiss banks agree to in the global settlement of 13 August 1998?
16327.e: The settlement ended class actions in the USA. The money was intended for Holocaust survivors and their descendants.
16327.m: In the 1998 global settlement the banks paid 1.25 billion dollars.

16328.q: Which picture of Switzerland in the Second World War did the Bergier Commission call into question?
a: That Switzerland was spared only thanks to its army and neutrality
That Switzerland took an active part in the war
That Switzerland was occupied by Germany
That Switzerland took in no refugees
16328.e: The commission showed that economic relations, gold deals and a harsh refugee policy also played a role. The Bonjour Report from 1965 onwards had already partly corrected this picture.
16328.m: The Bergier Commission showed that Switzerland was not spared thanks to the army alone.

16725.q: Apart from pensioners, who else receives AHV pensions?
16725.e: AHV stands for old-age and survivors’ insurance. Survivors are the widows, widowers and orphans of a person who has died. Unemployed people are covered by unemployment insurance.
16725.m: The AHV also pays pensions to widows, widowers and orphans.

16726.q: With what share of yes votes was the AHV Act accepted in 1947?
16726.e: The AHV Act received 80 per cent yes votes with a turnout of 79.7 per cent. That was a very clear result.
16726.m: The AHV was accepted in 1947 with about four fifths of the votes.

16728.q: Which vote in 1925 created the constitutional basis for the AHV?
