17330.e: Pluto used to be counted as a planet. Since 2006 it has been classed as a dwarf planet, because it is small and shares its orbit with many other bodies.

17331.q: What is the path called on which a planet circles the Sun?
17331.e: Every planet moves along its orbit around the Sun. This path is almost circular.
17331.m: A planet circles the Sun in an orbit.

17332.q: Which planet do we live on?
17332.e: We humans live on Earth. To this day we know of no other planet with life.
17332.m: We live on the planet Earth.

17333.q: Can you see some planets in the sky without a telescope?
17333.e: Some planets are so bright that you can see them with the naked eye. They look like bright stars but hardly twinkle.
17333.m: You can see some planets in the sky without a telescope.

17334.q: Which planet is the smallest in our solar system?
17334.e: Mercury is not much bigger than our Moon. No other planet is as small.

17335.q: How many moons does Mercury have?
17335.e: Mercury has no moon. It travels round the Sun all on its own.

17336.q: What does Mercury’s surface look like?
17336.e: Many lumps of rock have crashed into Mercury. That is why, like our Moon, it is covered in craters.
17336.m: Mercury’s surface is full of craters.

17337.q: How long does Mercury take to go once round the Sun?
17337.e: Mercury is fast and has a short path. It goes once round the Sun in about 88 days.
17337.m: A year on Mercury lasts only about 88 days.

17338.q: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
17338.e: On Venus it is over 400 degrees. Its thick layer of air holds in the heat like a blanket.

17339.q: What is Venus called when it shines brightly early in the morning?
17339.e: After the Sun and the Moon, Venus is the brightest light in the sky. In the morning it is called the morning star, in the evening the evening star.
17339.m: Venus is also called the morning star.

17340.q: Counting from the Sun, which number planet is Venus?
17340.e: Only one planet circles closer to the Sun than Venus. So it is the second planet.
17340.m: Venus is the second planet from the Sun.

17341.e: Venus is completely surrounded by thick clouds. That is why you cannot see its ground from outside.

17342.e: Venus was the ancient Romans’ goddess of love and beauty. The bright, beautiful planet was given her name.
17342.m: Venus bears the name of the Roman goddess of love.

17343.q: Which planet is called the “Red Planet”?
17343.e: Mars shines reddish in the sky. That is why it is called the Red Planet.

17344.e: There is a lot of iron in the ground on Mars, and it has rusted. This rusty dust makes the planet red.

17345.q: How many moons does Mars have?
17345.e: Mars has two small moons. They are called Phobos and Deimos.

17346.q: What do researchers use to explore the surface of Mars?
17346.e: Remote-controlled robot vehicles called rovers drive around on Mars. They take photos and examine rocks.

17347.q: What is the name of the giant volcano on Mars?
17347.e: Olympus Mons is one of the highest mountains in the whole solar system. It is much higher than any mountain on Earth.
17347.m: The giant volcano Olympus Mons is on Mars.

17348.q: What is the Great Red Spot on Jupiter?
17348.e: The Great Red Spot is a swirling storm. It is bigger than the whole Earth and has been observed for almost 150 years.
17348.m: The Great Red Spot is a giant storm.

17349.q: What is the name of Jupiter’s largest moon?
17349.e: Ganymede is the largest moon in the whole solar system. It is even bigger than the planet Mercury.
17349.m: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system.

17350.q: Counting from the Sun, which number planet is Jupiter?
17350.e: Four smaller planets circle closer to the Sun than Jupiter. So it is the fifth planet.
17350.m: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun.

17351.q: Roughly how long is a day on Jupiter?
17351.e: Jupiter spins very fast. One turn takes just under 10 hours.
17351.m: A day on Jupiter is very short.

17352.q: Which planet is famous for its large, bright rings?
17352.e: Saturn has the most beautiful and brightest rings of all the planets. You can see them even with a small telescope.
17352.m: Saturn is the planet with the famous rings.

17353.q: What are Saturn’s rings made of?
17353.e: The rings are made of countless chunks. Most are made of ice, and some also contain rock.
17353.m: Saturn’s rings are mainly made of ice.

17354.q: Counting from the Sun, which number planet is Saturn?
17354.e: Five planets circle closer to the Sun than Saturn. So it is the sixth planet.
17354.m: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun.

17355.q: What is the name of Saturn’s largest moon?
17355.e: Titan is Saturn’s largest moon. It is the only moon with a thick layer of air.

17356.q: What would happen to Saturn in a giant bathtub?
17356.e: Saturn is huge, but very light for its size. It is lighter than the same amount of water and would therefore float.
17356.m: Saturn is lighter than the same amount of water.

17357.q: What is special about the way Uranus spins?
a: It lies almost on its side
It does not spin at all
17357.e: Uranus is tilted a lot. So it rolls around the Sun almost lying down.
17357.m: Uranus spins almost lying on its side.

17358.e: A gas in its layer of air makes Uranus shine blue-green. This gas is called methane.

17359.q: What was used to discover Uranus in 1781?
17359.e: The scientist William Herschel discovered Uranus with his telescope. It was the first planet to be found with a telescope.
17359.m: Uranus was discovered with a telescope.

17360.q: Counting from the Sun, which number planet is Uranus?
17360.e: Six planets circle closer to the Sun than Uranus. So it is the seventh planet.
17360.m: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun.

17361.q: Does Uranus take longer than the Earth to go once round the Sun?
17361.e: Uranus is very far from the Sun and has a long way to go. One trip round takes about 84 Earth years.
17361.m: A year on Uranus lasts much longer than a year on Earth.

17362.q: Which planet is furthest from the Sun?
17362.e: Neptune is the outermost planet of our solar system. It is icy cold and dark there.

17363.q: On which planet do the strongest winds blow?
17363.e: On Neptune, storms rage at over 2000 kilometres per hour. That is more than twice as fast as a passenger plane.
17363.m: The strongest winds blow on Neptune.

17364.e: Neptune shimmers bluish, much like Uranus. The gas methane in its layer of air gives it this colour.

17365.q: Which space probe is the only one to have flown past Neptune?
17365.e: The space probe Voyager 2 flew past Neptune in 1989. It sent the first close-up pictures back to Earth.

17366.e: Neptune was the ancient Romans’ god of the sea. The blue planet is a reminder of the sea.
17366.m: Neptune bears the name of the Roman god of the sea.

17367.q: How many planets belong to our solar system?
17367.e: Our solar system has eight planets. The Earth is one of them.
17367.m: Our solar system has eight planets.

17368.q: What is at the centre of our solar system?
17368.e: All the planets travel around the Sun. That is why it is called the solar system.
17368.m: The Sun is at the centre of the solar system.

17369.q: What does a planet trail, like the one on the Uetliberg, show?
a: The phases of the Moon over a year
17369.e: On a planet trail, the Sun and planets are set up much smaller than in real life. As you walk, you notice how far apart the planets are.
17369.m: On a planet trail you walk through a scaled-down solar system.

17370.q: How old is our solar system?
a: Ancient, much older than the dinosaurs
About as old as the pyramids
17370.e: The Sun and the planets formed an unimaginably long time ago from a huge cloud of gas and dust. That was long before there were dinosaurs.
17370.m: Our solar system is much older than the dinosaurs.

17371.q: How long does the Earth take to spin once around itself?
17371.e: One complete turn of the Earth takes about 24 hours. That is exactly one day and one night.
17371.m: The Earth spins once around itself in about 24 hours.

17372.q: In which direction does the Sun rise in the morning?
17372.e: The Earth spins in such a way that the Sun appears in the east for us. In the evening it sets in the west.
17372.m: The Sun rises in the east.

17373.q: When it is midday in Switzerland, roughly what time is it in New Zealand?
17373.e: New Zealand is almost on the other side of the Earth. When the Sun is high in the sky here, it is about midnight there.
17373.m: On the other side of the Earth it is night when it is day here.

17374.q: In which month are the days longest in Switzerland?
17374.e: Around 21 June, the Sun is in our sky for the longest time. This day is called the summer solstice.
17374.m: In June our days are the longest.

a: Because the Earth's axis is tilted
Because the Earth is sometimes closer to the Sun
Because the Sun sometimes burns more strongly
17375.e: The Earth is tilted. That is why sometimes the northern half and sometimes the southern half of the Earth gets more sunlight.
17375.m: The tilted axis of the Earth causes the seasons.

17376.q: When it is summer here, which season is it in Australia?
17376.e: Australia is in the southern half of the Earth. There the seasons are exactly the other way round from ours.
17376.m: In Australia the seasons are reversed.

17377.q: In which month does spring begin here?
17377.e: Spring begins around 20 March. After that, the days become longer than the nights.

17378.q: What is the day called when day and night are about the same length?
17378.e: Twice a year, in spring and in autumn, day and night last almost the same length of time. This day is called the equinox.
17378.m: At the equinox, day and night are almost the same length.

17379.e: Long ago, people joined bright stars together with imaginary lines. That is how pictures such as animals or heroes came about.
17379.m: A constellation is a picture made of stars.

17380.q: Which group of seven bright stars looks like a plough or a cart with a long handle?
17380.e: Seven bright stars form the Plough. It is part of the constellation of the Great Bear and can be seen all year round from here.
17380.m: The Plough is made up of seven bright stars.

17381.q: Which star shows almost exactly where north is?
17381.e: The Pole Star is almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole. If you look at it, you are facing north.
17381.m: The Pole Star shows the way north.

17382.q: Which constellation shows a hunter with a belt of three stars?
17382.e: Orion is a hunter in the sky. Three bright stars in a row make up his belt. You can see him well in winter.
17382.m: Orion is the sky hunter with the belt of stars.

17383.q: When can you see constellations best?
a: On a night with thick clouds
In the early evening when it rains
17383.e: Stars shine only faintly. That is why you see constellations best when it is dark and there are no clouds in the sky.
17383.m: Constellations are best seen on clear, dark nights.

17384.q: Who was the first person in space in 1961?
17384.e: Yuri Gagarin from the Soviet Union flew once around the Earth on 12 April 1961. He was the first person in space.
17384.m: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space.

17385.q: Who was the first Swiss person in space?
17385.e: Claude Nicollier from Vevey flew into space on a Space Shuttle in 1992. Later he also helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope.
17385.m: Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss person in space.

17386.q: What are the clothes called that protect astronauts outside in space?
17386.e: A spacesuit provides air to breathe and protects against cold, heat and radiation. It is like a small spacecraft you can wear.
17386.m: The spacesuit protects astronauts in space.

17387.q: Why do astronauts float in the space station?
17387.e: The space station and the astronauts are constantly falling around the Earth together. That is why they do not feel their weight and float.

17388.q: Who was the first woman in space?
17388.e: Valentina Tereshkova from the Soviet Union flew into space in 1963. She orbited the Earth for almost three days.
17388.m: Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space.

17389.q: What does a rocket push out downwards so that it flies upwards?
17389.e: Fuel burns in the engine. The hot gases rush downwards and push the rocket upwards.
17389.m: Hot gases push a rocket upwards.

17390.q: What was the name of the first satellite that a rocket carried into space in 1957?
17390.e: Sputnik 1 was a small metal ball with antennas. It was launched by the Soviet Union in 1957 and sent out beeping signals.
17390.m: Sputnik 1 was the first satellite in space.

17391.q: What was the name of the huge rocket that took astronauts to the Moon?
17391.e: The Saturn V was one of the largest rockets ever built. It took the Apollo astronauts to the Moon.
17391.m: The Saturn V flew people to the Moon.

17392.q: What are the large rockets called that Europe sends into space?
17392.e: The Ariane rockets are launched from French Guiana in South America. They also contain parts made in Switzerland.

17393.q: What do people do during the countdown before a rocket launch?
a: They count forwards to a hundred
17393.e: During the countdown, the last seconds are counted backwards. At zero, the rocket lifts off.
17393.m: In a countdown you count backwards to zero.

17394.q: What is the name of the space station where people have lived all the time since 2000?
17394.e: ISS stands for International Space Station. Many countries built it together, and Europe is part of it too.
17394.m: Astronauts live on the ISS all the time.

17395.q: Roughly how many times a day does the ISS orbit the Earth?
17395.e: The ISS is very fast and needs only about an hour and a half for one lap. So it manages about 16 laps a day.
17395.m: The ISS orbits the Earth about 16 times a day.

17396.q: Roughly how high above the Earth does the ISS fly?
17396.e: The ISS orbits about 400 kilometres above the Earth. That is further than the distance from Geneva to St Gallen.
17396.m: The ISS flies about 400 kilometres high.

17397.q: Can you see the ISS from Switzerland with your bare eyes?
a: Yes, as a bright point of light
17397.e: In the evening or early morning, the ISS reflects sunlight. Then it moves quickly across the sky as a bright dot.
17397.m: You can sometimes see the ISS as a bright dot in the sky.

17398.q: Where does the ISS get its electricity from?
17398.e: The ISS has huge wings made of solar cells. They turn sunlight into electricity.
17398.m: The ISS gets its electricity from sunlight.

17399.q: According to current knowledge, how many years ago did the Big Bang happen?
17399.e: Measurements of the background radiation and of the expansion of the universe give an age of around 13.8 billion years. That is about three times as old as the Earth.
17399.m: The universe is around 13.8 billion years old.

17400.q: Which radiation is seen as the “afterglow” of the Big Bang?
a: the UV radiation of the stars
17400.e: The cosmic background radiation comes evenly from all directions of the sky. It was discovered in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson and is important evidence for the Big Bang.
17400.m: The cosmic background radiation is the echo of the Big Bang.

17401.q: Which astronomer showed in 1929 that most galaxies are moving away from us?
17401.e: Edwin Hubble found that galaxies further away are moving away from us faster. It follows that the universe is expanding.
17401.m: Edwin Hubble discovered that the universe is expanding.

17402.q: Which chemical element was formed most often shortly after the Big Bang?
17402.e: In the first minutes after the Big Bang, almost only hydrogen and helium formed. Heavier elements such as iron or carbon were made much later inside stars.
17402.m: Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.

17403.q: What does the Big Bang theory say?
a: The universe began very hot and dense and has been expanding ever since
The universe has always existed exactly as it is today
The Earth is the oldest object in the universe
All the stars formed in an explosion of the Sun
17403.e: According to the Big Bang theory, the universe was extremely hot and dense around 13.8 billion years ago. Since then it has been expanding and cooling down.
17403.m: Since the Big Bang, the universe has been expanding.

17404.q: What did our solar system form from?
a: from a cloud of gas and dust
from the remains of a comet
17404.e: A huge cloud of gas and dust pulled itself together through its own gravity. The Sun formed in its centre, and the planets formed from the rest.
17404.m: The Sun and the planets formed from a cloud of gas and dust.

17405.q: What shape did the spinning cloud of gas and dust take, from which our planets formed?
a: A hollow ring with no middle
17405.e: The collapsing cloud spun faster and faster and became flat like a disc. The planets grew in this disc.
17405.m: Planets form in a flat disc around a young star.

17406.q: How did the planets grow in the young disc around the Sun?
a: Small lumps collided and stuck together
They fell out of the Sun fully formed
17406.e: Grains of dust stuck together and became bigger and bigger lumps. These collided and finally formed the planets.
17406.m: Planets grew from many small lumps.

17407.q: Why are the four inner planets rocky planets?
a: Close to the Sun it was too hot for ice and light gases.
Close to the Sun there was only water.
The outer planets gave them their rock.
The Sun set fire to their gas layer at once.
17407.e: Near the young Sun, only rock and metal could stay solid. Further out it was cold enough for ice, and that is where the big gas planets formed.
17407.m: Rocky planets formed near the Sun, gas giants further out.

17408.q: According to the most widely accepted theory today, how did the Earth's Moon form?
a: when the young Earth collided with a body the size of Mars
when a passing comet was captured
when a piece split off from the Sun
when a volcano erupted on Earth
17408.e: A body about the size of Mars, often called Theia, crashed into the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris that was thrown out.
17408.m: The Moon probably formed after a huge collision with the Earth.

17409.q: The Earth spins once completely around itself (360 degrees) in about 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in one hour?
17409.e: 360 degrees ÷ 24 hours gives 15 degrees per hour. That is why a time zone is roughly 15 degrees of longitude wide.
17409.m: The Earth turns 15 degrees further every hour.

17410.q: In which direction does the Earth spin on its axis?
17410.e: The Earth spins towards the east. That is why the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west for us.
17410.m: Because the Earth spins towards the east, the Sun rises in the east.

17411.q: Which experiment made the Earth's rotation visible in Paris in 1851?
17411.e: Léon Foucault let a long pendulum swing. The direction of its swing seemed to turn slowly, because in reality the Earth was turning underneath it.
17411.m: Foucault's pendulum proves that the Earth rotates.

17412.q: Roughly how fast does a place on the equator move because of the Earth's rotation?
17412.e: The Earth's circumference at the equator is around 40,075 km. In 24 hours that gives 40,075 km ÷ 24 h, so about 1670 km/h.
17412.m: At the equator the ground spins at about 1670 km/h.

17413.q: How long does the Earth take to make one turn compared with the distant stars (a sidereal day)?
17413.e: Because the Earth is also moving around the Sun, it has to turn a little further for a solar day. Compared with the stars, one turn is therefore about 4 minutes shorter.
17413.m: A sidereal day is about 4 minutes shorter than a solar day.

17414.q: What is caused by the Earth spinning on its own axis?
17414.e: Because of the rotation, one half of the Earth always faces the Sun. There it is day, and on the other half it is night.
17414.m: The Earth's rotation causes the change between day and night.

17415.q: How long does the Earth take to go once around the Sun?
17415.e: One orbit takes around 365 days and 6 hours. The extra hours are balanced out every four years with a leap day.
17415.m: The Earth goes around the Sun in about 365 days and 6 hours.

17416.q: On average, how far is the Earth from the Sun?
17416.e: The average distance is around 149.6 million kilometres. This distance is also called one astronomical unit.
17416.m: One astronomical unit is about 150 million kilometres.

17417.q: What shape is the Earth's orbit around the Sun?
17417.e: According to Kepler's laws, planetary orbits are ellipses. However, the Earth's orbit is only slightly stretched and is almost a circle.
17417.m: The Earth's orbit is an ellipse that is almost a circle.

17418.q: What is the main reason for the seasons?
a: the tilt of the Earth's axis
the changing distance to the Sun
the changing brightness of the Sun
17418.e: The Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees. That is why in summer the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun and gets steeper sunlight and longer days.
17418.m: The tilted axis of the Earth is the reason for the seasons.

17419.q: Roughly how fast does the Earth move along its orbit around the Sun?
17419.e: The Earth travels almost a billion kilometres in a year. That gives around 30 km per second, which is over 100,000 km/h.
17419.m: The Earth races around the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second.

17420.q: When in the year is the Earth closest to the Sun?
17420.e: The Earth reaches the point of its orbit closest to the Sun, called the perihelion, every year in early January. Even so, it is winter in the northern hemisphere then.
17420.m: In January the Earth is closest to the Sun.

17421.q: Roughly how long is it from one full moon to the next?
17421.e: This period is called the synodic month and lasts around 29 days and 12 hours. The word “month” also comes from “moon”.
17421.m: A whole cycle of the Moon's phases lasts about 29.5 days.

17422.q: What is the phase of the Moon called when it can hardly be seen from Earth?
17422.e: At new moon, the side of the Moon lit by the Sun faces away from us. We only see the dark side, which is also in the bright daytime sky.
17422.m: At new moon, the Moon is invisible to us.

17423.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon from Earth?
a: The Moon spins once around itself in the same time it takes to orbit the Earth.
The Moon does not spin around itself at all.
The other side is always hidden by clouds.
The Earth spins exactly as fast as the Moon.
17423.e: This is called tidal locking. Over a long time, the Earth's gravity has slowed down the Moon's spin in this way.
17423.m: Because of tidal locking, the Moon always shows us the same side.

17424.q: What is the Moon called in the time between new moon and full moon?
17424.e: After new moon, a larger part of the lit side becomes visible every evening. The Moon waxes until it is full.
17424.m: Between new moon and full moon, the Moon is waxing.

17425.q: What causes the phases of the Moon?
a: our changing view of the half of the Moon lit by the Sun
the Earth's shadow on the Moon
Moon volcanoes switching on and off
17425.e: The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon. Depending on where the Moon is in its orbit, we see more or less of this bright half.
17425.m: The Moon's phases depend on how much of the lit side we can see.

17426.q: How much of the visible disc of the Moon is lit at half moon?
17426.e: At half moon we see exactly half of the Moon's disc lit up. Even so, this phase is also called the first or last quarter, because the Moon has completed a quarter of its orbit.
17426.m: At half moon, half of the Moon's disc is shining.

17427.q: During a solar eclipse, which body is between the other two?
17427.e: The Moon moves between the Sun and the Earth. Its shadow falls on the Earth and covers the Sun there completely or partly.
17427.m: In a solar eclipse, the Moon covers the Sun.

17428.q: What is the glowing crown of rays around the Sun called that you see during a total solar eclipse?
17428.e: The corona is the outermost, very thin layer of the Sun's atmosphere. Normally it is too faint to be seen next to the bright disc of the Sun.
17428.m: The Sun's corona becomes visible during a total solar eclipse.

17429.q: Why can the small Moon cover the much larger Sun almost exactly?
a: The Sun is about 400 times bigger, but also about 400 times further away.
The Sun is only about twice as big as the Moon.
The Moon shines by itself during an eclipse.
The Earth's atmosphere makes the Moon look bigger.
17429.e: The Sun's diameter is around 400 times that of the Moon. Because the Sun is also about 400 times further away, both look almost the same size in the sky.
17429.m: The Sun and the Moon look about the same size in the sky.

17430.q: Why does a bright ring stay visible during an annular solar eclipse?
a: The Moon is further from the Earth at that time and looks smaller.
The Sun is closer at that time and shines more strongly.
The Moon has a hole in the middle.
The Earth's shadow makes the edge bright.
17430.e: The Moon's orbit is an ellipse. When the Moon is far away, its disc is too small to cover the Sun completely, and a ring of Sun remains.
17430.m: When the Moon is far away, an annular solar eclipse happens.

17431.q: What can you safely use to watch a solar eclipse directly?
17431.e: Sunlight can seriously and permanently damage the retina. Only special, tested filters block enough light and invisible radiation.
17431.m: Never look at the Sun without a tested solar filter.

17432.q: During a lunar eclipse, which body is between the other two?
17432.e: The Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. The Moon moves through the Earth's shadow and goes dark.
17432.m: In a lunar eclipse, the Earth casts its shadow on the Moon.

17433.q: From where can you watch a total lunar eclipse?
a: from the whole night side of the Earth
only from a narrow strip of the Earth
only from the day side of the Earth
17433.e: The Moon is then really inside the Earth's shadow. Everyone who has the Moon above the horizon at that moment sees the eclipse at the same time.
17433.m: A lunar eclipse can be seen from the whole night side of the Earth.

17434.q: Why does the Moon still glow faintly during a total lunar eclipse?
a: The Earth's atmosphere bends red sunlight into the Earth's shadow.
The Moon has its own sources of light.
The stars light it from behind.
17434.e: Sunlight is bent in the Earth's atmosphere and directed into the shadow. Blue light is scattered away, and red light gets through, a bit like a red sunset.
17434.m: The Earth's atmosphere turns the eclipsed Moon red.

17435.q: What is the Moon often called in everyday language during a total lunar eclipse?
17435.e: Because of its reddish colour, people speak of a “blood moon”. A “supermoon”, on the other hand, is a full moon that is especially close to the Earth.
17435.m: The reddish eclipsed Moon is often called a blood moon.

17436.q: Why is there not a lunar eclipse at every full moon?
a: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees to the Earth's orbit.
The Moon is always too far away at full moon.
The Sun is not bright enough at full moon.
The Earth spins too fast at full moon.
17436.e: Usually the Moon passes just above or below the Earth's shadow. Only when it is close to the points where the two orbits cross does an eclipse happen.
17436.m: Because the Moon's orbit is tilted, eclipses are fairly rare.

17437.q: Who published the law of universal gravitation in 1687?
17437.e: In his work “Principia”, Isaac Newton explained that the same force makes the apple fall and keeps the Moon in its orbit.
17437.m: Isaac Newton was the first to describe gravity with a law.

17438.q: Roughly how large is the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface?
17438.e: Without air resistance, a falling object gets about 9.81 m/s faster every second. On other bodies in space, this value is larger or smaller.
17438.m: On Earth the acceleration due to gravity is about 9.81 metres per second squared.

17439.q: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon?
17439.e: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change. On the Moon only the weight is smaller, because the Moon pulls less strongly.
17439.m: Mass stays the same everywhere; only weight changes.

17440.q: Roughly how many times smaller is weight on the Moon than on Earth?
17440.e: The Moon has much less mass than the Earth and therefore pulls less strongly. An object there weighs only about a sixth as much as on Earth.
17440.m: On the Moon you weigh about a sixth of what you weigh on Earth.

17441.q: What mainly causes low and high tide on the coasts?
17441.e: The Moon pulls on the water of the oceans and creates bulges of water. As the Earth spins, these move across the coasts, and the Sun makes the effect stronger or weaker.
17441.m: The Moon is the main reason for the tides.

17442.q: What does the gravitational force between two bodies depend on?
a: on their masses and their distance
on their shape and their age
17442.e: The larger the masses, the more strongly they attract each other. If the distance doubles, the force drops to a quarter.
17442.m: Large masses and small distances make the pull strong.

17443.q: Where is the asteroid belt of our solar system?
17443.e: In the asteroid belt, millions of chunks of rock orbit the Sun. Jupiter's gravity stopped them from joining together into a planet.
17443.m: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.

17444.q: What is the largest object in the asteroid belt called, which today counts as a dwarf planet?
17444.e: Ceres is almost 1000 kilometres across and round. Since 2006 it has been counted as a dwarf planet.
17444.m: Ceres is the largest body in the asteroid belt.

17445.q: What are asteroids mainly made of?
17445.e: Asteroids are solid chunks, some rather rocky, others very rich in metal. They are left over from the time when the planets formed.
17445.m: Asteroids are chunks of rock and metal orbiting the Sun.

17446.q: Which animals died out after an asteroid impact around 66 million years ago?
17446.e: An asteroid about 10 kilometres across struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. The effects changed the climate, and the dinosaurs, apart from the birds, died out.
17446.m: An asteroid impact ended the age of the dinosaurs.

17447.q: What did NASA successfully test in 2022 with the DART mission?
a: deflecting an asteroid by crashing a probe into it
capturing an asteroid into an orbit around Earth
drilling for gold on an asteroid
17447.e: The DART probe crashed into the small asteroid Dimorphos. This changed its orbit by a measurable amount, a test for defending against dangerous asteroids.
17447.m: DART tested how to push an asteroid off course.

17448.q: What did the OSIRIS-REx space probe bring back to Earth in 2023?
17448.e: OSIRIS-REx collected material from the asteroid Bennu. In September 2023 the sample capsule landed in the desert in Utah.
17448.m: OSIRIS-REx brought material from an asteroid to Earth.

17449.q: What is the core of a comet mainly made of?
17449.e: A comet's core is a mixture of frozen water, other kinds of ice, dust and rock. That is why it is also called a “dirty snowball”.
17449.m: A comet is a dirty snowball made of ice and dust.

17450.q: In which direction does a comet's tail point?
a: always in the direction it is flying
17450.e: The solar wind and the pressure of sunlight blow gas and dust away from the core. That is why the tail always points away from the Sun.
17450.m: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.

17451.q: Roughly how long does Halley's Comet take to go once around the Sun?
17451.e: Edmond Halley realised that the same comet comes back regularly. Its orbit takes around 75 to 76 years.
17451.m: Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years.

17452.q: Which ESA space probe was the first to put a lander on a comet in 2014?
17452.e: The Rosetta probe accompanied the comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko, and its lander Philae touched down in November 2014. On board was also the measuring instrument ROSINA from the University of Bern.
17452.m: Rosetta brought the first lander to a comet.

17453.q: What is the huge cloud at the edge of the solar system called, where many long-period comets come from?
17453.e: The Oort Cloud is a spherical shell of billions of icy bodies far beyond Neptune. From there, comets sometimes fall into the inner solar system.
17453.m: Many comets come from the distant Oort Cloud.

17454.q: What is the glowing cloud of gas called that forms around a comet's core near the Sun?
17454.e: When the comet gets close to the Sun, ice turns to gas and forms a cloud around the core. This cloud is called the coma and can become larger than a planet.
17454.m: The cloud of gas around a comet's core is called the coma.

17455.q: What do you call a chunk from space that falls all the way to the ground?
17455.e: A meteor is only the streak of light in the sky. If part of the object reaches the ground, this piece is called a meteorite.
17455.m: A meteorite is a stone from space that has reached the ground.

17456.q: What is the meteor shower called that can be seen especially well every August?
17456.e: In August, the Earth passes through the dust trail of the comet Swift-Tuttle. The particles burn up in the air and seem to come from the constellation of Perseus.
17456.m: The Perseids bring lots of shooting stars in August.

17457.q: Above which Russian city did a meteor explode in February 2013, shattering many windows?
17457.e: An object about 20 metres across broke apart in the atmosphere above Chelyabinsk. The shock wave injured around 1500 people, mostly from broken glass.
17457.m: The Chelyabinsk meteor exploded high above the city in 2013.

17458.q: What are iron meteorites mainly made of?
17458.e: Iron meteorites come from the metal core of asteroids that broke apart. They are made mainly of iron with some nickel.
17458.m: Iron meteorites contain a lot of nickel as well as iron.

17459.q: What is the well-known iron meteorite called, of which many pieces were found in the canton of Bern?
17459.e: The first piece of the Twannberg meteorite was found in 1984 in a field near Twann, and many more have been found since. It is considered the largest meteorite find in Switzerland.
17459.m: The Twannberg meteorite is Switzerland's best-known meteorite.

17460.q: What type of galaxy is the Milky Way?
17460.e: The Milky Way has a bar-shaped core from which spiral arms spread out. Seen from the side, it is a flat disc.
17460.m: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy.

17461.q: Roughly how many stars does the Milky Way contain?
17461.e: Estimates are around 100 to 400 billion stars. The Sun is just one of them.
17461.m: The Milky Way is made up of hundreds of billions of stars.

17462.q: What is at the centre of the Milky Way?
a: a second sun made of ice
a large empty space with no matter
17462.e: At the centre lies the black hole Sagittarius A*, with around 4 million times the mass of the Sun. The discovery won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020.
17462.m: A huge black hole sits at the heart of the Milky Way.

17463.q: Roughly how long does the Sun take to go once around the centre of the Milky Way?
17463.e: The Sun moves around the centre of the galaxy at over 200 km per second. Even so, one orbit takes around 230 million years because the distance is so huge.
17463.m: One orbit of the Sun around the centre of the Milky Way is called a galactic year.

17464.q: Where is our solar system in the Milky Way?
a: in a spiral arm, the Orion Arm
in the halo far outside the disc
in the bar in the middle
17464.e: The solar system lies in the disc, around 26,000 light years from the centre. It is in the Orion Arm, a smaller spiral arm.
17464.m: The Sun orbits in the Orion Arm of the Milky Way.

17465.q: What is the name of the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way?
17465.e: The Andromeda Galaxy has about the same mass as the Milky Way and, in good conditions, is the most distant object you can see with the naked eye. It lies in the constellation of Andromeda.
17465.m: The Andromeda Galaxy is our large neighbouring galaxy.

17466.q: Roughly how far away from us is the Andromeda Galaxy?
17466.e: The light we see from Andromeda today is around 2.5 million years old. So we see the galaxy as it was back then.
17466.m: Looking at the Andromeda Galaxy is looking into the past.

17467.q: Which two galaxies can be seen with the naked eye from the southern hemisphere as bright patches?
a: the Large and the Small Magellanic Cloud
the Andromeda and the Triangulum Galaxy
the Sombrero and the Cigar Galaxy
the Whirlpool and the Pinwheel Galaxy
17467.e: The two Magellanic Clouds are small companion galaxies of the Milky Way. They are named after the seafarer Ferdinand Magellan.
17467.m: The Magellanic Clouds are companions of the Milky Way.

17468.q: Which space telescope has been observing very distant galaxies in infrared light since the end of 2021?
17468.e: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched on 25 December 2021. With its large mirror and infrared light, it can see very young galaxies from the early days of the universe.
17468.m: The James Webb Telescope looks far back to the time of the first galaxies.

17469.q: According to current estimates, how many galaxies are there in the observable universe?
17469.e: Deep images from space telescopes show thousands of galaxies even in small patches of sky. Scaled up, that gives hundreds of billions, and some estimates go up to trillions.
17469.m: There are unimaginably many galaxies in the universe.

17470.q: What does a light year measure?
17470.e: A light year is the distance light travels in one year. This unit is needed because distances between stars in kilometres would be awkwardly huge.
17470.m: A light year is a unit of length, not of time.

17471.q: Roughly how long is a light year?
17471.e: Light travels around 9.46 trillion kilometres in a year. That is over 60,000 times the distance between the Earth and the Sun.
17471.m: A light year is around 9.5 trillion kilometres.

17472.q: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
17472.e: Light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to us. So we always see the Sun as it was a good 8 minutes ago.
17472.m: Sunlight travels about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.

17473.q: What is the nearest star after the Sun called?
17473.e: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light years away. It is a small red dwarf star and cannot be seen with the naked eye.
17473.m: Proxima Centauri is our nearest neighbouring star.

17474.q: Light travels about 300,000 km per second. Roughly how far does it get in one minute?
17474.e: A minute has 60 seconds. 300,000 km × 60 gives 18,000,000 km, so 18 million km.
17474.m: In one minute light travels about 18 million kilometres.

17475.q: Roughly how long does light take to travel from the Moon to the Earth?
17475.e: On average the Moon is around 384,400 km away. 384,400 km ÷ 300,000 km/s gives about 1.3 seconds.
17475.m: Moonlight needs only just over a second to reach us.

17476.q: Which space probe is the human-made object furthest from the Earth?
17476.e: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and in 2012 became the first probe to reach interstellar space. Today it is over 25 billion kilometres away (as of 2026).
17476.m: Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object.

17477.q: Which space probe was the first to fly past the dwarf planet Pluto in 2015?
17477.e: New Horizons was launched in 2006 and reached Pluto in July 2015. Among other things, its pictures showed a large heart-shaped area of ice.
17477.m: New Horizons sent the first close-up pictures of Pluto.

17478.q: Which NASA rover landed on Mars in February 2021?
17478.e: Perseverance is searching Jezero Crater for signs of past life and collecting rock samples. It also brought along the small helicopter Ingenuity.
17478.m: The Perseverance rover has been exploring Mars since 2021.

17479.q: Which planet is photographed from orbit by the CaSSIS camera of the University of Bern?
17479.e: CaSSIS travels on board the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, which was launched in 2016. The camera takes colour 3D pictures of the surface of Mars.
17479.m: A camera from Bern photographs Mars from space.

17480.q: Which space probe has come closer to the Sun than any other human-made object?
17480.e: NASA's Parker Solar Probe flew past only around 6 million kilometres from the Sun's surface in December 2024. It was faster than any other human-made object.
17480.m: The Parker Solar Probe flies through the Sun's outer atmosphere.

17482.q: At roughly what height do geostationary satellites orbit above the equator?
17482.e: At a height of around 35,800 km, a satellite takes exactly as long to circle the Earth as the Earth takes to turn once. So from Earth it seems to stand still in the sky.
17482.m: Geostationary satellites seem to stand still above one point on Earth.

17483.q: What was the name of the first satellite built entirely in Switzerland and launched in 2009?
17483.e: SwissCube was developed at the ETH Lausanne (EPFL) together with other universities. The small cube-shaped satellite is only about 10 cm along each edge.
17483.m: SwissCube was the first Swiss satellite.

17484.q: What are navigation satellites, such as those of the European Galileo system, used for?
a: lighting up the night side of the Earth
measuring the depth of the sea
17484.e: A receiver, for example in a mobile phone, picks up signals from several satellites at the same time. From how long the signals take, it works out where it is.
17484.m: Navigation satellites help you find your exact location.

17485.q: Which Swiss astronaut helped repair the Hubble Space Telescope in 1993 and 1999?
17485.e: Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss person to fly into space, four times in all on the Space Shuttle. On two flights he helped to service the Hubble telescope.
17485.m: Claude Nicollier is the best-known Swiss astronaut.

17486.q: In which year did people land on the Moon for the first time?
17486.e: The lunar module landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969. Many people all over the world followed the event on television.
17486.m: In July 1969, people set foot on the Moon for the first time.

17487.q: What was the name of the mission of the first crewed Moon landing?
17487.e: Three astronauts flew to the Moon on Apollo 11, and two of them landed. Apollo 13 had to turn back without landing after an explosion.
17487.m: Apollo 11 brought the first people to the Moon.

17488.q: Who was the second person to step onto the Moon during the first Moon landing?
17488.e: Buzz Aldrin climbed out of the lunar module Eagle just under 20 minutes after the commander. Michael Collins stayed in the command module in orbit around the Moon.
17488.m: Buzz Aldrin was the second person on the Moon.

17489.q: Which experiment from the University of Bern did the Apollo 11 astronauts set up on the Moon?
17489.e: The sail made of aluminium foil caught particles of the solar wind and was then brought back to Earth. According to the University of Bern, it was even set up before the American flag.
17489.m: A solar wind sail from Bern was part of the first Moon landing.

17490.q: How many people have walked on the Moon so far?
17490.e: Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo missions each landed two astronauts on the Moon. Nobody has walked on the Moon since (as of 2026).
17490.m: Twelve people have walked on the Moon so far.

17491.q: At roughly what height does the International Space Station ISS orbit the Earth?
17491.e: The ISS flies at a height of around 400 km. In good weather you can see it from Switzerland as a bright, fast-moving dot in the sky.
17491.m: The ISS orbits the Earth at a height of about 400 kilometres.

17492.q: Roughly how long does the ISS take to go once around the Earth?
17492.e: The space station flies at about 28,000 km/h. That way it manages one lap around the Earth in around an hour and a half.
17492.m: The ISS goes around the Earth in about an hour and a half.

17493.q: Since when has the ISS been lived on by people without a break?
17493.e: On 2 November 2000 the first long-term crew came on board. Since then, astronauts have lived there all the time.
17493.m: The ISS has been lived on all the time since 2000.

17494.q: The ISS flies at around 7.7 km per second. Roughly how far does it get in one minute?
17494.e: A minute has 60 seconds. 7.7 km × 60 gives 462 km, so about 460 km.
17494.m: The ISS travels around 460 kilometres in one minute.

17495.q: Which European organisation is a partner in the ISS?
17495.e: The European Space Agency ESA contributed, among other things, the Columbus research laboratory. Switzerland is a founding member of ESA.
17495.m: ESA represents Europe on the International Space Station.

17496.q: Why do the astronauts float in the ISS?
a: They are in free fall around the Earth together with the station.
At a height of 400 km there is no Earth gravity.
The station is filled with helium.
17496.e: At the height of the ISS, the Earth's gravity is still almost 90 per cent as strong as on the ground. But the station and the crew fall around the Earth together, so they feel weightless.
17496.m: You float in the ISS because everything falls around the Earth together.

17597.q: How many fingers do you have on one hand?
17597.e: On each hand there is a thumb and four other fingers. Together that makes five fingers.
17597.m: I have five fingers on each hand.

17598.q: Which part of the body connects the head to the trunk?
17598.e: The neck holds up the head. Thanks to it you can turn your head and nod.
17598.m: The neck connects the head to the body.

17599.q: What is the joint in the middle of the leg called?
17599.e: The knee is between the thigh and the lower leg. Thanks to it you can bend your leg.
17599.m: With my knee I can bend my leg.

17600.q: What is the joint in the middle of the arm called?
17600.e: The elbow is between the upper arm and the forearm. You use it to bend your arm.
17600.m: With my elbow I can bend my arm.

17601.e: The thumb is the strongest finger. With it we can grab and hold things well.
17601.m: My thumb helps me grab things.

17603.q: Which sense tells you whether something is soft or hard?
17603.e: When you touch something, you feel with your skin whether it is soft, hard, rough or smooth.
17603.m: With my sense of touch I feel what something is like.

17604.q: Which sense helps you enjoy music?
17604.e: Music is made of sounds. You take in sounds with your ears.
17604.m: I take in music with my hearing.

17605.q: What do you call the parts of the body we use to sense things?
17605.e: Eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin pick up signals from the world around us. That is why they are called sense organs.
17605.m: With my sense organs I take in the world.

17606.q: Which sense warns you about burnt food before you see it?
17606.e: The smell of burning reaches the nose quickly. So you often notice from the next room that something is burning.
17606.m: My nose can warn me of danger.

17607.q: What is the black hole in the middle of the eye called?
17607.e: Light enters the eye through the pupil. In the dark it gets bigger, in bright light smaller.
17607.m: Light comes into my eye through the pupil.

17608.q: Which part of the eye decides eye colour?
17608.e: The iris is the coloured ring around the pupil. It can be, for example, blue, green or brown.
17608.m: The iris gives my eyes their colour.

17609.q: What protects the eye when we blink?
17609.e: When you blink, the eyelid closes briefly. It spreads tear fluid and keeps dust away.
17609.m: When I blink, the eyelid protects my eye.

17610.q: What do our eyes need in order to see?
17610.e: Our eyes take in light. In total darkness we cannot see anything.
17610.m: Without light I cannot see anything.

17611.q: What helps many people to see clearly again?
17611.e: Glasses have special lenses. They help the eye to see things clearly.

17612.q: What is the thin skin in the ear that vibrates with sounds called?
17612.e: Sounds make the eardrum vibrate. These vibrations are passed on into the inner parts of the ear.
17612.m: The eardrum vibrates when sounds come into the ear.

17613.q: Apart from hearing, what is the inner ear also important for?
17613.e: In the inner ear there is a balance organ. It notices how we move and how our head is positioned.
17613.m: My ear also helps me keep my balance.

17614.q: Where in the body is the smallest bone?
17614.e: The smallest bone is called the stirrup. It sits in the middle ear and helps with hearing.
17614.m: The smallest bone is in my ear.

17615.q: What protects your ears from very loud noise?
17615.e: Very loud noise can damage your hearing for good. Ear protection makes the noise quieter.
17615.m: When it is very loud, I protect my ears.

17616.q: What helps people who are hard of hearing to hear better?
17616.e: A hearing aid makes sounds louder. That way people who are hard of hearing can follow conversations better.
17616.m: A hearing aid makes sounds louder.

17617.q: What are the little hairs in your nose good for?
17617.e: Nose hairs catch dust and tiny particles from the air. That keeps the lungs cleaner.

17618.q: Why does food often taste bland when you have a cold?
a: Because your nose cannot smell well
17618.e: Smell and taste work closely together. If your nose is blocked, lots of things taste weaker.

17619.q: What does your nose do with the air you breathe in?
17619.e: In the nose, the air is warmed and moistened. That is good for the lungs.
17619.m: The nose warms the air you breathe.

17620.q: How many nostrils does a person have?
17620.e: The nose has two nostrils. Between them is the wall called the septum.

17621.q: Which taste goes with a lemon?
17621.e: Lemons contain a lot of acid. That is why they taste sour.

17622.e: Honey contains a lot of sugar. Sugar tastes sweet.

17623.q: What is on the tongue and helps with tasting?
17623.e: There are thousands of tiny taste buds on the tongue. We taste our food with them.
17623.m: I taste with my taste buds.

17624.q: Apart from tasting, what does the tongue help with?
17624.e: The tongue moves very easily. Without it we could not say many sounds.

17625.q: Why do we sweat when we are hot?
17625.e: Sweat evaporates on the skin. As it does so, it cools the body down.

17626.q: What protects the skin from sunburn in summer?
17626.e: Sun cream blocks some of the sun's rays. A hat, clothes and shade protect the skin too.
17626.m: In summer I protect my skin from the sun.

17627.q: What is unique to every person?
17627.e: The fine lines on your fingertips are different for every person. Even twins have different fingerprints.
17627.m: My fingerprint belongs only to me.

17628.q: What do you call it when the tiny hairs on your skin stand up in the cold?
17628.e: When you are cold or get a fright, tiny muscles in the skin tighten. Then the tiny hairs stand up.
17628.m: When it is cold I sometimes get goose bumps.

17630.q: What do we think and learn with?
17630.e: The brain processes everything we see, hear and feel. It also stores what we learn.
17630.m: I think and learn with my brain.

17631.q: What protects your head when you ride a bike?
17631.e: A helmet cushions knocks if you fall. That way it protects your head and brain.
17631.m: I wear a helmet when I ride my bike.

17632.q: What does the brain need to recover well?
17632.e: During sleep the brain rests and sorts out what we have learnt. Afterwards we can concentrate better.
17632.m: Sleep is good for my brain.

17633.q: How do messages get from the brain to the hands?
17633.e: Nerves run like cables through the whole body. They pass messages between the brain and the parts of the body.
17633.m: Nerves carry messages through my body.

17634.e: The heart is a pump. It pumps blood around the whole body.
17634.m: My heart pumps blood around my body.

17635.q: What is the heart mainly made of?
17635.e: The heart is a strong muscle. It tightens again and again and so pumps the blood along.

17636.e: The heart is in the ribcage, a little to the left of the middle. You can sometimes feel it beating there.
17636.m: My heart is in my chest.

17637.q: What happens to your heartbeat when you run fast?
17637.e: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen. That is why the heart beats faster.
17637.m: When I do sport, my heart beats faster.

17638.q: Where can you feel your pulse easily?
17638.e: At the wrist, blood flows close under the skin. There you can feel every heartbeat as your pulse.
17638.m: I can feel my pulse at my wrist.

17639.q: How many lungs does a person have?
17639.e: People have a right lung and a left lung. Both are in the ribcage.

17640.q: Which organ takes oxygen out of the air?
17640.e: When you breathe in, air flows into the lungs. There the oxygen from the air gets into the blood.
17640.m: My lungs take oxygen out of the air.

17641.q: What is very harmful to the lungs?
17641.e: Tobacco smoke contains many poisonous substances. They damage the lungs and make people ill.

17642.q: What protects the lungs from the outside?
17642.e: The ribs form the ribcage. It surrounds the lungs like a cage.

17643.q: Where does food end up after you swallow it?
17643.e: After you swallow, the food slides down into the stomach. There it is digested further.
17643.m: Swallowed food goes into the stomach.

17644.q: What does the stomach do with food?
a: It pumps it into the heart
It sends it to the nose
17644.e: The stomach kneads the food and mixes it with gastric juice. That turns it into a mush.
17644.m: My stomach turns food into a mush.

17645.q: Why does your tummy sometimes rumble?
17645.e: An empty stomach still moves. Air and liquid are pushed back and forth, and we hear that.
17645.m: A rumbling tummy often means you are hungry.

17646.q: What does gastric juice contain that makes bacteria harmless?
17646.e: Gastric juice is very acidic. The acid kills many germs in food.

17647.q: Roughly how many bones does an adult have?
17647.e: An adult human has about 206 bones. Babies have more, because some bones grow together later.

17648.q: What do you call all the bones together?
17648.e: All the bones together make up the skeleton. It supports the body and gives it its shape.

17649.e: The skull is a hard case of bone. Inside it lies the delicate brain.

17650.q: Where is the longest bone in the body?
17650.e: The thigh bone is the longest and one of the strongest bones. It carries a large part of the body's weight.
17650.m: The longest bone is in the thigh.

17651.q: What do people often wear when they have broken an arm?
17651.e: A plaster cast keeps the broken bone still. That way it can grow back together properly.
17651.m: A plaster cast helps a broken bone heal.

17652.q: What do we need to move an arm?
17652.e: Muscles pull on the bones. That way we can move our arms, legs and fingers.

17653.q: What happens to a muscle when it works?
17653.e: A working muscle gets shorter and thicker. As it does, it pulls on a bone.
17653.m: A muscle tightens when it works.

a: Through sitting for a long time
17654.e: When we use our muscles often, they get stronger. Sport and playing outside help with this.

17655.q: What do you call sore muscles the day after lots of sport?
17655.e: After unusual effort, muscles often hurt the next day. This is called muscle soreness, and it goes away by itself after a few days.
17655.m: Muscle soreness goes away after a few days.

17656.q: What is the muscle at the front of the upper arm called?
17656.e: The biceps is at the front of the upper arm. It bends the arm at the elbow.

17657.q: How many milk teeth does a child have?
17657.e: Children have 20 milk teeth. Later they are replaced one by one by permanent teeth.
17657.m: A child has twenty milk teeth.

17658.q: How many times a day should you brush your teeth?
17658.e: Dentists recommend brushing your teeth at least twice a day. Best in the morning and in the evening before bed.
17658.m: I brush my teeth at least twice a day.

17659.q: What is especially bad for your teeth?
17659.e: Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. The acid attacks the teeth.
17659.m: Too much sugar is bad for your teeth.

17660.q: What is the hard white layer on the teeth called?
17660.e: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the whole body. It protects the tooth.

17661.q: What is the disease called in which holes form in the teeth?
17661.e: With tooth decay, the tooth is attacked by acid. Holes form, and the dentist has to treat them.
17661.m: Tooth decay makes holes in the teeth.

17662.e: Blood is red because it contains a huge number of red blood cells. They give the blood its colour.

17663.q: What does blood carry around the body?
17663.e: Blood collects oxygen from the lungs. It takes it to every part of the body.
17663.m: Blood brings oxygen into my body.

17664.q: In which tubes does blood flow around the body?
17664.e: Blood flows in blood vessels, which are also called veins and arteries. They reach right into your fingertips.
17664.m: My blood flows in my blood vessels.

17665.q: What forms when a small wound heals?
17665.e: The blood clots at the wound and becomes firm. This crust closes the wound until new skin has grown.
17665.m: A crust protects a healing wound.

17666.q: Roughly how much blood does an adult have?
17666.e: An adult has about 5 to 6 litres of blood. Children have less, because they are smaller.
17666.m: An adult has about five litres of blood.

17667.q: Which gas from the air do we need to live?
17667.e: Our body needs oxygen to get energy. Without oxygen we could only survive for a short time.

17668.q: Which gas do we mainly breathe out?
17668.e: When we breathe out, we give off carbon dioxide. It is made in the body as a waste product.
17668.m: When I breathe out, I give off carbon dioxide.

17669.q: What is the tube through which air flows into the lungs called?
17669.e: The windpipe leads from the neck into the chest. There it splits and leads into both lungs.
17669.m: Air comes into the lungs through the windpipe.

17670.q: What rises and falls when you breathe deeply?
17670.e: When you breathe in, the chest expands, and when you breathe out, it gets smaller again. You can feel this with your hand.
17670.m: When I breathe, my chest moves.

17671.q: What gets faster when you run?
17671.e: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen. That is why we breathe faster and more deeply.
17671.m: When I work hard, I breathe faster.

17672.e: Food is already broken up by the teeth in the mouth. That is where digestion begins.

17673.q: Through which tube does food get from the mouth to the stomach?
17673.e: The food pipe is a tube made of muscle. It pushes food down into the stomach.
17673.m: The food pipe leads to the stomach.

17674.q: Which long organ comes after the stomach?
17674.e: After the stomach, the food mush moves into the gut. There the nutrients are taken into the blood.
17674.m: After the stomach comes the gut.

17675.q: What is the liquid in your mouth that helps with eating called?
17675.e: Saliva makes food moist and slippery. That makes it easier to swallow.

17676.q: Why should you chew your food well?
a: So that it is easier to digest
So that there is more of it
17676.e: Well-chewed food is in small pieces. Then the stomach has less work to do.
17676.m: Food that is well chewed is half digested.

17677.q: Roughly how many hours of sleep do school-age children need each night?
17677.e: Experts recommend about 9 to 12 hours of sleep for children aged 6 to 12. Children need more sleep than adults.

17678.q: What do we often experience while we sleep?
17678.e: During sleep the brain processes lots of impressions. We often dream while it does, even if we forget it by the morning.
17678.m: I often dream while I sleep.

17679.e: Darkness and quiet tell the body that it is time to sleep. Screens, on the other hand, keep you awake.
17679.m: I sleep better in a dark, quiet room.

17680.q: What happens to children's bodies mainly while they sleep?
a: They get as cold as ice
17680.e: During sleep the body makes particularly a lot of growth hormone. That is why sleep is very important for children.
17680.m: My body grows while I sleep.

17681.q: How do people often feel after too little sleep?
17681.e: People who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate. They get tired and grumpy more quickly.
17681.m: When I have slept well, I can concentrate better.

17682.q: According to experts, at least how long should children be active every day?
17682.e: The World Health Organization recommends at least 60 minutes of activity a day for children and teenagers. Playing counts too.
17682.m: I am active for at least an hour every day.

17683.q: What is a healthy way to get to school?
17683.e: If you walk or cycle to school, you move every day. That strengthens your heart and muscles.

17684.q: What should you do before sport?
17684.e: Warming up gets your muscles and joints ready for the effort. That way you are less likely to get injured.

17685.q: What is best to drink after sport?
17685.e: During sport the body loses water through sweat. Water replaces the liquid without any sugar.

17686.q: Which vitamin is found in large amounts in oranges?
17686.e: Oranges and other citrus fruits contain a lot of vitamin C. It is important for our body's defences.
17686.m: Oranges provide lots of vitamin C.

17687.q: How many portions of vegetables and fruit are recommended per day?
17687.e: In Switzerland, five portions a day are recommended: three portions of vegetables and two portions of fruit. One portion is about a handful.
17687.m: I eat five portions of vegetables and fruit every day.

17688.q: Which mid-morning snack is especially healthy?
17688.e: An apple provides vitamins and fills you up. Sweets, on the other hand, contain a lot of sugar.
17688.m: An apple is a healthy mid-morning snack.

17689.q: What do milk and cheese provide for your bones?
17689.e: Dairy products contain a lot of calcium. Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

17690.q: What does the food pyramid show?
a: How to eat a balanced diet
17690.e: The food pyramid shows what you should eat a lot of and what you should eat little of. At the bottom is what you need most.
17690.m: The food pyramid helps me eat a balanced diet.

17691.q: When should you always wash your hands?
a: Before going to sleep in bed
17691.e: After using the toilet there may be germs on your hands. That is why you always wash your hands thoroughly afterwards.
17691.m: After the toilet I always wash my hands.

17692.q: What makes your hands properly clean when you wash them?
17692.e: Soap loosens dirt and grease from the skin. Water then rinses the germs away.

17693.q: Where should you sneeze if you have no tissue?
a: Into the crook of your elbow
17693.e: If you sneeze into the crook of your elbow, you spread fewer germs. Your hands stay clean and do not infect others.
17693.m: Without a tissue, I sneeze into the crook of my elbow.

17694.q: Why should everyone use their own toothbrush?
a: So that no germs are passed on
So that the toothpaste tastes better
17694.e: Germs from the mouth stick to a toothbrush. If you share it, illnesses can be passed on.

17695.q: What should you do before eating?
17695.e: Lots of germs collect on your hands. They should be clean before eating, so the germs do not get into your mouth.
17695.m: I wash my hands before eating.

17696.q: Which is the longest bone in the human body?
17696.e: The thigh bone (femur) is the longest and one of the strongest bones in the body.
17696.m: The thigh bone is the longest human bone.

17697.q: Where is the smallest human bone?
17697.e: The stirrup in the middle ear is only a few millimetres long. It helps to pass sound on to the inner ear.
17697.m: The stirrup in the ear is the smallest bone.

17698.q: How many pairs of ribs does a person usually have?
17698.e: People usually have 12 pairs of ribs, so 24 ribs. Together with the breastbone they form the ribcage.
17698.m: The ribcage is made of 12 pairs of ribs and the breastbone.

17699.q: What is made in the red bone marrow?
17699.e: Red and white blood cells and platelets are made in the red bone marrow.
17699.m: Red bone marrow is the factory for our blood cells.

17700.q: Which mineral makes bones hard and firm?
17700.e: Bones contain a lot of calcium in the form of calcium phosphate. This substance gives them their hardness.

17701.q: Which type of joint is found in the shoulder and the hip?
17701.e: In a ball-and-socket joint, a ball-shaped end of bone sits in a socket. That is why you can move your arm and leg in many directions.
17701.m: Ball-and-socket joints allow movement in all directions.

17702.q: Which type of joint, like a door hinge, only allows bending and straightening?
17702.e: A hinge joint only moves in one plane, much like a door hinge. Examples are the joints between the bones of the fingers.
17702.m: A hinge joint only moves back and forth in one direction.

17703.q: What covers the joint surfaces of bones so that they glide smoothly?
17703.e: Smooth cartilage covers the ends of the bones in a joint. It reduces friction and cushions knocks.
17703.m: Cartilage protects the ends of the bones in a joint.

17704.q: What is the fluid that lubricates a joint called?
17704.e: The joint fluid (synovial fluid) is made by the joint capsule. It makes sure the joint moves easily.
17704.m: Joint fluid keeps our joints moving.

17705.q: In a joint, what connects two bones to each other?
17705.e: Ligaments are tough bands of connective tissue that connect bone to bone. They keep the joint stable.
17705.m: Ligaments hold the bones in a joint together.

17706.q: Which human joint is a saddle joint?
a: The joint at the base of the thumb
17706.e: The saddle joint of the thumb is at the base of the thumb, between the wrist bones and the hand bone. It lets you place the thumb opposite the other fingers.
17706.m: Thanks to the saddle joint we can grip with our thumb.

17707.q: Which three types of muscle are there in the human body?
17707.e: Skeletal muscles move the body, the heart muscle pumps blood and smooth muscles work, for example, in the gut.
17707.m: Humans have skeletal muscles, smooth muscles and the heart muscle.

17708.q: What connects a muscle to a bone?
17708.e: Tendons pass the force of the muscle on to the bone. The best known is the Achilles tendon at the heel.

17709.q: Which muscle straightens the arm when the biceps is relaxed?
17709.e: The biceps and triceps are opposing muscles. The biceps bends the arm and the triceps straightens it.
17709.m: Muscles work together in opposing pairs.

17710.q: Why does every skeletal muscle need an opposing muscle?
a: Because muscles can only pull, not push
Because muscles tear after every movement
Because muscles only work once a day
Because muscles need no energy themselves
17710.e: A muscle can only tighten. To move the joint back again, another muscle on the opposite side has to pull.
17710.m: A muscle can only pull and never push.

17711.q: What is a skeletal muscle made of on the inside?
17711.e: A skeletal muscle is built from many bundles of fibres. Each muscle fibre is a long cell that can shorten.
17711.m: Muscles are made of many long muscle fibres.

17712.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
17712.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart into the body. Veins bring it back to the heart.
17712.m: Arteries lead away from the heart, veins lead back to it.

17713.q: What are the tiniest blood vessels, where substances are exchanged, called?
17713.e: Capillaries are extremely thin. Oxygen and nutrients pass through their walls into the cells.
17713.m: In the capillaries, blood and cells exchange substances.

17714.e: Red blood cells contain the red pigment haemoglobin. Oxygen attaches to it.
17714.m: Red blood cells are the oxygen carriers in the blood.

a: They help the blood to clot
17715.e: Platelets (thrombocytes) stick together at a wound and help to close it.
17715.m: Platelets stop bleeding when you are injured.

17716.q: Roughly how much blood does an adult have?
17716.e: An adult has about 4.5 to 6 litres of blood, which is about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight.
17716.m: An adult has about 5 to 6 litres of blood.

17717.q: Where does blood flow in the pulmonary circulation?
a: From the heart to the lungs and back
From the heart to the brain and back
From the liver to the gut
From the kidneys to the bladder
17717.e: In the small or pulmonary circulation, the blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives off carbon dioxide.
17717.m: In the pulmonary circulation the blood is loaded with oxygen.

17719.q: Roughly how many times a minute does an adult's heart beat at rest?
17719.e: An adult's resting pulse is usually about 60 to 80 beats per minute; about 50 to 100 counts as normal. In children it is higher.
17719.m: At rest, an adult heart beats about 60 to 80 times per minute.

17720.q: A heart beats 70 times a minute. How many times does it beat in an hour?
17720.e: An hour has 60 minutes. So you calculate 70 times 60, which makes 4,200 beats.
17720.m: A heart beats several thousand times an hour.

17721.q: What are the heart valves for?
a: They filter poisons out of the blood
17721.e: The heart valves work like valves on a pipe. They only let blood flow in one direction.
17721.m: Heart valves make blood flow in one direction.

17722.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood into the main artery and so into the whole body?
17722.e: The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. Its wall is especially thick and strong.
17722.m: The left ventricle supplies the whole body with blood.

a: Electrical signals in the heart itself
17723.e: In the right atrium there is a natural pacemaker, the sinus node. It regularly sends out electrical signals that make the heart muscle tighten.
17723.m: The heart sets its own rhythm with electrical signals.

17724.q: Where in the lungs does gas exchange take place?
17724.e: In the tiny air sacs (alveoli), oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the air.
17724.m: Oxygen gets into the blood in the air sacs.

17725.q: Which muscle is the most important for breathing in?
17725.e: The diaphragm separates the chest from the belly. When it tightens and moves down, air flows into the lungs.
17725.m: The diaphragm is our most important breathing muscle.

17726.q: What stops food getting into the windpipe when you swallow?
17726.e: The epiglottis closes the entrance to the windpipe when you swallow. That way the food slides into the food pipe.
17726.m: The epiglottis protects the windpipe when you swallow.

17727.q: Roughly what percentage of the air we breathe in is oxygen?
17727.e: Air is made up of about 78 per cent nitrogen and about 21 per cent oxygen.
17727.m: Air contains about one fifth oxygen.

17728.q: Which gas do we breathe out in larger amounts than we breathe in?
17728.e: Cells make carbon dioxide when they produce energy. It is taken by the blood to the lungs and breathed out.
17728.m: When we breathe out, we give off carbon dioxide.

17729.q: Which nutrient is already broken down by saliva in the mouth?
17729.e: Saliva contains the enzyme amylase. It starts to break starch down into sugar. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time.
17729.m: Digestion already begins in the mouth.

17730.q: Which acid does the stomach make?
17730.e: The stomach lining makes hydrochloric acid. It kills many germs and helps to digest protein.
17730.m: Stomach acid kills germs and helps with digestion.

17731.q: In which organ are most nutrients taken into the blood?
17731.e: The small intestine has many folds and tiny finger-like villi. This gives it a huge surface so it can take in lots of nutrients.
17731.m: The small intestine takes in most of the nutrients.

17732.q: What is the main job of the large intestine?
a: It removes water from the food mush
17732.e: In the large intestine, water and salt are taken out of what is left of the food. What remains is the thickened faeces.
17732.m: The large intestine takes water back out of the food mush.

17733.e: The liver makes bile, and the gall bladder only stores it. Bile helps to digest fats.
17733.m: The liver makes bile for digesting fat.

17734.q: What is the technical term for a nerve cell?
17734.e: Neurons are cells that receive and pass on electrical signals. The brain is made of billions of them.

17735.q: What does the central nervous system consist of?
17735.e: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. The nerves in the rest of the body belong to the peripheral nervous system.
17735.m: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system.

17736.q: What is the contact point where a nerve cell passes a signal on to the next cell called?
17736.e: At the synapse, messenger substances are released. They pass the signal on to the next cell.
17736.m: Nerve cells pass on signals at synapses.

17737.q: Why do we pull our hand away from a hot hob in a flash?
a: Because of a reflex through the spinal cord
Because the muscles feel the heat
17737.e: In a reflex, the signal is already switched in the spinal cord. The movement starts before the brain consciously registers the pain.
17737.m: Reflexes protect us from danger in a flash.

17738.q: Which part of the nervous system gets the body ready for fight or flight under stress?
17738.e: The sympathetic nervous system speeds up heartbeat and breathing. Its opposite number, the parasympathetic nervous system, brings rest and recovery.
17738.m: The sympathetic nervous system activates the body under stress.

17739.q: Which part of the brain is especially important for balance and coordinating movement?
17739.e: The cerebellum fine-tunes movements. It helps you keep your balance, for example, when riding a bike.

17740.q: Which part of the brain controls vital processes such as breathing and heartbeat?
17740.e: The brainstem connects the brain and spinal cord. It automatically controls breathing, heartbeat and swallowing.

17741.q: Which side of the body is mainly controlled by the left half of the brain?
a: The right side of the body
The left side of the body
17741.e: The nerve pathways cross over on their way to the body. That is why the left half of the brain mainly controls the right side.
17741.m: Each half of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.

17742.q: Roughly how heavy is an adult's brain?
17742.e: An adult brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms. That is only about 2 per cent of body weight.
17742.m: Our brain weighs a little more than one kilogram.

17743.q: Which part of the brain is especially important for storing new things in your memory?
17743.e: The hippocampus lies deep in the temporal lobe. It helps to move new experiences and knowledge into long-term memory.
17743.m: The hippocampus helps with learning and remembering.

17744.q: Why is enough sleep important for the brain?
a: Because it strengthens what you have learnt while you sleep
Because it needs no energy while you sleep
Because it makes new bones while you sleep
Because it makes blood while you sleep
17744.e: During sleep the brain processes the impressions of the day. What you have learnt is strengthened in your memory.
17744.m: If you sleep well, you can learn better.

17745.q: What is the body's first protective barrier against germs?
17745.e: Unbroken skin and the mucous membranes keep many germs out before they even get into the body.
17745.m: The skin is our first wall of protection against germs.

17746.q: What do you call white blood cells that surround and break down germs?
17746.e: Phagocytes (macrophages) recognise invaders, swallow them up and digest them.
17746.m: Phagocytes eat up germs that have got in.

17747.q: Which proteins does the immune system make to mark particular germs?
17747.e: Antibodies are made by certain white blood cells. They fit exactly to one germ and mark it for the body's defences.
17747.m: Antibodies recognise and mark very particular germs.

17748.q: Why do many people only get chickenpox once?
a: Because memory cells recognise the germ again
Because the germ dies out afterwards
Because the blood dilutes the germ
17748.e: After the illness, memory cells stay in the body. If you come into contact with the germ again, they fight it very quickly.
17748.m: The immune system remembers germs it already knows.

a: An overreaction to substances that are actually harmless
17749.e: With an allergy, the immune system fights harmless substances such as pollen. This leads, for example, to sneezing or itching.
17749.m: With an allergy, the immune system reacts too strongly.

17750.q: Why can a fever be useful during an infection?
a: It makes it harder for many germs to multiply
17750.e: The raised temperature slows down many germs and speeds up the body's defences. A very high fever, however, must be treated by a doctor.
17750.m: Fever is one of the body's defence reactions.

17751.q: Which of these groups does NOT belong to the germs that cause disease?
17751.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites can cause diseases. Vitamins, on the other hand, are vital nutrients.
17751.m: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites can make you ill.

17752.q: Which diseases can ticks pass on in Switzerland?
17752.e: Ticks can pass on the tick-borne encephalitis virus and Borrelia bacteria. That is why you should check yourself after spending time in the woods.
17752.m: After being in the woods, you check your body for ticks.

17753.q: What do you call it when germs are passed on by coughing or sneezing?
17753.e: When you cough and sneeze, tiny droplets with germs get into the air. Other people breathe them in.
17753.m: Sneezing into the crook of your elbow protects others from droplets.

17754.q: What do you call the time between catching an illness and the first signs of it?
17754.e: During the incubation period, the germs multiply in the body before you feel any symptoms.
17754.m: The incubation period lies between infection and the outbreak of the illness.

17755.e: Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites (plasmodia). They are passed on by Anopheles mosquitoes.
17755.m: Malaria is passed on by mosquitoes.

17756.q: Why are viruses not considered living things in their own right?
a: They can only multiply inside other cells
They are made only of fat
17756.e: Viruses have no metabolism of their own. They need a host cell that makes new viruses for them.
17756.m: Viruses need other cells in order to multiply.

17757.q: Why do antibiotics not help against flu?
a: Because flu is caused by viruses
Because flu does not last long enough
Because antibiotics only work against fungi
Because flu is not an illness
17757.e: Antibiotics work against bacteria. Flu, however, is caused by influenza viruses.
17757.m: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

17758.q: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
17758.e: Measles is caused by the measles virus and is very contagious. The other diseases are caused by bacteria.
17758.m: Measles is a contagious viral disease.

17759.q: How big are viruses usually compared with bacteria?
17759.e: Most viruses are so tiny that you can only see them with an electron microscope. Bacteria are usually much bigger.
17759.m: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria.

17760.q: Which germs usually cause an ordinary cold?
17760.e: Colds are usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses. They normally get better by themselves after a few days.
17760.m: A cold is usually caused by viruses.

17761.q: What do bacteria lack compared with human cells?
